In 2011, experts in North and South Korea met to discuss the potential for a significant eruption in the near future, as the last eruption was in 1903 and the volcano is expected to erupt around every 100 years.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-27) The Government of North Korea invited several volcanologists, including James Hammond, [Clive Oppenheimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Oppenheimer "Clive Oppenheimer"), and [Kayla Iacovino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kayla_Iacovino "Kayla Iacovino"), to study the mountain for recent volcanic activity.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-28)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-29) This made Iacovino the first foreign female researcher to conduct research in North Korea.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-30)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-31) The researchers began publishing their research in 2016 and in February 2020 formed the Mt. Paektu Research Center.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-32)

There are five known species of plants in the lake on the peak, and some 168 have been counted along its shores. The forest on the Chinese side is ancient and almost unaltered by humans. [Birch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birch "Birch") predominates near the [tree line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_line "Tree line"), and [pine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pine "Pine") lower down, mixed with other species. There has been extensive [deforestation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation") on the lower slopes on the North Korean side of the mountain.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

The area is a known habitat for [Siberian tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_tiger "Siberian tiger"), [bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear "Bear"), [wolves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf "Wolf"), and [wild boars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_boar "Wild boar").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-33) The [Ussuri dholes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ussuri_dhole "Ussuri dhole") may have been extirpated from the area. Deer in the mountain forests, which cover the mountain up to about 2,000 meters (6,600 ft), are of the Paekdusan [roe deer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_roe_deer "Siberian roe deer") kind. Many wild birds such as [black grouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_grouse "Black grouse"), [owls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owl "Owl"), and [woodpecker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodpecker "Woodpecker") are known to inhabit the area. The mountain has been identified by [BirdLife International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BirdLife_International "BirdLife International") as an [Important Bird Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Important_Bird_Area "Important Bird Area") (IBA) because it supports a population of [scaly-sided mergansers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scaly-sided_merganser "Scaly-sided merganser").[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-bli-34)

The mountain has been worshipped by the surrounding peoples throughout history. A considerable percentage of the [Koreans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koreans "Koreans") and [Manchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchu_people "Manchu people") consider it sacred, especially the [Heaven Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaven_Lake "Heaven Lake") in its crater.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-Fravel2008-35)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-:6-36)

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/Emblem_of_North_Korea.svg/250px-Emblem_of_North_Korea.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Emblem_of_North_Korea.svg)

Mount Paektu on the national [emblem of North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emblem_of_North_Korea "Emblem of North Korea").

The mountain has been considered sacred by Koreans throughout history.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-:6-36) According to [Korean mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_mythology "Korean mythology"), it was the birthplace of [Dangun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dangun "Dangun"), the founder of [Gojoseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn "Old Chosŏn") (2333–108 BC), whose parents were said to be [Hwanung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwanung "Hwanung"), the Son of Heaven, and [Ungnyeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ungnyeo "Ungnyeo"), a bear who had been transformed into a woman.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-37) Many subsequent kingdoms of Korea, such as [Buyeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buyeo_Kingdom "Buyeo Kingdom"), [Goguryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo "Goguryeo"), [Balhae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae "Balhae"), [Goryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goryeo "Goryeo") and Joseon recognized this myth.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-38)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-39)

The Goryeo dynasty (936–1392) first called the mountain _Baekdu_,[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-40) recording that the [Jurchens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurchen_people "Jurchen people") across the Yalu River were made to live outside of Mount Baekdu. The Joseon dynasty (1392–1910) recorded volcanic eruptions in 1597, 1668, and 1702. In the 15th century, [King Sejong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sejong_the_Great_of_Joseon "Sejong the Great of Joseon") strengthened the fortification along the Tumen and Yalu rivers, making the mountain a natural border with the northern peoples.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-41) Some Koreans claim that the entire region near Mount Paektu and the Tumen River belongs to Korea and parts of it were illegally given away by Japanese colonialists to China through the [Gando Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gando_Convention "Gando Convention").\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

Mount Baekdu is mentioned in the national anthems of both North and South Korea and in the Korean folk song "[Arirang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arirang "Arirang")".

Dense forest around the mountain provided bases for Korean armed resistance against the [Japanese occupation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_under_Japanese_rule "Korea under Japanese rule"), and later communist guerrillas during the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War"). [Kim Il Sung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Il_Sung "Kim Il Sung") organized his resistance against the Japanese forces there, and North Korea claims that [Kim Jong Il](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Jong_Il "Kim Jong Il") was [born there](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektusan_Secret_Camp "Paektusan Secret Camp"),[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-42) although records outside of North Korea suggest that he was born in the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union").[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-43)[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-44)

The peak has been featured on the state [emblem of North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emblem_of_North_Korea "Emblem of North Korea") since 1993, as defined in Article 169 of the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Constitution_of_the_Democratic_People%27s_Republic_of_Korea "Socialist Constitution of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea"), which describes Mt. Paektu as "the sacred mountain of the revolution".[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-45) The mountain is often referred to in slogans such as: "Let us accomplish the Korean revolution in the revolutionary spirit of Paektu, the spirit of the blizzards of Paektu!"[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-46) [North Korean media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korean_media "North Korean media") celebrates natural phenomena witnessed at the mountain as portentous,[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-47) and [weather forecasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_forecasting "Weather forecasting") aired by state broadcaster [Korean Central Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Central_Television "Korean Central Television") list [Paektusan Secret Camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektusan_Secret_Camp "Paektusan Secret Camp"), claimed birthplace of [Kim Jong Il](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Jong_Il "Kim Jong Il"), behind only the capital of [Pyongyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongyang "Pyongyang").[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-48) The mountain's name is used for various products, such as the [Paektusan rocket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektusan_/(rocket/) "Paektusan (rocket)"), the Paektusan computer, and the Mt Paektu handgun.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-49)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-50)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-51)

In the 2019 South Korean [disaster film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disaster_film "Disaster film") _[Ashfall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashfall_/(film/) "Ashfall (film)")_, the mountain erupts and causes severe earthquakes in the Korean peninsula.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-52)

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/MYK-1-%E9%95%BF%E7%99%BD%E5%B1%B1.png/500px-MYK-1-%E9%95%BF%E7%99%BD%E5%B1%B1.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MYK-1-%E9%95%BF%E7%99%BD%E5%B1%B1.png)

Painting from the [Manchu Veritable Records](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%BB%A1%E6%B4%B2%E5%AE%9E%E5%BD%95 "zh:满洲实录") with the names of Mount Paektu in Manchu, Chinese and Mongolian

Mount Changbai was regarded as the most sacred mountain in the [shamanist religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shamanism_in_the_Qing_dynasty "Shamanism in the Qing dynasty") of the [Manchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchus "Manchus"), and their ancestors [Sushen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sushen_people "Sushen people") and [Jurchens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurchens "Jurchens").[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-jlsda-53) The Jin dynasty bestowed the title "the King Who Makes the Nation Prosperous and Answers with Miracles" (興國靈應王) on the mountain in 1172 and it was entitled "the Emperor Who Cleared the Sky with Tremendous Sagehood" (開天宏聖帝) in 1193. A temple for the mountain god was constructed on the northern side.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-changchun-8)

The Manchu clan [Aisin Gioro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aisin_Gioro "Aisin Gioro"), which founded the [Qing dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty "Qing dynasty") of China, claimed their progenitor [Bukūri Yongšon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buk%C5%ABri_Yong%C5%A1on "Bukūri Yongšon") was conceived near Paektu Mountain. In 1682, 1698, 1733, 1754 and 1805, Qing emperors visited Jilin and paid homage to the mountain. The rites at Mount Changbai were heavily influenced by the ancient [Feng Shan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feng_Shan "Feng Shan") ceremonies, in which Chinese emperors offered sacrifices to heaven and earth at [Mount Tai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Tai "Mount Tai"). The [Kangxi Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangxi_Emperor "Kangxi Emperor") claimed that Mount Tai and Changbai belong to the same mountain range, which runs from northeast to southwest but is partially submerged under the sea before reaching [Shandong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shandong "Shandong"). The geography and [feng shui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feng_shui "Feng shui") of Mount Changbai thus provided legitimacy to the Aisin Gioro clan's rule over China.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-jlsda-53)

_Baishan Heishui_, "white mountain and black river", referring to Mount Changbai and the [Heilongjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heilongjiang_River "Heilongjiang River"), has been a traditional name for [Northeast China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_China "Northeast China") since the [Jin dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jin_dynasty_/(1115%E2%80%931234/) "Jin dynasty (1115–1234)").[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-54)

Sovereignty disputes
--------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paektu_Mountain&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Sovereignty disputes")\]

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Apprx._PRC-DPRK_border_around_Baekdu-Changbai_Mountain.PNG/500px-Apprx._PRC-DPRK_border_around_Baekdu-Changbai_Mountain.PNG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Apprx._PRC-DPRK_border_around_Baekdu-Changbai_Mountain.PNG)

Map showing the [Chinese-North Korean border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China-North_Korea_border "China-North Korea border") region around Paektu Mountain

According to _[Annals of the Joseon Dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annals_of_the_Joseon_Dynasty "Annals of the Joseon Dynasty")_, the [Yalu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalu_River "Yalu River") and [Tumen Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumen_River "Tumen River") were set as the borders in the era of the founder of Joseon Dynasty, [Taejo of Joseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taejo_of_Joseon "Taejo of Joseon") (1335–1408).[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-55) Because of the continuous entry of Korean people into Gando, a region in [Manchuria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchuria "Manchuria") that lay north of the Tumen, Manchu and Korean officials surveyed the area and negotiated a border agreement in 1712. To mark the agreement, they built a monument describing the boundary at a watershed, near the south of the crater lake at the mountain peak. Volume 8 of the Annals of King Taejo, 2nd article of Gyemyo, 14 December, 4th year of King Taejo, 1395, 28th year of Ming Hongwu Since the 19th century, interpretations of the inscription have been relevant in some territorial disputes.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

The 1909 [Gando Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gando_Convention "Gando Convention") between China and Japan, when [Korea was under Japanese rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_under_Japanese_rule "Korea under Japanese rule"), recognized the north and east of the mountain as Chinese territory.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-:7-56)

In 1962 and 1964, China and North Korea negotiated two treaties in secret that outlined their modern borders. Both treaties especially focused on the sovereignty of Paektu and Heaven Lake. As a result of the treaties, North Korea received 280 km2 (110 mi2)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-57) of land on and around Paektu, 9 out of 16 peaks, and 54.5% of Heaven Lake.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-58)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-59)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-:7-56) Neither treaty is recognized by the governments of Taiwan or South Korea.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-:7-56)

As of 2013, South Korea formally claimed the caldera lake and the inside part of the ridge.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-60) However, some South Korean groups argue that recent activities conducted on the Chinese side of the border, such as economic development, cultural festivals, infrastructure development, promotion of the tourism industry, attempts at registration as a [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site"), and bids for a Winter Olympic Games, constitute attempts to claim the mountain as Chinese territory.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-Chosun-61)[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-Donga-62) These groups object to China's use of the name _Mount Changbai_.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-Jin-7) Some groups also regard the entire mountain as Korean territory that was given away by North Korea in the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War").[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-Donga-62)

During the [2007 Asian Winter Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Asian_Winter_Games "2007 Asian Winter Games"), which were held in [Changchun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changchun "Changchun"), China, a group of South Korean athletes held up signs during the award ceremony which stated "Mount Paektu is our territory". Chinese sports officials delivered a letter of protest on the grounds that political activities violated the spirit of the Olympics and were banned in the charter of the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") and the [Olympic Council of Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Council_of_Asia "Olympic Council of Asia"). Officials from the South Korean athletic team apologized to China.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-63)[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-64)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-65)

Most Chinese, Russian, South Korean and international visitors climb the mountain from the Chinese side. The North Korean side of the mountain is also popular among visitors to North Korea.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] The Chinese tourism area is classified as a [AAAAA scenic area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AAAAA_scenic_area "AAAAA scenic area") by the [China National Tourism Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_National_Tourism_Administration "China National Tourism Administration").[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-66)

There are a number of monuments on the North Korean side of the mountain. Paektu Spa is a natural spring and is used for bottled water.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Pegae Hill is a camp site of the [Korean People's Revolutionary Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_People%27s_Revolutionary_Army "Korean People's Revolutionary Army") allegedly led by [Kim Il Sung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Il_Sung "Kim Il Sung") during their struggle against [Japanese colonial rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_under_Japanese_rule "Korea under Japanese rule").\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Secret camps are also now open to the public. There are several waterfalls, including the Hyongje Falls which splits into two about a third of the way from the top.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] In 1992, on the occasion of the 80th birthday of Kim Il Sung, a large sign with the words "Holy mountain of the revolution" written in metal letters was erected on the side of the mountain.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] North Koreans\[_[who?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_\] claim that there are 216 steps leading to the top of the mountain, symbolizing [Kim Jong Il](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Jong_Il "Kim Jong Il")'s 16 February birth date, but this claim is disputed.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-67) On the North Korean side of the mountain, there is a funicular system with two cars.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-68) This was updated with new funicular cars built by the [Kim Chong-t'ae Electric Locomotive Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Chong-t%27ae_Electric_Locomotive_Works "Kim Chong-t'ae Electric Locomotive Works"), with the new cars successfully running on the funicular from 30 October 2020.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-69)[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paektu_Mountain#cite_note-70)

One Hundred Mountains: The meaning of Mt Paektu =============== [One Hundred Mountains](https://onehundredmountains.blogspot.com/) ================================================================== On and around Japan's Hyakumeizan and other mountains Wednesday, January 17, 2018 --------------------------- ### The meaning of Mt Paektu **How North Korea taps into the symbolic voltage of a mysterious volcano** Has Kim Jong-un taken up winter mountaineering? Exactly a month ago, he was again bestriding the Korean peninsula’s highest peak. A local newspaper, the _Rodong Sinmun_, reported that "His eyes reflected the strong beams of the gifted great person seeing in the majestic spirit of Mount Paektu the appearance of a powerful socialist nation which dynamically advances full of vigour without vacillation at any raving dirty wind on the planet."
Kim Jong-un bestrides Mt Paektu in December 2017
It’s easy to mock the style of North Korean pronouncements. But this may run the risk of underestimating their effectiveness, warns B R Myers, a North Korea-watcher based at Dongseo University in Busan, South Korea. In his view, the regime’s “ideology has generally enjoyed the support of the North Korean people through good times and bad”, adding that about half of the refugees who make it over the border to China end up by voluntarily returning home. Mt Paektu (the "white-headed peak") figures prominently in this propaganda. Visits to its snow-covered summit by the Supreme Leader often preface or follow important decisions, [alleges a popular UK newspaper](https://www.thesun.co.uk/news/5118518/mount-paektu-north-korea-kim-jong-un-missile-test/). Kim Jong-un last visited the peak in September 2016, right after the country’s fifth nuclear test. He was also there [in April 2015](https://onehundredmountains.blogspot.ch/2015/04/the-meizan-militant.html), just before executing a former defense chief, and in November 2013, before executing his own uncle, among other top officials.
North Korean commemorative stamp showing
Kim Jong Il atop his native mountain
And this is to say nothing of the mountain’s ubiquity as a backdrop for the Kim dynasty in all manner of official productions, from postage stamps to oil paintings. In his book, _The cleanest race – how North Koreans see themselves and why it matters_, B R Myers offers a convincing explanation for this prominence. Many see North Korea as a hardline Marxist-Leninist regime. Yet this is misleading, Myers says. For, when Kim Il-sung established his regime in the late 1940s, he chose not follow the model of his Soviet mentors but reached instead for Japan’s pre-war emperor cult, to which Korea had been intensively exposed during the country’s period as a colony.
Painting of (l to r) Mrs Kim, the infant Kim Jong-un and Kim Jong-Il 
This thesis explains a lot. It makes clear why members of the Kim dynasty are often depicted riding on a white horse – typically in a mountainous setting – an imperial motif that can be traced back as far as Napoleon. As for Mt Paektu, it simply replaced Mt Fuji as a symbol of national prowess. This, in turn, explains why official sources so assiduously insist on Mt Paektu as the birthplace of Kim Jong-il, the present Supreme Leader's progenitor. In doing so, they tap into a legend that a mythical founder of the Korean nation descended on the peak thousands of years ago. In effect, “Kim Il-sung turned his whole family into a divine entity. He knew theocracies last longer than any type of regime,” says Song Bong-sun, a historian at Korea University in South Korea, [as quoted in the _Taipei Times_](http://www.taipeitimes.com/News/world/archives/2012/04/09/2003529904/1). Even the snow in our header picture fits this narrative, as a symbol of the cultural and ideological purity that North Korea preserves from corruption by the foreign-dominated south. So the answer to our opening question – has Kim Jong-un taken up mountaineering – is clearly “no”. Rather, he’s revealed himself as a master of misapplied [meizanology](https://onehundredmountains.blogspot.ch/2016/07/definition-of-terms.html) – the art and science of divining a mountain’s meaning. And, in Kim's case, of exploiting it too.
The majestic spirit of Mt Paektu ("White head peak")
Photo: Wikipedia
Of course, Mt Paektu is no Mt Fuji. Sited on the remote northern border, it never figured as centrally in Korea's classical literature and art as Mt Fuji did in Japan’s. And at 2,744 metres, it tops out a full kilometre below its Japanese counterpart – although its altitude is curiously similar to that of another "white mountain", Hakusan (2,702 metres), one of Japan’s three most sacred peaks.
A crater lake from central casting (Landsat image)
Even so, Mt Paektu does have a "majestic spirit", to borrow the _Rodong Sinmun's_ words_._ It has mystery – nobody is quite sure how a volcano managed to grow so far from an obvious plate boundary – and it has a magnificent crater lake, on a scale that hints at the [incalculable menace lurking beneath](https://www.nytimes.com/2016/12/09/science/north-korea-mount-paektu-volcano.html). But suggestions that a gigantic eruption [might be triggered by nearby bomb tests](https://www.forbes.com/sites/robinandrews/2017/08/23/heres-how-north-korea-could-accidentally-trigger-a-volcanic-supereruption/#1e65bf00d558) – thus hoisting the regime with its own petard – are probably wishful thinking. In the end, you almost have to applaud how adeptly the three Kims have co-opted their top mountain into shoring up their legitimacy. At the same time, one wonders how long it will take their regime’s arch-antagonist – himself no slouch at self-aggrandisement – to take a leaf out of their meizanological playbook. Or, on second thoughts, perhaps [it really is better not to go there](http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2017/07/26/mount-trump-social-media-reacts-donald-trump-jokes-added-mount/). **References** B R Myers, _The cleanest race - How North Koreans see themselves – and why it matters_, Melville House, 2010. The **Jeulmun pottery period** ([Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"): 즐문 토기 시대) is an archaeological era in [Korean prehistory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistoric_Korea "Prehistoric Korea") broadly spanning the period of 8000–1500 BC.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-1) This period subsumes the [Mesolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesolithic "Mesolithic") and [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") cultural stages in Korea,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-Choe_and_Bale_2002-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-3) lasting c. 8000–3500 BC ("Incipient" to "Early" phases) and 3500–1500 BC ("Middle" and "Late" phases), respectively.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-4) Because of the early presence of pottery, the entire period has also been subsumed under a broad label of "Korean Neolithic".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-Lee_2001-5) The [Jeulmun pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery "Jeulmun pottery") period is named after the decorated [pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pottery "Pottery") vessels that form a large part of the pottery assemblage consistently over the above period, especially 4000–2000 BC. _Jeulmun_ (즐문; 櫛文) means "Comb-patterned". A boom in the archaeological excavations of Jeulmun period sites since the mid-1990s has increased knowledge about this important formative period in the prehistory of [East Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asia "East Asia"). The Jeulmun was a period of hunting, gathering, and small-scale cultivation of plants.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-6) Archaeologists sometimes refer to this life-style pattern as "broad-spectrum [hunting and gathering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter-gatherer "Hunter-gatherer")". [![Image 1: Jeulmun pottery period is located in Continental Asia](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Map_Asia_physical_%28continental%29.png/330px-Map_Asia_physical_%28continental%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_Asia_physical_/(continental/).png "Jeulmun pottery period is located in Continental Asia") ![Image 2: Jeulmun pottery period](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Orange_dot_%28semi-transparent%29.png/40px-Orange_dot_%28semi-transparent%29.png) The Ubaid culture and contemporary cultures circa 5000 BC [![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Jeulmunmap.png/250px-Jeulmunmap.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jeulmunmap.png) Map of archaeological sites in the southern Korea peninsular during the Jeulmun period [![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/KoreanEarthenwareJar4000BCEAmsa-DongNearSeoul.jpg/250px-KoreanEarthenwareJar4000BCEAmsa-DongNearSeoul.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KoreanEarthenwareJar4000BCEAmsa-DongNearSeoul.jpg) Korean earthenware vessel in the classic _Jeulmun_ comb-pattern style. Various patterns cover the majority of the vessel surface. C. 4000 BC, [Amsa-dong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsa-dong "Amsa-dong"), [Seoul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul "Seoul"). [British Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Museum "British Museum"). [![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Korea-Neolithic.age-Pot-01.jpg/250px-Korea-Neolithic.age-Pot-01.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Korea-Neolithic.age-Pot-01.jpg) Classic Jeulmun vessel with wide mouth, c. 3500 BC. From [National Museum of Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Korea "National Museum of Korea"). The origins of the Jeulmun are not well known, but raised-clay pattern [Yunggimun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yunggimun "Yunggimun") pottery (융기문토기; 隆起文土器) appears at southern sites such as Gosan-ni in [Jeju Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeju_Province "Jeju Province") and Ubong-ni on the seacoast in [Ulsan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulsan "Ulsan"). Some archaeologists describe this range of time as the "Incipient Jeulmun period" and suggest that the Gosan-ni pottery dates to 10,000 BC.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-Choe_and_Bale_2002-2)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-7) Samples of the pottery were radiocarbon dated, and although one result is consistent with the argument that pottery emerged at a very early date (i.e., 10,180±65 BP \[AA-38105\]), other dates are somewhat later.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-8) If the earlier dating holds true, Yunggimun pottery from Gosan-ni would be, along with central and southern China, the [Japanese Archipelago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Archipelago "Japanese Archipelago"), and the [Russian Far East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Far_East "Russian Far East"), among a group of the oldest known [pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pottery "Pottery") in world [prehistory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistory "Prehistory"). Kuzmin suggests that more [absolute dating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_dating "Absolute dating") is needed to gain a better perspective on this notion.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-9) The Early Jeulmun period (c. 6000–3500 BC) is characterized by deep-sea fishing, hunting, and small semi-permanent settlements with [pit-houses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pit-house "Pit-house"). Examples of Early Jeulmun settlements include Seopohang, [Amsa-dong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsa-dong "Amsa-dong"), and Osan-ri.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-10) Radiocarbon evidence from coastal shellmidden sites such as [Ulsan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulsan "Ulsan") Sejuk-ri, [Dongsam-dong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dongsam-dong_Shell_Midden "Dongsam-dong Shell Midden"), and Ga-do Island indicates that shellfish were exploited, but many archaeologists maintain that shellmiddens (or [shellmound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shellmound "Shellmound") sites) did not appear until the latter Early Jeulmun.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-Lee_2001-5) Choe and Bale estimate that at least 14 Middle Jeulmun period (c. 3500–2000 BC) sites have yielded evidence of cultivation in the form of carbonized plant remains and agricultural stone tools.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-11) For example, Crawford and Lee, using [AMS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_spectrometry "Mass spectrometry") dating techniques, directly dated a domesticated [foxtail millet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foxtail_millet "Foxtail millet") (_Setaria italica_ ssp. _italica_) seed from the Dongsam-dong Shellmidden site to the Middle Jeulmun.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-12) Another example of Middle Jeulmun cultivation is found at Jitam-ri (Chitam-ni) in [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea"). A pit-house at Jitam-ri yielded several hundred grams of some carbonized cultigen that North Korean archaeologists state is [millet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millet "Millet").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-14) However, not all archaeologists accept the grains as [domesticated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesticated "Domesticated") millet because it was gathered out of context in an unsystematic way, only black-and-white photos of the find exist, and the original description is in [Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language") only. Cultivation was likely a supplement to a subsistence regime that continued to heavily emphasize deep-sea fishing, shellfish gathering, and hunting. "Classic Jeulmun" or _Bitsalmunui_ pottery (빗살무늬토기) in which comb-patterning, cord-wrapping, and other decorations extend across the entire outer surface of the vessel, appeared at the end of the Early Jeulmun and is found in West-central and South-coastal Korea in the Middle Jeulmun. The [subsistence pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsistence_pattern "Subsistence pattern") of the Late Jeulmun period (c. 2000–1500 BC) is associated with a de-emphasis on exploitation of shellfish, and the settlement pattern registered the appearance of interior settlements such as Sangchon-ri (see [Daepyeong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daepyeong "Daepyeong")) and Imbul-ri. Lee suggests that environmental stress on shellfish populations and the movement of people into the interior prompted groups to become more reliant on cultivated plants in their diets.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-15) The subsistence system of the interior settlements was probably not unlike that of the incipient Early [Mumun pottery period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumun_pottery_period "Mumun pottery period") (c. 1500–1250 BC), when small-scale [shifting cultivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shifting_cultivation "Shifting cultivation") ("[slash-and-burn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slash-and-burn "Slash-and-burn")") was practiced in addition to a variety of other subsistence strategies. The Late Jeulmun is roughly contemporaneous with [Lower Xiajiadian culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Xiajiadian_culture "Lower Xiajiadian culture") in [Liaoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning "Liaoning"), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"). Archaeologists have suggested that [Bangudae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangudae_Petroglyphs "Bangudae Petroglyphs") and Cheonjeon-ri, a substantial group of petroglyph panels in Ulsan, may date to this sub-period, but this is the subject of some debate. Kim Jangsuk suggests that the hunter-gatherer-cultivators of the Late Jeulmun were gradually displaced from their "resource patches" by a new group with superior slash-and-burn cultivation technology and who migrated south with _Mumun_ or undecorated pottery (무문토기; 無文土器). Kim explains that the pattern of land use practiced by the Mumun pottery users, the dividing up of land into sets of slash-and-burn fields, eventually encroached on and cut off parts of hunting grounds used by Jeulmun pottery users.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_note-16) * [Prehistory of Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistory_of_Korea "Prehistory of Korea") * [List of archaeological periods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_archaeological_periods "List of archaeological periods") * [Jōmon pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C5%8Dmon_pottery "Jōmon pottery") * [Pit-Comb Ware culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pit-Comb_Ware_culture "Pit-Comb Ware culture") 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period#cite_ref-1)** Bale, Martin T. 2001. Introduction
------------

Archaeology of the 21st century has transcended the conventional notion that prehistoric communities were static entities. It is now concurred that community is dynamic and constitutes a critical venue, not only physical but also ideological and conceptual, for human lives and interactions. But a consensus on its definition and, more significantly, how to approach community archaeologically remains elusive. Many of these challenges stem from the fuzziness of defining community. Perceptions of and involvement in a community vary among individuals and contexts, and the social roles of a community are in a state of constant flux. Multiple types and layers of communities coexist within a society on various scales and levels, and individuals participate in diverse communities across different contexts. Individuals may hold different notions of community depending on the contexts of their interactions—communities rooted in economic interactions may differ from those based on ideological or ritualistic interactions. Similarly, communities characterized by daily interactions may be distinct from those marked by sporadic interactions.

Although recent attention to community in archaeology (e.g., Birch [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR23 "Birch, J. (2014). From Prehistoric Villages to Cities: Settlement Aggregation and Community Transformation, Routledge, New York."); Feinman and Neitzel [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR57 "Feinman, G. M., and Neitzel, J. E. (2023). The social dynamics of settling down. Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 69: 101468."); Kolb and Snead [1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR117 "Kolb, M. J., and Snead, J. E. (1997). It's a small world after all: Comparative analyses of community organization in archaeology. American Antiquity 62: 609–628."); Yaeger and Canuto [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR198 "Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (2012). Introducing an archaeology of communities. In Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (eds.), Archaeology of Communities, Routledge, London, pp. 1–15.")) marks an important achievement, the inherent fluidity and plurality of communities present numerous practical challenges. These issues were rarely recognized in earlier archaeological works, which often interpreted the physical village as equivalent to the socially dynamic community. Archaeologists no longer equate community, which “can take multiple and diverse forms” (Yaeger and Canuto [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR198 "Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (2012). Introducing an archaeology of communities. In Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (eds.), Archaeology of Communities, Routledge, London, pp. 1–15.")), solely with a village or residential cluster (Birch [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR23 "Birch, J. (2014). From Prehistoric Villages to Cities: Settlement Aggregation and Community Transformation, Routledge, New York."); Yaeger and Canuto [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR198 "Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (2012). Introducing an archaeology of communities. In Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (eds.), Archaeology of Communities, Routledge, London, pp. 1–15.")), but they still are confronted with the dilemma of establishing links between material data and community and how to archaeologically recognize and investigate past communities. To address this issue, Kolb and Snead ([1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR117 "Kolb, M. J., and Snead, J. E. (1997). It's a small world after all: Comparative analyses of community organization in archaeology. American Antiquity 62: 609–628.")) propose three archaeologically visible functions of community: social reproduction, subsistence production, and self-identification/social recognition. Yaeger and Canuto ([2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR198 "Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (2012). Introducing an archaeology of communities. In Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (eds.), Archaeology of Communities, Routledge, London, pp. 1–15.")) criticize these indices as overly functionalistic. They instead identify four methodological challenges in exploring past communities: correlating spatial and social units; addressing issues of scale and sampling; recognizing interaction patterns; and grappling with the question of palimpsests (Yaeger and Canuto [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR198 "Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (2012). Introducing an archaeology of communities. In Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (eds.), Archaeology of Communities, Routledge, London, pp. 1–15."), p. 9). While these suggestions, despite their differing foci, can encompass various aspects of community, recognizing community from the archaeological data remains a difficult task. Among the above four challenges Yaeger and Canuto ([2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR198 "Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (2012). Introducing an archaeology of communities. In Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (eds.), Archaeology of Communities, Routledge, London, pp. 1–15.")) list, we suggest that correlating spatial and social units may be the most realistic starting point to archaeologically exploring communities, although the four challenges interwind in complicated ways. While, as stated above, the village and the community are distinct concepts, it may be suggested that the village plays a necessary role in archaeological understandings of communities. Villages, as spatial clusters of households, serve as hubs where multiple individuals engage with one another daily, irrespective of the nature of their interactions (Ortman and Coffey [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR163 "Ortman, S. G., and Coffey, G. D. (2017). Settlement scaling in middle-range societies. American Antiquity 82: 662–682.")). Villages can encompass individuals with diverse identities and perceptions of community, while multiple villages interacting and sharing some degree of identity may collectively form a community. For example, large, aggregated communities may begin to impact smaller communities in their periphery, resulting in increased interactions between members of several communities. Although the reasons for aggregation may vary depending on context, it inevitably leads to altered forms of interaction, regardless of whether all members of a village community perceive themselves to belong to the same community. While a village cannot simply be equated with a community, we suggest that the village provides valuable insights into understanding community formation. Even though archaeological detection of village lifespan and the question of palimpsests remain problems that must be addressed, investigation of how villages formed and changed serves as a starting point for exploring community formation and change through time.

On exploring the relationship between the formation of village and community, Feinman and Neitzel’s ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR57 "Feinman, G. M., and Neitzel, J. E. (2023). The social dynamics of settling down. Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 69: 101468.")) recent discussion deserves special consideration. Rather than attempting to directly bridge community to the archaeological record, they are more concerned with decisions made by individuals and households in given social contexts. They suggest that “individuals and households make choices about where to live and who to affiliate with based on opportunities and challenges” (Feinman and Neitzel [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR57 "Feinman, G. M., and Neitzel, J. E. (2023). The social dynamics of settling down. Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 69: 101468."), p. 7). The choices made by decision-making units, which they call “affiliative decisions,” involve “whether the advantages of staying with the larger cohort outweighed the costs of reconfigured social arrangements.” While the affiliative decisions vary depending on many factors that affect the costs and benefits of staying in a particular place, Feinman and Neitzel ([2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR57 "Feinman, G. M., and Neitzel, J. E. (2023). The social dynamics of settling down. Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 69: 101468.")) emphasize the relationship between demography and interaction. According to them, if population increases or becomes closely packed over demographic thresholds and the size of the interactive network exceeds the capacity for information processing, new social institutions for adjustment may emerge, leading to substantial changes in the nature, range, and intensity of interactions among decision-making units (see also Ortman and Coffey [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR163 "Ortman, S. G., and Coffey, G. D. (2017). Settlement scaling in middle-range societies. American Antiquity 82: 662–682.")). Although the focus is not directly on the formation of community but the transition from mobile to sedentary lifeways, their model can be heuristically applied to understandings of the connection between the formation of village and community. Indeed, the formation and growth/decline of villages and ever-changing intra- and supra-village interactions are processes that are closely related to the spatio-temporal dynamics of demography. Demographic dynamics include not only changes in population but also the aggregation and/or dispersion of affiliative decision-making units that may facilitate new venues of interaction, leading to changes in various aspects of community.

In this paper, we undertake a review of archaeological works concerned with community formation during the Neolithic and Bronze Age periods of Korea, spanning 8000 to 100 BC. We aim to highlight major achievements and research trends in the prehistoric archaeology of Korea and delve into how community formation has been conceptualized in Korea and some of the epistemological and methodological issues that have arisen along with these conceptualizations. Over the past three decades, a wealth of archaeological data has been amassed in South Korea, making it one of the most extensively investigated regions in the world. Archaeologists in South Korea have conducted thousands of excavations across large swathes of the southern Korean Peninsula largely due to surges in land development. The density of excavated sites in South Korea is among the highest globally, with more than 800 sites dated to the Neolithic and more than 3200 to the Bronze Age (Cultural Heritage Administration [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR52 "Cultural Heritage Administration. (2024). 문화재청 국가유산 보존관리지도 [Cultural Heritage GIS Service]. Retrieved 2024-04-05 from 
https://gis-heritage.go.kr
"); G.-A. Lee [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR130 "Lee, G.-A. (2017). The Chulmun period of Korea: Current findings and discourse on Korean Neolithic culture. In Habu, J., Lape, P. V., and Olsen, J. W. (eds.), Handbook of East and Southeast Asian Archaeology, Springer, New York, pp. 451–481.")), although very little is known about North Korea. While most investigations are rescue excavations, permission for excavations and the quality of investigations are systematically managed by government regulations.

Similar to other countries in northeast Asia, the archaeology of Korea has been dominated by a culture-historical approach based mainly on pottery typology (Choi et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR36 "Choi, J., Lee, Y., Lee, J., and Kim, J. (2017). Radiocarbon dating and the historical archaeology of Korea: An alternative interpretation of Hongryeonbong Fortress II in the Three Kingdoms period, central Korea. Journal of Field Archaeology 42: 1–12."); Yi [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR203 "Yi, S. (2022). Archaeology of Korea - An Outline with Emphasis on Prehistory, Sahoipyoungnon Academy, Seoul.")). Pottery typology serves as the primary means of establishing chronologies, defining “cultural groups,” and tracing the origins of diffusion and migration. Diffusion and migration are typically employed as explanatory frameworks for changes in material culture, subsistence, and technology, although this paradigm has been continuously criticized (J. Kim [2014b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR103 "Kim, J. (2014b). 한국고고학의 편년과 형태변이에 대한 인식 [Chronology and understanding of formal variability in Korean archaeology]. Journal of the Korean Ancient Historical Society 83: 5–32."); Seong et al. [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR174 "Seong, C., Moon, S., and Yang, H. (2018). 물질문화의 유형과 고고학 분석의 단위 - 한국 청동기시대 유형론을 중심으로 [The use and abuse of the concepts of assemblage and complex in Korean Bronze Age archaeology]. Journal of the Korean Archaeological Society 109: 326–357.")). As large-scale rescue excavations in the 21st century revealed large numbers of settlement sites of various sizes across the southern half of the Korean Peninsula, settlement patterns began to be incorporated into archaeological research, albeit largely limited to descriptions of the spatial distribution of villages and hierarchical arrangements of sites according to their sizes, leaving the processes and causes of village development and community formation largely unexplored. However, as we review, some recent works have endeavored to elucidate the emergence and growth of villages during the Neolithic and Bronze Age and explore changes in the relationship between villages and communities, although much of this work has been published exclusively in Korean, limiting its exposure to the international community. These efforts owe much to the substantial accumulation of radiocarbon dates and their application toward understanding spatio-temporal population dynamics, a methodology that has been applied widely in other regions (e.g., Crema et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR51 "Crema, E. R., Bevan, A., and Shennan, S. (2017). Spatio-temporal approaches to archaeological radiocarbon dates. Journal of archaeological Science 87: 1–9."); Palmisano et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR164 "Palmisano, A., Bevan, A., and Shennan, S. (2017). Comparing archaeological proxies for long-term population patterns: An example from central Italy. Journal of Archaeological Science 87: 59–72."); Shennan [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR178 "Shennan, S. (2018). The First Farmers of Europe: An Evolutionary Perspective, Cambridge University Press, Cambridge."); Shennan et al. [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR179 "Shennan, S., Downey, S. S., Timpson, A., Edinborough, K., Colledge, S., Kerig, T., Manning, K., and Thomas, M. G. (2013). Regional population collapse followed initial agriculture booms in mid-Holocene Europe. Nature Communications 4: 2486."); Timpson et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR191 "Timpson, A., Colledge, S., Crema, E., Edinborough, K., Kerig, T., Manning, K., Thomas, M. G., and Shennan, S. (2014). Reconstructing regional population fluctuations in the European Neolithic using radiocarbon dates: A new case-study using an improved method. Journal of Archaeological Science 52: 549–557.")). Korea’s radiocarbon database contains more than 17,000 dates, providing a comprehensive dataset for exploring population dynamics critical to understanding changes in population organization over time (Hwang [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR75 "Hwang, J. (2021). 한국고고학과 방사성탄소연대 [Radiocarbon dating in Korean archaeology]. The Yongnam Archaeological Review 90: 5–30.")).

Contextualizing the Neolithic and Bronze Age of Korea in Northeast Asia
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

The prehistory of Korea is commonly divided into the Paleolithic, Neolithic (8000–1500 BC), Bronze Age (1500–100 BC), and Iron Age (first century BC–AD third century), which broadly aligns with periodization schema used throughout northeast Asia (China, Mongolia, Korea, and the Russian Far East) with the important exception of Japan. The use of the term "Neolithic" in northeast Asia differs significantly from its use in western Eurasia, where the arrival of the Neolithic is mainly demarcated by the domestication of plants and animals and the transition to agriculture and animal husbandry (Banning [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR21 "Banning, E. B. (1998). The Neolithic period: Triumphs of architecture, agriculture, and art. Near Eastern Archaeology 61: 188–237."); Bar-Yosef [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR22 "Bar-Yosef, O. (1998). On the nature of transitions: The Middle to Upper Palaeolithic and the Neolithic revolution. Cambridge Archaeological Journal 8: 141–163."); Byrd [1994](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR30 "Byrd, B. F. (1994). Public and private, domestic and corporate: The emergence of the southwest Asian village. American Antiquity 59: 639–666."); Weisdorf [2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR195 "Weisdorf, J. L. (2005). From foraging to farming: Explaining the Neolithic Revolution. Journal of Economic Surveys 19: 561–586."); Zvelebil [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR206 "Zvelebil, M. (2001). The agricultural transition and the origins of Neolithic society in Europe. Documenta Praehistorica 28: 1–26.")). In northeast Asia, the beginning of the Neolithic is instead marked by the appearance of pottery (Kuzmin [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR124 "Kuzmin, Y. K. (2010). The neolithic of the Russian Far East and neighbouring East Asia: Definition, chronology, and origins. Bulletin of the Indo-Pacific Prehistory Association 30: 157–162.")), which emerged by at least 13,000 BC (Craig et al. [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR47 "Craig, O. E., Saul, H., Lucquin, A., Nishida, Y., Taché, K., Clarke, L., et al. (2013). Earliest evidence for the use of pottery. Nature 496: 351–354."); Yanshina and Kovalenko [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR201 "Yanshina, O. V., and Kovalenko, S. V. (2022). New data and insights into how pottery appeared along the Amur River. Quaternary International 608–609: 154–177.")) but with significant diachronic variation from region to region. For example, while Pleistocene pottery is known from China, Japan, and the Russian Far East (Shoda et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR183 "Shoda, S., Lucquin, A., Yanshina, O., Kuzmin, Y., Shevkomud, I., Medvedev, V., et al. (2020). Late Glacial hunter-gatherer pottery in the Russian Far East: Indications of diversity in origins and use. Quaternary Science Reviews 229: 106124."); Yanshina [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR200 "Yanshina, O. V. (2017). The earliest pottery of the eastern part of Asia: Similarities and differences. Quaternary International 441: 69–80."); Yanshina and Kovalenko [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR201 "Yanshina, O. V., and Kovalenko, S. V. (2022). New data and insights into how pottery appeared along the Amur River. Quaternary International 608–609: 154–177.")), the earliest examples of pottery in Korea appeared by 8000–7000 BC (Kim et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR109 "Kim, M.-J., Go, J.-W., Bang, M.-B., Hong, W., and Lee, G.-K. (2020). Absolute chronology of Gosan-ri-type pottery, the oldest manufactured pottery in Korea. Radiocarbon 62: 1715–1722.")), by which pottery had become more-or-less a universal feature of Neolithic technology throughout northeast Asia. More significantly, the earliest examples of pottery production and use throughout northeast Asia are not related to the development of agriculture or animal husbandry and seem to have instead been first taken up by hunter-gatherer-fishers (Craig et al. [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR47 "Craig, O. E., Saul, H., Lucquin, A., Nishida, Y., Taché, K., Clarke, L., et al. (2013). Earliest evidence for the use of pottery. Nature 496: 351–354."); Gibbs et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR61 "Gibbs, K., Isaksson, S., Craig, O. E., Lucquin, A., Grishchenko, V. A., Farrell, T. F. G., et al. (2017). Exploring the emergence of an ‘aquatic’ Neolithic in the Russian Far East: Organic residue analysis of early hunter-gatherer pottery from Sakhalin Island. Antiquity 91: 1484–1500."); Shoda et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR182 "Shoda, S., Lucquin, A., Ahn, J.-h., Hwang, C.-j., and Craig, O. E. (2017). Pottery use by Early Holocene hunter-gatherers of the Korean Peninsula closely linked with the exploitation of marine resources. Quaternary Science Reviews 170: 164–173.")). When evidence for plant domestication first appeared, rather than a regional transition toward agricultural economies, the Neolithic in northeast Asia was characterized by an eclectic patchwork of diverse cultivated crops and large regional and chronological variations both in their importance and the ways in which they were utilized.

The earliest seed crops known to have been domesticated in northeast Asia are foxtail millet (_Setaria italica_) and broomcorn millet (_Panicum miliaceum_), which show evidence of cultivation as early as 8000 BC in northern China (Yang et al. [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR199 "Yang, X., Wan, Z., Perry, L., Lu, H., Wang, Q., Zhao, C., et al. (2012). Early millet use in northern China. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 109: 3726–3730.")). Some of the earliest domesticated millet is from Xinglongwa settlements (ca. 6200–5400 BC), located in the West Liao River basin, which have been associated with pottery production, millet cultivation, hunting and gathering, and potential pig husbandry (Liu et al. [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR152 "Liu, X., Jones, M. K., Zhao, Z., Liu, G., and O'Connell, T. C. (2012). The earliest evidence of millet as a staple crop: New light on neolithic foodways in North China. American Journal of Physical Anthropology 149: 283–290.")). Farther south in the Yi-Luo River basin, early examples of mixed millet and rice cultivation—rice having been introduced from southern China—are associated with Peiligang settlements (ca. 7000–5000 BC), which also show evidence of millet and rice cultivation alongside hunting and gathering and possible pig husbandry (Zhang et al. [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR205 "Zhang, J., Lu, H., Gu, W., Wu, N., Zhou, K., Hu, Y., Xin, Y., and Wang, C. (2012). Early mixed farming of millet and rice 7800 years ago in the Middle Yellow River region, China. PLoS One 7: e52146.")). Within a couple of millennia, increasingly complex societies that were highly dependent on agriculture and pig husbandry had developed in both the West Liao River basin and Yi-Luo and Yellow River basins, represented by the succeeding Hongshan (ca. 4700–2900 BC) and Yangshao (ca. 5000–3000 BC) periods, respectively (Deng et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR53 "Deng, C., Gao, Z., Wu, Q., Zhou, Y., and Guo, Y. (2024). Millet agriculture and social complexity in the Central Plains of the Neolithic (9000–5000 BP): Isotopic reconstruction of human diet from the Shanggangyang site in China. Journal of archaeological Science 161: 105893."); Liu and Chen [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR151 "Liu, L., and Chen, X. (2012). The Archaeology of China: From the Late Paleolithic to the Early Bronze Age, Cambridge University Press, New York."); Liu et al. [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR152 "Liu, X., Jones, M. K., Zhao, Z., Liu, G., and O'Connell, T. C. (2012). The earliest evidence of millet as a staple crop: New light on neolithic foodways in North China. American Journal of Physical Anthropology 149: 283–290.")).

Toward the end of the Hongshan and Yangshao periods, domesticated millets appeared throughout much of northeast Asia, including along its coastal peripheries, although the precise processes and routes behind their spread are not well known (but see Hudson et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR73 "Hudson, M., Li, T., Nelson, S., Robbeets, M., and Zhushchikhovskaya, I. (2020). Tracing population movements in ancient East Asia through the linguistics and archaeology of textile production. Evolutionary Human Sciences 2: e5."); Li et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR146 "Li, T., Ning, C., Zhushchikhovskaya, I. S., Hudson, M. J., and Robbeets, M. (2020). Millet agriculture dispersed from northeast China to the Russian Far East: Integrating archaeology, genetics, and linguistics. Archaeological Research in Asia 22: 100177."); Robbeets et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR170 "Robbeets, M., Bouckaert, R., Conte, M., Savelyev, A., Li, T., An, D.-I., et al. (2021). Triangulation supports agricultural spread of the Transeurasian languages. Nature 599: 616–621.")). However, rather than leading toward full-fledged agricultural transitions, foxtail and broomcorn millets were incorporated into existing hunting-gathering-fishing economies in many areas and were combined with small-scale cultivation of other indigenous crops. For instance, foxtail and broomcorn millet both arrived in Korea and Russia’s Primorsky Krai by approximately 3500 BC (G.-A. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR145 "Leipe, C., Long, T., Sergusheva, E. A., Wagner, M., and Tarasov, P. E. (2019). [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR146 "Li, T., Ning, C., Zhushchikhovskaya, I. S., Hudson, M. J., and Robbeets, M. (2020). (2006). Dietary reconstruction at the neolithic Konam-ri and Daejuk-ri sites by trace element analysis. Journal of the Korean Ancient Historical Society 53: 23–41."); Choy et al. [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR38 "Choy, K., An, D., and Richards, M. P. (2012). Journal of Archaeological Science 36: 1312–1318.")), foraging of staple plant foods such as acorns, walnuts, and chestnuts (Ahn [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR6 "Ahn, S.-M. (2012). 식물유체로 본 선사, 고대 견과류 이용의 변화 -도토리, 참나무와 밤, 밤나무를 중심으로 [Exploitation patterns of nuts and nut-yielding trees from Neolithic to ancient periods in Korea based on plant remains]. Bulletin of the Indo-Pacific Prehistory Association 30: 157–162."), [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR125 "Kuzmin, Y. V. (2013). V. (2013). The beginnings of prehistoric agriculture in the Russian Far East: Current evidence and concepts. Documenta Praehistorica XL: 1–12."); G.-A. Lee [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR129 "Lee, G.-A. (2013). Archaeological perspectives on the origins of azuki (Vigna angularis). (eds.), Handbook of East and Southeast Asian Archaeology, Springer, New York, pp. 451–481.")). Interestingly, there is no evidence that foxtail millet and broomcorn millet reached Japan until the last phases of the Jomon period (ca. 13,000–900 BC) (Nasu and Momohara [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR157 "Nasu, H., and Momohara, A. W. (2011). Advances in understanding early agriculture in Japan. In Kuzmin, Y. (ed.), Across the Seas in Prehistoric Northeast Asia: Obsidian as a Commodity for the Study of Human Migrations, Springer Nature, Singapore, pp. 53–58.")). While there was a great deal of variation in the subsistence activities throughout the several-millennia span of Japan’s Jomon period, Jomon inhabitants likely cultivated and domesticated another species of millet, barnyard millet (_Echinochloa esculenta_), independently, while mainly relying on hunting, gathering, and fishing of berries, acorns, chestnuts, and horse chestnuts to support, in some phases, large village communities (Bleed and Matsui [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR25 "Bleed, P., and Matsui, A. (2010). Why didn't agriculture develop in Japan? A consideration of Jomon ecological style, niche construction, and the origins of domestication. Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory 17: 356–370."); Crawford [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR48 "Crawford, G. W. (2011). Advances in understanding early agriculture in Japan. Current Anthropology 52: S331–S345.")). Furthermore, unlike in much of northern China, pig husbandry and the rearing of other domesticated animals besides dogs appear to have begun much later in Korea, Japan, and Primorsky Krai, after the fully fledged transitions to agriculture of their respective Bronze Ages (or in the case of Japan, the Yayoi period) (Price and Hongo [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR169 "Price, M., and Hongo, H. (2020). The archaeology of pig domestication in Eurasia. Journal of Archaeological Research 28: 557–615.")).

A lack of evidence for the spread of domesticated foxtail and broomcorn millets makes the picture unclear farther north, for example, in present-day Mongolia and Siberia. Nonetheless, the growing body of archaeobotanical, zooarchaeological, and stable isotopes data from peripheral coastal and insular northeast Asia—Korea, Japan, and Primorsky Krai—suggest that rather than referring broadly to a Neolithic of northeast Asia, it would be more appropriate to emphasize the spatial and diachronic variability among Neolithics of northeast Asia, particularly in terms of subsistence lifeways and the roles plant cultivation and animal husbandry played in these. While there does not appear to be a point in time in which a single, common subsistence lifeway characterized all the Neolithics of northeast Asia contemporaneously, the common thread that tied them together from their beginnings was the universality and importance of pottery production (Popov et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR168 "Popov, A. N., Tabarev, A. V., and Mikishin, Y. A. (2014). Neolithization and ancient landscapes in southern Primorye, Russian Far East. Journal of World Prehistory 27: 247–261."); Sato and Natsuki [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR171 "Sato, H., and Natsuki, D. (2017). Human behavioral responses to environmental condition and the emergence of the world's oldest pottery in east and northeast Asia: An overview. Quaternary International 441: 12–28."); Uchiyama et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR192 "Uchiyama, J., Gillam, J. C., Hosoya, L. A., Lindström, K., and Jordan, P. (2014). Investigating neolithization of cultural landscapes in East Asia: The NEOMAP Project. Journal of World Prehistory 27: 197–223.")).

In Korea, the transition to a fully agricultural economy occurred abruptly, following the introduction of rice cultivation in the mid-second millennium. Most likely domesticated in southern China by 8000–7000 BC, rice had spread northward and was taken up by Neolithic societies in northern China, as seen in the Peiligang and Yangshao traditions (Deng et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR53 "Deng, C., Gao, Z., Wu, Q., Zhou, Y., and Guo, Y. (2024). Millet agriculture and social complexity in the Central Plains of the Neolithic (9000–5000 BP): Isotopic reconstruction of human diet from the Shanggangyang site in China. Journal of archaeological Science 161: 105893.")). From around 1500 BC, rice appeared abruptly on the Korean Peninsula and spread rapidly accompanied by an entirely new material culture assemblage, including undecorated, coarse-ware Mumun pottery, large semi-subterranean longhouses, and new polished stone tools, including semilunar reaping knives and daggers. This association of a new economy and material culture is referred to as the Bronze Age by Korean archaeologists, as evidence of bronze items—mostly consisting of ritual and ceremonial items such as daggers and mirrors—first appeared in this period, associated with rice, but remained rare until the latest phase of the period. The Bronze Age also witnessed a rapid florescence in the number and size of archaeological sites, suggesting a boom in population and the aggregation of large-scale village communities (Oh et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR162 "Oh, Y., Conte, M., Kang, S., Kim, J., and Hwang, J. (2017). Population fluctuation and the adoption of food production in prehistoric Korea: Using radiocarbon dates as a proxy for population change. Radiocarbon 59: 1761–1770.")). Social complexity significantly increased during the Bronze Age. Following the Bronze Age, the Iron Age, also known as the Proto-Three-Kingdoms period, began around 100 BC with the introduction of iron from China, followed by the development of states during the subsequent Three-Kingdoms period (AD third-seventh century).

The emergence of states was a long-delayed process in Korea and Japan, and the trajectories of state formation in northeast Asia show considerable diversity. Although the date of state formation is debated due to varying definitions of early states and differing interpretations of historical records (Allan [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR11 "Allan, S. (2007). Erlitou and the formation of Chinese civilization: Toward a new paradigm. Journal of Asian Studies 66: 461–496."); Shelach and Jaffe [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR176 "Shelach, G., and Jaffe, Y. (2014). The earliest states in China: A long-term trajectory approach. Journal of Archaeological Research 22: 327–364.")), it is argued that the Bronze Age of the Central Plains of China witnessed the formation of states as early as 1800 BC (Liu [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR150 "Liu, L. (2009). State emergence in early China. Annual Review of Anthropology 38: 217–232.")). In present-day northeast China, adjacent to the Korean Peninsula, historical texts record that an early state called Gojoseon emerged in the first millennium BC. Many lines of archaeological and historical evidence suggest that Bronze Age inhabitants of Korea engaged in interaction with various polities in contemporaneous China during the Western Zhou (11th–eighth century BC), Spring and Autumn period (770–481 BC), Warring States period (481–221 BC), and Qin/Han period of China (Korean Archaeological Society [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR120 "Korean Archaeological Society. (2022). 한국 고고학 강의 [Lectures on the Archaeology of Korea], 10th ed., Sahoepyeongron, Seoul.")). These interactions likely influenced the process of community formation on the Korean Peninsula but did not directly result in the emergence of states.

The Neolithic and Bronze Age of Korea are delineated by a major shift in subsistence lifeways that, we believe, contributed to completely different trajectories of community formation. While plant cultivation is a component of both periods, the Neolithic is characterized by the continuity of a tradition of hunting, gathering, and fishing that goes back to the turn of the Holocene, whereas the Bronze Age saw a rapid and more complete commitment to agriculture following the arrival of new crops, rice (_Oryza sativa_), wheat (_Triticum_ sp.), and barley (_Hordeum_ sp.). For these reasons, the use of the terms Neolithic and Bronze Age may seem to fail to capture the context of the two periods within the broader context of northeast Asian prehistory. As such, many East Asian researchers favor the alternative terms, "Chulmun period" and "Mumun period," and we use them to denote the Neolithic and Bronze Age, as it is commonly used by archaeologists working in Korea.

We review works on the Chulmun period and Mumun period separately, primarily due to the aforementioned differences and perceived discontinuity between the two periods. Although both periods witnessed the emergence of large villages, the scale of the villages and causes and processes behind their establishment differ significantly. Emphasis is placed on how the nature and scale of villages changed over time, how changes in the scale and organization of villages were related to land use, subsistence practices, social complexity, the spatial diversity of processes of aggregation and subsequent responses, and most importantly how archaeologists working in Korea understand the formation of community throughout both periods. Numerous debates on the formation of community during the Chulmun and Mumun periods revolve around epistemological considerations concerning the relationship between villages as spatial clusters of dwellings and communities as “the conjunction of people, places, and premise” (as per Yaeger and Canuto [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR198 "Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (2012). Introducing an archaeology of communities. In Yaeger, J., and Canuto, M. A. (eds.), Archaeology of Communities, Routledge, London, pp. 1–15.")). Similarly, archaeologists of Korean prehistory hold varied views on the relationship between the emergence of large villages and community formation.

Our review is organized to first provide an overview of general understandings and interpretations of the archaeology of each period chronologically. However, because processes of community formation, both within and beyond the village, are interwoven with many other social, economic, and political aspects of prehistoric lifeways, our discussions address multiple broader themes that we find pertinent to understandings of community formation, including, but not necessarily limited to, foraging and farming, mobility and sedentism, dispersion and aggregation, and sociopolitical complexity and scalar stress. Special attention is given to spatio-temporal dynamics of demography across these periods, as both a potential driver and a potential outcome of major changes in Chulmun and Mumun lifeways. While investigating past population dynamics remains challenging, researchers have worked to statistically mitigate problems associated with using radiocarbon data as a proxy for population and/or occupation intensity (e.g., Carleton and Groucutt [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10814-024-09204-7#ref-CR31 "Carleton, W.
