### Ritual Contacts

From the Middle phase onwards, Jōmon culture saw a remarkable increase in archaeological remains relating to ritual behaviour. Clay figurines, for example, are known from the Incipient phase but become much more common from the Middle Jōmon (Bausch, [2010b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR20 "Bausch, I. R. (2010b). Fragmentation practices in central Japan: Middle Jomon clay figurines at Shakado. In D. Gheorghiu & A. Cyphers (Eds.), Zoomorphic miniature figures in Eurasia, Africa and Meso-America: Morphology, materiality, technology, function and context (pp. 99–112). Archaeopress."); Habu, [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR48 "Habu, J. (2004). Ancient Jomon of Japan. Cambridge University Press."), pp. 144–151). Until the Middle phase, such figurines had only been found as far west as Shiga prefecture, but from the Late Jōmon they are found across west Japan, except for Okinawa (Matsumoto, [2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR128 "Matsumoto, N. (2005). Jōmon no mura to shakai (縄文のムラと社会: Jōmon villages and society). Iwanami. In Japanese."), p. 153). At least 30 clay masks (or fragments) are known from Late and Final Jōmon sites, mainly in the Tohoku area (Habu, [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR48 "Habu, J. (2004). Ancient Jomon of Japan. Cambridge University Press."), p. 155). Matsumoto ([2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR129 "Matsumoto, N. (2011). The cognitive foundation of long distance interaction and its relation to social contexts. In N. Matsumoto, H. Bessho, & M. Tomii (Eds.), Coexistence and cultural transmission in East Asia (pp. 31–47). Left Coast Press.")) argues that the Late–Final Jōmon distribution of eastern Japan-made jadeite beads in Kyushu and Okinawa was mirrored by the eastward expansion of Kyushu-made tubular greenstone beads, which found their way to western Honshu sites as distant as Nishida in Gifu. A large quantity and variety of polished stone rods are also associated with the Middle–Final phases (Habu, [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR48 "Habu, J. (2004). Ancient Jomon of Japan. Cambridge University Press."), pp. 151–155). Although earlier generations of archaeologists saw close links between Late–Final Jōmon stone circles and monuments from northeast China and Siberia (e.g., Komoto, [1982](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR106 "Komoto, M. (1982). Megalithic monuments in ancient Japan. In B.-M. Kim (Ed.), Megalithic cultures in Asia (pp. 4–40). Hanyang University Press.")), clear evidence of such a link is lacking. Dolmens from the Korean peninsula do spread to northwest Kyushu at the beginning of the Yayoi period but they are often associated with native Jōmon skeletal remains and isotope analyses of those remains suggests a continuing dependence on marine foods rather than agricultural crops (Mihara et al., [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR134 "Mihara, S., Miyamoto, K., Nakamura, T., & Koike, H. (2004). 14C age determination for human bones during the Yayoi period: The calibration ambiguity around 2400 BP and the marine reservoir effect. Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research B, 223–224, 700–704.")).

Although the possibility of earlier examples has been raised, the first uncontroversial ritual tooth ablation in Japan dates from the end of the Middle Jōmon. This custom then flourished during the Late and Final phases and into the Yayoi (Han & Nakahashi, [1996](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR50 "Han, K., & Nakahashi, T. (1996). A comparative study of ritual tooth ablation in ancient China and Japan. Anthropological Science, 104(1), 43–64."); Nakahashi, [1999](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR143 "Nakahashi, T. (1999). Transition from the Jomon to the Yayoi period in the northern Kyushu and Yamaguchi region as viewed from ritual tooth ablation and skeletal morphology. In K. Omoto (Ed.), Interdisciplinary perspectives on the origins of the Japanese (pp. 127–142). International Research Center for Japanese Studies.")). The widespread distribution of tooth ablation in Japan at this time is shown by its presence at the Late Jōmon Funadomari site on Rebun Island, Hokkaido (Matsumura et al., [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR133 "Matsumura, H., Anezaki, T., & Ishida, H. (2001). A morphometric analysis of Jomon skeletons from the Funadomari site on Rebun island, Hokkaido, Japan. Anthropological Science, 109, 1–21.")). Forked teeth filing is also known at some sites around Nagoya (Harunari, [1986](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR52 "Harunari, H. (1986). Rules of residence in the Jōmon period, based on the analysis of tooth extraction. In R. J. Pearson, G. L. Barnes, & K. L. Hutterer (Eds.), Windows on the Japanese past: Studies in archaeology and prehistory (pp. 293–310). Center for Japanese Studies, University of Michigan.")). Tooth ablation is known in Shandong and coastal areas of northeast China from around 5400 BC. Research comparing tooth ablation patterns at Yayoi sites, such as Doigahama, with Neolithic sites of the Shandong region in northern China, such as Dawenkou, shows basic similarities in the age at commencement of ablation (approximately 12–15 years) and in the prevalence of the extraction of upper lateral incisors (Han & Nakahashi, [1996](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR50 "Han, K., & Nakahashi, T. (1996). A comparative study of ritual tooth ablation in ancient China and Japan. Anthropological Science, 104(1), 43–64."), pp. 49–50). The adoption of this custom in Jōmon society can be argued to represent a major change since it must have been traumatic for those undergoing the tooth removals (Takenaka et al., [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR191 "Takenaka, M., Mine, K., Tsuchimochi, K., & Shimada, K. (2001). Tooth removal during ritual tooth ablation in the Jomon period. Bulletin of the Indo-Pacific Prehistory Association, 21, 49–52.")). If this custom was indeed introduced from, or influenced by, China, then it seems likely that it derived prestige from its ‘international’ identifications. A parallel here might be with the standardised filed front teeth possessed by some Viking men (cf. Arcini, [2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR8 "Arcini, C. (2005). The Vikings bare their filed teeth. American Journal of Physical Anthropology, 128, 727–733."), [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR9 "Arcini, C. (2007). Reconstructing daily life in past populations. In A. Kaliff (Ed.), Archaeology in the east and the west: Papers presented at the Sino–Sweden archaeology forum, Beijing in September 2005 (pp. 261–274). Stockholm: National Heritage Board.")). A common interpretation of Jōmon tooth ablation—that it was related to coming-of-age ceremonies and post-marital residence patterns (Harunari, [1986](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR52 "Harunari, H. (1986). Rules of residence in the Jōmon period, based on the analysis of tooth extraction. In R. J. Pearson, G. L. Barnes, & K. L. Hutterer (Eds.), Windows on the Japanese past: Studies in archaeology and prehistory (pp. 293–310). Center for Japanese Studies, University of Michigan."))—is not supported by recent research, which suggests a connection with lineage-based subsistence procurement groups (Kusaka et al., [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR115 "Kusaka, S., Ikarashi, T., Hyodo, F., Yumoto, T., & Katayama, K. (2008). Variability in stable isotope ratios in two Late-Final Jomon communities in the Tokai coastal region and its relationship with sex and ritual tooth ablation. Anthropological Science, 116, 171–181."); Temple et al., [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR192 "Temple, D. H., Kusaka, S., & Sciulli, P. W. (2011). Patterns of social identity in relation to tooth ablation among prehistoric Jomon foragers from the Yoshigo site, Aichi prefecture, Japan. International Journal of Osteoarchaeology, 21, 323–335.")). Mizoguchi ([2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR139 "Mizoguchi, K. (2017). Anthropomorphic clay figurines of the Jomon period of Japan. In T. Insoll (Ed.), The Oxford handbook of prehistoric figurines (pp. 521–544). Oxford University Press."), p. 539) suggests that in the Late Jōmon, the difficulties of maintaining ‘intra- and inter-communal collaboration and negotiations over limited and shrinking resource bases’ might have resulted in ‘_signifiers inscribed on the body_ in the form of ritual tooth extraction bec\[oming\] necessary as a medium with which to give orders to the world.’

### Linguistic Interaction

A final category of interaction between Jōmon Japan and the East Asian mainland during the period considered here is linguistic. Given the archaeological connections outlined above, some language contact—perhaps including the borrowing of loan words for new objects and ideas—almost certainly occurred. Language contact with coastal China is also a possibility at this time but actual linguistic evidence suggests that contact with the Korean peninsula was more extensive.

Although the question of whether Japanese and Korean are related to the Tungusic, Mongolic and Turkic languages is still debated, the genealogical relationship between Japanese and Korean is gaining acceptance among linguists (Whitman, [1985](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR206 "Whitman, J. (1985). The phonological basis for the comparison of Japanese and Korean. Ph.D. dissertation. Cambridge: Harvard University."); Unger, [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR200 "Unger, J. M. (2009). The role of contact in the origins of the Japanese and Korean languages. University of Hawai‘i Press."); Ratté, [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR40 "Francis-Ratté, A. (2016). Proto-Korean-Japanese: A new reconstruction of the common origin of the Japanese and Korean languages. Ph.D. dissertation. Ohio: The Ohio State University.")). Proto-Japonic, the ancestor of Mainland Japanese and the Ryukyuan languages, has been associated with the language of the immigrants who established Yayoi culture on the Japanese Islands (Hudson, [1999](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR62 "Hudson, M. J. (1999). Ruins of identity: Ethnogenesis in the Japanese Islands. University of Hawai‘i Press."); Whitman, [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR228 "Whitman, J. (2012). The relationship between Japanese and Korean. In N. Tranter (Ed.), The languages of Japan and Korea (pp. 24–38). Routledge.")). By contrast, proto-Koreanic, the ancestor of the contemporary Korean dialects, Middle Korean, as well as some fragmentary recorded historical languages, such as those of Silla and Paekche, can be viewed as the language of the farmers who brought millet agriculture to Korea (Robbeets, [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR169 "Robbeets, M. (2017). The language of the Transeurasian farmers. In M. Robbeets & A. Savelyev (Eds.), Language dispersal beyond farming (pp. 93–121). John Benjamins.")) (Fig. [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#Fig2)). From this perspective, the separation of proto Japano-Koreanic into Japonic and Koreanic probably occurred on the Liaodong peninsula in northeast China between 3500 and 2000 BC (Robbeets, [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR169 "Robbeets, M. (2017). The language of the Transeurasian farmers. In M. Robbeets & A. Savelyev (Eds.), Language dispersal beyond farming (pp. 93–121). John Benjamins.")).

Ainu and Nivkh have been regarded as marginal pockets of earlier language types whose lineages became isolated at the time of the expansion of Japonic, Koreanic and other Transeurasian languages (Fortescue, [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR39 "Fortescue, M. (2013). Polysynthesis in the Arctic/Sub-Arctic: How recent is it? In B. Bickel, L. A. Grenoble, D. A. Peterson, & A. Timberlake (Eds.), Language typology and historical contingency: Festschrift for Johanna Nichols (pp. 241–264). John Benjamins."); Nichols, [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR153 "Nichols, J. (2011). Forerunners to globalization: The Eurasian steppe and its periphery. In C. Hasselblatt, P. Houtzagers, & R. van Pareren (Eds.), Language contact in times of globalization (pp. 177–195). Rodopi.")). Ainuic, the language ancestral to Ainu, has been associated with one of the indigenous languages spoken by Jōmon populations (Hudson, [1999](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR62 "Hudson, M. J. (1999). Ruins of identity: Ethnogenesis in the Japanese Islands. University of Hawai‘i Press."); Vovin, [1993](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR203 "Vovin, A. (1993). A reconstruction of proto-Ainu. Brill."), p. 190). Indeed, linguistic evidence suggests a language shift whereby some of the ancestral speakers of Ainu abandoned their native language and adopted proto-Japonic as a new target language, whereas speakers of ancestral Nivkh replaced their native language with proto-Koreanic. This evidence comes from atypical structural features in Japanese and Korean that are likely to have developed through substratum interference from pre-Ainu and pre-Nivkh, respectively (Robbeets, [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR169 "Robbeets, M. (2017). The language of the Transeurasian farmers. In M. Robbeets & A. Savelyev (Eds.), Language dispersal beyond farming (pp. 93–121). John Benjamins.")). Among others, these features include—for Korean—the occurrence of initial consonant clusters, two distinctive tones and three laryngeal contrast sets and—for Japanese—the distinction between intentional and non-intentional action in certain verb affixes, productive noun-incorporation, and the occurrence of prefixing morphology in spite of being verb-final. Even if Korean shares these structural parallels with Nivkh, implying language shift, there are no lexical parallels between the two languages, implying mutual loanwords (Janhunen, [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR76 "Janhunen, J. (2016). Reconstructio externa linguae Ghiliacorum. Studia Orientalia, 117, 3–27.")).

Nevertheless, we find some lexical lookalikes between Ainu and Korean, which are suggestive of prehistoric language contact between the ancestral speakers of the two languages. (The following abbreviations are used in this section: J: Japanese; K: Korean, OJ: Old Japanese; pA: proto-Ainuic; pK: proto-Koreanic.) Such potential loanwords include terms for natural landmarks such as (1) K _na:y_ ‘river' and Ainu _náy_ ‘river, stream’; (2) K _yem_ ‘small stony island, small rocks sticking out of the water’ and Ainu _yá_ 'dry land (as opposed to sea), shore, high rock’; words for housing and locality such as (3) K _aph_ ‘front, fore part’ and Ainu _apá_ ‘doorway, entrance’; (4) K _kot_ ‘place, locality, site’ and Ainu _kotán_ ‘village, town, country, place’; terms for fauna such as (5) K _say_ ‘bird’ and Ainu _say_ ‘flock, flight of birds’; terms relating to the body such as (6) K _nwun_ ‘eye’ and Ainu _núu_ ‘eye’; (7) K _ni_ ‘tooth’ and Ainu _nii_ ‘tooth’; (8) K _alh_\- ‘suffer from’ and Ainu _árka_ ‘painful, sore, hurting’; words for food production such as (9) K _a:m_ ‘hot cereal; thick rice soup’ and Ainu _amám_ ‘cereals, rice’; and (10) K _swi_:- ‘to turn sour, spoil (intr.)’ and Ainu _síw_ ‘to be bitter’. See the supplementary information for a detailed description of these etymologies.

Most of these lookalikes are nouns and belong to the cultural vocabulary, which is suggestive of borrowing in a sporadic to moderate contact setting (Thomason & Kaufman, [1988](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR194 "Thomason, S. G., & Kaufman, T. (1988). Language contact, creolization, and genetic linguistics. University of California Press.")). Even if body part terms are usually considered as basic vocabulary, it may be possible to interpret the borrowing of ‘tooth’ and ‘eye’ within the cultural context of ritual tooth ablation. The direction of the borrowing seems to be from ancestral Koreanic into ancestral Ainuic, because some Korean forms have a broader meaning (e.g., (5) K ‘bird’ vs. Ainu ‘flight of birds’); they preserve primary or less cultural meanings (e.g., (3) K ‘fore part, front’ vs. Ainu ‘doorway, entrance’; (4) K ‘place, locality, site’ vs. Ainu ‘village, town’); they are morphologically complex (e.g., (8) pK \*_alk-a_ (suffer.from-FIN) ‘suffers from’ → pA \*_árka_ ‘painful’); the phonological correlation supports the directionality (e.g. (3) pK \*-_lp-_ in \*_alpʌ-k_ ‘fore part, front’ is imitated as pA \*-_p- in_ pA \*_apa_ ‘doorway, entrance’); two synonymous basic vocabulary items coexist in Ainu (e.g., (6) pA \*_núu_ ‘eye’ and pA \*_sík_ ‘eye’; (7) pA \*_nii_ ‘tooth’ and pA \*_imak_ ‘tooth’); or they have a Japanese cognate supporting their originality (e.g., K _yem_ ‘small stony island, small rocks sticking out of the water’ is cognate to J _yama_ ‘mountain’). The direction of the borrowing implies that the speakers of Koreanic were technologically superior or socially more prestigious than the speakers of Ainuic.

It is not possible to pinpoint the exact time of these borrowings, but there are indications of upper and lower limits. Parallels such as K _a:m_ ‘hot cereal; thick rice soup’ and Ainu _amam_ ‘cereal grain or rice’ suggest that the borrowing occurred later than the introduction of cereal cultivation to the Korean pensinsula (i.e. after 3500 BC) and probably after the introduction of rice cultivation (i.e. after 1500 BC). Most Korean–Ainu lookalikes described above lack a potential Japanese parallel, and if there is a Japanese cognate (e.g. J _yama_ ‘mountain’), the Ainu forms are semantically or formally closer to the Korean lookalike than to its Japanese cognate. This suggests that the contacts between Koreanic and Ainuic speakers took place _after_ the separation between Japonic and Koreanic (i.e. after 2000 BC) and without intermediary Japonic speakers. As far as the upper time limit is concerned, the contacts must pre-date the Ainu migration to Sakhalin in the thirteenth century AD (Hudson, [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR63 "Hudson, M. J. (2017). The historical ecology of colonialism and violence in Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, AD 1200–1900. In J. Habu, P. Lape, & J. Olsen (Eds.), Handbook of East and Southeast Asian archaeology (pp. 695–706). Springer.")) because the Ainu words have cognates in Sakhalin Ainu. Moreover, they pre-date the time of the Old Japanese _Manyōshū_ poetry (i.e., AD 500–759) because some of the Ainu loanwords have in turn been transmitted into Old Japanese (e.g. (1) Ainu _náy_ ‘river’ → OJ _na_ ‘river’; (2) Ainu _yá_ ‘dry land, shore’ → OJ _ya_ ‘shore’). The relative lack of Japanese intermediate loans suggests that the Ainuic and Koreanic speakers were in direct contact, probably at a time before the spread of Japonic speakers over the Japanese Islands (i.e., before 200 BC). Therefore, the prehistoric contact between Koreanic and Ainuic speakers presumably took place on the Japanese archipelago between 1500 and 200 BC, in Late–Final Jōmon contexts.

Using Heggarty’s ([2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR54 "Heggarty, P. (2007). Linguistics for archaeologists: Principles, methods and the case of the Incas. Cambridge Archaeological Journal, 17, 311–340.")) proposal that Quechua formed a _lingua franca_ for the Inca empire, Jennings ([2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR78 "Jennings, J. (2011). Globalizations and the ancient world. Cambridge University Press."), p. 129) suggests that one feature of ancient globalisations might be the development of such bridge languages. Here, however, we do not find any evidence for a Jōmon _lingua franca_ as the limited body of around ten potential borrowings from Koreanic into Ainuic only implies low to moderate contact between ancestral speakers of Korean and Ainu. Given the limited intensity of the contacts (mainly nouns, some inflected verb forms, plus cultural vocabulary) and the cultural sphere of the vocabulary, it is more parsimonious to see these borrowings within a restricted context of trade and cultural exchange. We hypothesise that some Late–Final Jōmon Ainuic speakers, familiarising themselves with Koreanic for the purpose of cultural exchange and trade, were responsible for introducing Koreanic words into Ainuic.

Discussion
----------

Interaction between Jōmon Japan and the Eurasian mainland had occurred since the beginning of the Jōmon period and indeed from the Palaeolithic before that, but the Late–Final Jōmon phases saw an increase in the diversity of objects and, presumably, of ideas which reached Japan. Geographically, it is not the case that all of these objects first entered Jōmon Japan through Kyushu or Hokkaido, the islands closest to the mainland. Given known ocean currents around Japan, several of the examples summarised above—including finds from northeast Honshu or southern Shikoku—might reflect drift or accidental voyages from the mainland (cf. Im, [1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR69 "Im, H.-J. (1995). The new archaeological data concerned with the cultural relationship between Korea and Japan in the Neolithic age. Korea Journal, 35(3), 31–39.")). For reference it might be useful here to cite a Second World War plan to float fuel and food to Japan only using ocean currents. This plan was developed after Japanese scientists found that 90% of bottles set adrift on the east coast of Korea reached the northern coast of Honshu (Tsutsui, [2003](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR195 "Tsutsui, W. M. (2003). Landscapes in the dark valley: Toward an environmental history of wartime Japan. Environmental History, 8, 294–311."), pp. 303–304). While some voyages to Japan were no doubt accidental, however, several of the objects discussed above can be considered as prestige goods, suggesting more structured patterns of interaction. The Korea Straits were probably the main focal point of exchange networks between Japan and the continent in the latter half of the Jōmon (Bausch, [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR21 "Bausch, I. R. (2016). Prehistoric networks across the Korea strait (5000–1000 BCE): ‘Early globalization’ during the Jomon period in northwest Kyushu? In T. Hodos (Ed.), The Routledge handbook of archaeology and globalization (pp. 413–437). Routledge."); Miyamoto, [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR136 "Miyamoto, K. (2008). Prehistoric interaction between the Korean peninsula and the Japanese archipelago through Tsushima and Iki islands. Bulletin of the Society for East Asian Archaeology, 2, 13–17.")). However, Bausch’s previous work found that there was no progressive increase in connectivity over time. Korea Strait interaction declined in the Middle Jōmon but then reached its peak from the end of the Middle into the Late phases (Bausch, [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR21 "Bausch, I. R. (2016). Prehistoric networks across the Korea strait (5000–1000 BCE): ‘Early globalization’ during the Jomon period in northwest Kyushu? In T. Hodos (Ed.), The Routledge handbook of archaeology and globalization (pp. 413–437). Routledge."), pp. 425–426). In the second half of the Late Jōmon, the network focus shifted to eastern Japan (Matsumoto, [2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR128 "Matsumoto, N. (2005). Jōmon no mura to shakai (縄文のムラと社会: Jōmon villages and society). Iwanami. In Japanese.")).

Kobayashi ([1992](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR102 "Kobayashi, T. (1992). Regional organization in the Jomon period. Arctic Anthropology, 29, 82–95.")) suggested that ‘new information’ from the Korean peninsula in the Late Jōmon led to a ‘conservative’ strengthening of Jōmon traditions as part of a ‘resistance movement’ to the new cultural influences. Here, however, we have argued that the Late–Final social changes represent a much more complex phenomenon, which involved both ‘traditional’ and radically new manifestations. Furthermore, as noted by Teramae ([2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR193 "Teramae, N. (2017). Bunmei ni kōshita Yayoi no hitobito (文明に抗した弥生の人びと: The Yayoi people who resisted civilisation). Yoshikawa Kōbunkan. In Japanese."), pp. 53–54), eastern Jōmon cultural traits cannot be seen as ‘traditional’ in the west of the archipelago: for Late–Final Jōmon people living in Kyushu, eastern style clay figurines and stone rods represented a ‘foreign’ cultural incursion. More broadly, the evidence for Middle–Final Jōmon interaction between Japan and the continent discussed here suggests a rather different pattern from that proposed for forager/farmer frontiers in Europe (cf. Zvelebil & Rowley-Conwy, [1984](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR216 "Zvelebil, M., & Rowley-Conwy, P. (1984). Transition to farming in northern Europe: A hunter-gatherer perspective. Norwegian Archaeological Review, 17, 104–128.")). The later Jōmon did not see the patterned exchange of raw materials and goods found in the Mesolithic–Neolithic transition in northern Europe (Zvelebil, [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR215 "Zvelebil, M. (2008). Innovating hunter-gatherers: The Mesolithic in the Baltic. In G. Bailey & P. Spikins (Eds.), Mesolithic Europe (pp. 18–59). Cambridge University Press.")). The types of interaction described above are also not consistent with interpretations of the forager to farmer transition made by many Japanese archaeologists, who assume that rice or other cereal crops would be quickly adopted once available. Kondō ([1962](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR107 "Kondō, Y. (1962). Yayoi bunka (弥生文化: Yayoi culture). In S. Ienaga (Ed.), Iwanami kōza Nihon rekishi 1 (岩波講座日本歴史1: The Iwanami course on Japanese history) (Vol. 1, pp. 139–188). Tokyo: Iwanami. In Japanese.")), for example, proposed that a relative paucity of natural resources in western Japan led to a generalised subsistence adaptation which easily adopted rice agriculture when it became available. Eastern Jōmon populations, in contrast, were argued to have been more specialised, and scheduling and other demands made it harder for them to adopt farming (Akazawa, [1982](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR4 "Akazawa, T. (1982). Cultural change in prehistoric Japan: Receptivity to rice agriculture in the Japanese archipelago. In F. Wendorf & A. F. Close (Eds.), Advances in world archaeology (Vol. 1, pp. 151–212). Academic Press."), [1986](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR5 "Akazawa, T. (1986). Hunter-gatherer adaptations and the transition to food production in Japan. In M. Zvelebil (Ed.), Hunters in transition: Mesolithic societies of temperate Eurasia and their transition to farming (pp. 151–165). Cambridge University Press."), [1988](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR229 "Akazawa, T. (1988). Variability in the types of fishing adaptation of the later Jomon hunter-gatherers c. 2500–300 bc. In G. N. Bailey & J. Parkington (Eds.), The archaeology of prehistoric coastlines (pp. 78–92). Cambridge University Press. ")). Recent research suggests that an expansion in the cultivation of legumes in the western Jōmon was not mirrored by the adoption of millet from the Korean peninsula as predicted by Kondō and Akazawa. Late–Final Jōmon societies did, however, develop a concern with long-distance connections and appear to have imitated several types of material culture from Bronze Age Eurasia, including stone ‘swords’ based on metal prototypes, black-burnished pottery which may have been influenced by metal vessels, and pottery tripods. These objects were probably not made in isolation but suggest conscious relationships between different craft activities (cf. Sofaer, [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR184 "Sofaer, J. (2010). Technology and craft. In T. Earle & K. Kristiansen (Eds.), Organizing Bronze Age societies: The Mediterranean, central Europe, and Scandinavia compared (pp. 185–217). Cambridge University Press.")). There was also an increase in mobility, especially maritime mobility from the Late Jōmon phase.

The Late–Final Jōmon ‘accommodation to the foreign’ has parallels with western Eurasia in the Bronze Age (cf. Kristiansen and Larsson, 2005). The extent to which Japan can be said to have been part of a Bronze Age world system is, however, unclear. There is considerable evidence for trade and exchange _within_ Japan during this period but, with some exceptions, the possibility of trading contacts with the mainland has rarely been discussed (Bausch, [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR21 "Bausch, I. R. (2016). Prehistoric networks across the Korea strait (5000–1000 BCE): ‘Early globalization’ during the Jomon period in northwest Kyushu? In T. Hodos (Ed.), The Routledge handbook of archaeology and globalization (pp. 413–437). Routledge.")). The specialist craft production found in the Late–Final Jōmon included ceramics, shell beads, jadeite ornaments, greenstone beads, polished stone axes, lacquerware and salt (Kinoshita, [2003](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR230 "Kinoshita, N. (2003). Shell trade and exchange in the prehistory of the Ryukyu archipelago. Bulletin of the Indo-Pacific Prehistory Association, 23, 67–72."); Bausch, [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR18 "Bausch, I. R. (2004). Some considerations on Jomon serpentinite polished adze and jadeite ornament production sites along the Japan Sea coast. Bulletin of the International Jomon Culture Conference, 1, 15–24."), 2010; Sakaguchi, [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR173 "Sakaguchi, T. (2011). Mortuary variability and status differentiation in the Late Jomon of Hokkaido based on the analysis of shuteibo (communal cemeteries). Journal of World Prehistory, 24, 275–308."); Kawashima, [2015b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR86 "Kawashima, T. (2015b). Prehistoric salt production Japan. In R. Brigand & O. Weller (Eds.), Archaeology of salt: Approaching an invisible past (pp. 125–138). Sidestone."); Matsumoto, [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR129 "Matsumoto, N. (2011). The cognitive foundation of long distance interaction and its relation to social contexts. In N. Matsumoto, H. Bessho, & M. Tomii (Eds.), Coexistence and cultural transmission in East Asia (pp. 31–47). Left Coast Press."), [2018a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR130 "Matsumoto, N. (2018a). Japan: The earliest evidence of complex technology for creating durable coloured goods. Open Archaeology, 4, 206–216.")). The existence of very long-distance networks at this time is clear and Final Jōmon Kamegaoka pottery from the Tohoku region is found as far south as Okinawa (Shitara, [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR180 "Shitara, H. (2018). Nansei shotō no Ōborakei doki to sono shūhen (南西諸島の大洞系土器とその周辺: On the Ōbora type pottery of the Ryukyu Islands). Tōkyō Daigaku Kōkogaku Kenkyūshitsu Kenkyū Kiyō, 31, 47–60. In Japanese with English summary.")), some 2000 km as the crow flies, equivalent to the distance from Paris to Athens. Habu ([2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR49 "Habu, J. (2010). Seafaring and the development of cultural complexity in northeast Asia: Evidence from the Japanese archipelago. In A. Anderson, J. H. Barrett, & K. V. Boyle (Eds.), The global origins and development of seafaring (pp. 159–189). McDonald Institute for Archaeological Research.")) raises the possibility that the increase in dugout canoe numbers from the Late Jōmon was associated with craft specialisation and long-distance trade. Funadomari on Rebun Island seems to have served as a specialist Late Jōmon production site for flat shell beads. In the 1950s, it was suggested that these flat shell beads had diffused from the continent to Japan (cf. Kikuchi, [1986](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR94 "Kikuchi, T. (1986). Continental culture and Hokkaido. In R. J. Pearson, G. L. Barnes, & K. L. Hutterer (Eds.), Windows on the Japanese past: Studies in archaeology and prehistory (pp. 149–162). Center for Japanese Studies, University of Michigan.")). The opposite route now seems more likely, but this proposal awaits detailed analyses of beads from continental sites (Fujisawa, [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR43 "Fujisawa, T. (2013). Kaisei hiradama (貝製平玉: Flat shell beads). Kikan Kōkogaku, 125, 85–87. In Japanese.")). Sakaguchi ([2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR173 "Sakaguchi, T. (2011). Mortuary variability and status differentiation in the Late Jomon of Hokkaido based on the analysis of shuteibo (communal cemeteries). Journal of World Prehistory, 24, 275–308."), p. 301) raises the possibility that the Ishikari plain in southwest Hokkaido may have been a regional centre for long-distance trade in the Late Jōmon. Sites such as Kashiwagi B have produced very carefully-made polished stone rods with knobs at both ends. While usually interpreted as ritual objects, the possibility that such rods could be balance-beams for weighing commodities also needs to be considered.

Vandkilde ([2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR201 "Vandkilde, H. (2016). Bronzization: The Bronze Age as pre-modern globalization. Praehistorische Zeitschrift, 91, 103–123.")) argues that the Bronze Age spanned a ‘hyper-region’ of connectivity which was not centred on core–periphery relationships. While further work is needed on possible world system relations in East Asia, the idea of ancient globalisation, or what Vandkilde calls ‘bronzisation’, may be a useful way to explore the changes in Jōmon society at this time. Vandkilde ([2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR201 "Vandkilde, H. (2016). Bronzization: The Bronze Age as pre-modern globalization. Praehistorische Zeitschrift, 91, 103–123."), p. 106) notes that, ‘bronze easily crossed boundaries between different techno-economic systems, social solutions, and cultural groupings’, leading to a Bronze Age ‘metacultural beyond’ wherein the transcultural values of bronze became entangled with cultures over a wide area. Bronze ‘invited translations of the transculturally exotic, hence making objects co-active in local strategies of power and distinction’; as a result, ‘the Bronze Age is particularly rich in objects that were neither imports nor truly indigenous’ (Vandkilde, [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR201 "Vandkilde, H. (2016). Bronzization: The Bronze Age as pre-modern globalization. Praehistorische Zeitschrift, 91, 103–123."), p. 108). Even after the end of the Jōmon, there are a number of categories of material culture which were made to imitate bronze objects. These include shell bracelets and ceramic and stone mirrors. The concept of ‘bronzisation’ suggests the need for a re-evaluation of the strict typological approaches used in Japanese archaeology to examine both short- and long-distance influences on material culture.

One apparent difference between the process of ‘bronzisation’ proposed here for Late–Final Jōmon Japan and the situation on the Eurasian continent relates to violence and warfare. It has been widely argued that the Bronze Age marks the emergence of militarised societies, with professional specialists in warfare who used the new metal technology to deadly effect (Horn & Kristiansen, [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR59 "Horn, C., & Kristiansen, K. (Eds.). (2018). Warfare in Bronze Age society. Cambridge University Press."); Kristiansen, [1999](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR110 "Kristiansen, K. (1999). The emergence of warrior aristocracies in later European prehistory. In J. Carman & A. Harding (Eds.), Ancient warfare: Archaeological perspectives (pp. 175–189). Sutton Publishing.")). Molloy and Horn ([2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR140 "Molloy, B. & Horn, C. (2020). Weapons, warriors and warfare in Bronze Age Europe  In G. Fagan, L. Fibiger, M. Hudson & M. Trundle (Eds.), The Cambridge world history of violence (Vol. 1: The prehistoric and ancient worlds, pp. 117–141). Cambridge: Cambridge University Press."), p. 117) write that ‘the transformation of warfare in the Bronze Age was perhaps the most profound in human history and indeed for human history.’ In Japan, there was a significant increase in violence and warfare in the Yayoi period (Hudson, [1990](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR61 "Hudson, M. J. (1990). From Toro to Yoshinogari: Changing perspectives on Yayoi period archeology. In G. Barnes (Ed.), Hoabinhian, Jomon, Yayoi, early Korean states: Bibliographic reviews of Far Eastern archaeology 1990 (pp. 63–111). Oxbow."); Hudson et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR67 "Hudson, M. J., Schulting, R., & Gilaizeau, L. (2020). The origins of violence and warfare in the Japanese Islands. In G. Fagan, L. Fibiger, M. Hudson, & M. Trundle (Eds.), The Cambridge world history of violence (Volume 1, The prehistoric and ancient worlds, pp. 160–177). Cambridge University Press.")), but it is widely assumed that levels of violence in the Jōmon period were low, and a recent review of previously published osteological reports has supported that conclusion (Nakao et al., [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR145 "Nakao, H., Tamura, K., Arimatsu, Y., Nakagawa, T., Matsumoto, N., & Matsugi, T. (2016). Violence in the prehistoric period of Japan: The spatio-temporal pattern of skeletal evidence for violence in the Jomon period. Biology Letters, 12, e20160028.")). However, few of the studies used by Nakao et al. ([2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR145 "Nakao, H., Tamura, K., Arimatsu, Y., Nakagawa, T., Matsumoto, N., & Matsugi, T. (2016). Violence in the prehistoric period of Japan: The spatio-temporal pattern of skeletal evidence for violence in the Jomon period. Biology Letters, 12, e20160028.")) were systematic analyses of violent trauma and it is clear that further such analyses will increase the skeletal evidence for violence in Jōmon society (Hudson et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR67 "Hudson, M. J., Schulting, R., & Gilaizeau, L. (2020). The origins of violence and warfare in the Japanese Islands. In G. Fagan, L. Fibiger, M. Hudson, & M. Trundle (Eds.), The Cambridge world history of violence (Volume 1, The prehistoric and ancient worlds, pp. 160–177). Cambridge University Press.")). Such evidence will enable us to develop a better understanding of how the Bronze Age contacts discussed in this paper influenced patterns of violence and warfare in Japan.

Jennings ([2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR78 "Jennings, J. (2011). Globalizations and the ancient world. Cambridge University Press."), pp. 123–141, [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR79 "Jennings, J. (2016). Distinguishing past globalizations. In T. Hodos (Ed.), The Routledge handbook of archaeology and globalization (pp. 12–28). Routledge.")) suggests eight hallmarks of ancient globalisation: time/space compression, deterritorialisation, standardisation, unevenness, homogenisation, cultural heterogeneity, re-embedding of local culture, and vulnerability. We suggest that each of these was to some extent present in Japan in the Late–Final Jōmon periods (Table [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#Tab5)).

Conclusions
-----------

Many of the objects analysed in this paper have a long history of research within Japanese archaeology, and various opinions have been expressed on their relationship with the cultures of the East Asian continent. Our aim here has not been to ‘settle’ this debate, and discussion of many of these artefacts will no doubt continue. Rather, the main objective of this paper has been to provide something that has been missing from the literature so far: a broad framework for thinking about relations between Japan and the rest of Eurasia during the Bronze Age. The Bronze Age was the time when a new demand for metal ores and other raw materials transformed Eurasian trade economies, moving them away from their previous focus on alluvial city states (Scott, [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR177 "Scott, J. C. (2017). Against the grain: A deep history of the earliest states. Yale University Press.")). In a process which Scott ([2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR177 "Scott, J. C. (2017). Against the grain: A deep history of the earliest states. Yale University Press.")) calls the ‘Golden Age of the Barbarians’ and Hudson ([2020b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR65 "Hudson, M. J. (2020b). Language dispersals and the ‘secondary peoples’ revolution’: A historical anthropology of the Transeurasian unity. In M. Robbeets & A. Savelyev (Eds.), The Oxford guide to the Transeurasian languages (pp. 806–813). Oxford University Press.")) calls the ‘secondary peoples’ revolution’, the resulting Bronze Age trade networks and population dispersals engendered new economic forms, such as nomadic pastoralism, as well as the spread of full-scale agriculture to previously peripheral regions. Based on an analysis of Middle to Final Jōmon Japan, we argue that these developments can be termed Bronze Age ‘globalisation’ or, following Vandkilde ([2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR201 "Vandkilde, H. (2016). Bronzization: The Bronze Age as pre-modern globalization. Praehistorische Zeitschrift, 91, 103–123.")), ‘bronzisation’. Despite the highly peripheral location of the Japanese Islands in Eurasian prehistory, the Jōmon example discussed here shows just how powerful bronze was as a globalised transculture. Jōmon bronzisation may have led to shared values and perhaps began to break down previously resilient foraging modes of thought (cf. Barnard, [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10963-021-09156-6#ref-CR14 "Barnard, A. (2007). From Mesolithic to Neolithic modes of thought. In A. Whittle & V. Cummings (Eds.), Going over: The Mesolithic-Neolithic transition in north-west Europe (pp. 5–19). Oxford University Press.")). The perspective of bronzisation provides a new way of looking at the Jōmon which could potentially help to further integrate Japan into the broader story of Eurasian history.

**Lute-shaped bronze dagger culture** is the provisional designation of an [archeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archeology "Archeology") complex of the [Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") in [Northeast China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_China "Northeast China") and the northern part of the [Korean Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Peninsula "Korean Peninsula").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning_bronze_dagger_culture#cite_note-1) Its classification is controversial. While some believe it to be sufficiently distinct to be labelled as a separate culture, others associate the findings with the [Upper Xiajiadian culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Xiajiadian_culture "Upper Xiajiadian culture").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning_bronze_dagger_culture#cite_note-Byington_2016-2) Artifacts from the culture are found primarily in the [Liaoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning "Liaoning") area of [northeast China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_China "Northeast China") and in the [Korean peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_peninsula "Korean peninsula"). Various other bronze artifacts, including ornaments and weapons, are associated with the culture, but the daggers are viewed as the most characteristic. Liaoning bronzes contain a higher percentage of zinc than those of the neighboring bronze cultures.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning_bronze_dagger_culture#cite_note-3) [Lee Chung-kyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lee_Chung-kyu&action=edit&redlink=1 "Lee Chung-kyu (page does not exist)") (1996) considers that the culture is properly divided into five phases: Phases I and II typified by lute-shaped daggers, Phases IV and V by slender daggers, and Phase III by the transition between the two. Of these, remains from Phases I, II and III can be found in some amounts in both the Korean peninsula and northeast China, but remains from Phases IV and V are found almost exclusively in Korea. Lute-shaped daggers ------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Liaoning_bronze_dagger_culture&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Lute-shaped daggers")\] [![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Bronze_dagger.jpg/330px-Bronze_dagger.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bronze_dagger.jpg) Liaoning-style violin-shaped bronze knives from Korea held at the [War Memorial (Seoul)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Memorial_/(Seoul/) "War Memorial (Seoul)"). The early phase consists of an early period of bronze manufacture without daggers originated from the spreading processes of [Siberian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberia "Siberia") [Seima-Turbino Type bronzeware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seima-Turbino_phenomenon "Seima-Turbino phenomenon") throughout [Eurasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasia "Eurasia") continent, followed by a period of producing what is now called lute- or violin-shaped daggers by Korean scholars (Bipahyungdonggeom, [비파형동검](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EB%B9%84%ED%8C%8C%ED%98%95%EB%8F%99%EA%B2%80 "ko:비파형동검")).[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning_bronze_dagger_culture#cite_note-4) The earliest period of production of lute-shaped daggers is dated to the 14th century BCE. The earliest artifacts from this period are found exclusively in [Liaoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning "Liaoning") of [northeast China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_China "Northeast China") and seem only gradually to have spread to the Korean peninsula.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning_bronze_dagger_culture#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning_bronze_dagger_culture#cite_note-6) By Lee's (1996) Phase II, however, a distinctive notched form of dagger begins to emerge in southern Korea, suggesting that by this time independent bronze production had begun in that region. Some argue it to be a regional variation of a much larger distribution of similar daggers that range from [Hebei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebei "Hebei") and [Inner Mongolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Mongolia "Inner Mongolia") in the west to the Korean peninsula in the east. Many scholars consider it to be a style shared by a number of groups, rather than representing a single culture.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning_bronze_dagger_culture#cite_note-7) Evidence gained from pottery indicates that the bronze dagger "culture" of this time actually included several distinct cultural groups. One distinct pottery tradition is found in northeast China and northwestern Korea, another in the [Taedong River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taedong_River "Taedong River") valley, another in the southwest around the [Chungcheong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chungcheong "Chungcheong") provinces including the Geum River, and yet another throughout the rest of the southern Korean peninsula including [Jeju island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeju_Island "Jeju Island"). Slender daggers --------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Liaoning_bronze_dagger_culture&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Slender daggers")\] [![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Distribution_of_Bronze_Swords_in_Northeast_Asia.svg/250px-Distribution_of_Bronze_Swords_in_Northeast_Asia.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Distribution_of_Bronze_Swords_in_Northeast_Asia.svg) Distribution of Violin-shaped daggers (비파형동검) and Slender daggers (세형동검) This later part of the Liaoning bronze dagger culture is often referred to as the "Korean bronze dagger culture," since it was largely restricted to the Korean peninsula. At this point the Liaoning culture artifacts begin to disappear from the northeast China area. A new form of dagger begins to turn up on the Korean peninsula, straight and slender (Sehyungdonggeom, [세형동검](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%84%B8%ED%98%95%EB%8F%99%EA%B2%80 "ko:세형동검")). [![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e9/Tpgudehdrja.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tpgudehdrja.jpg) Sehyungdonggeom, also called Korean style dagger (Preserved in a museum in Gyeonggi.) The greatest concentration of bronze daggers is found in the [Geum River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geum_River "Geum River") valley of [South Chungcheong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Chungcheong "South Chungcheong") province. Away from this area, the daggers become progressively fewer. This appears to indicate that most daggers were produced in the Geum valley, and the other cultures of the peninsula acquired them primarily by trade. Trade also took place by sea, with artifacts from the Later Phase found in [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") archeological sites as well. Lee (1996) divides this phase into two distinct sections: one dating to the 3rd century BCE in which the production of slender bronze daggers predominated, and one dating to the 2nd century BCE in which daggers are often accompanied by bronze mirrors with geometric designs and halberds influenced by the Chinese [Qin state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_/(state/) "Qin (state)"). In the first part, a single pottery culture typified by clay-band applique is found throughout the Korean peninsula, but in the second part distinctive pottery types emerge in the northwest and the remainder of the peninsula. Historical identity ------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Liaoning_bronze_dagger_culture&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Historical identity")\] The disappearance of the Liaoning bronze dagger culture from Liaoning appears to coincide with the [State of Yan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Yan "State of Yan")'s conquest of that area. The Korean bronze dagger culture of the Later Phase appears to correspond with the state of [Jin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jin_/(Korean_history/) "Jin (Korean history)"), which occasionally enters Chinese annals as a contemporary of [Wiman Joseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiman_Joseon "Wiman Joseon"). Lee (1984, p. 13) views this as the period of emergence of the "walled-town states" in Korean culture, a hierarchical political structure in contrast to the tribal system which had prevailed during the [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") period. Other archaelologists have associated the culture with the ancient [Shanrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanrong "Shanrong") people, a group that lived on the periphery of Yan. 33.content:
Ancient China's interactions with Japan and Korea shaped East Asian civilization. Trade routes like the Silk Road and maritime networks fostered exchanges of goods, ideas, and cultural practices. These connections influenced economic, social, and political development.

China's cultural dominance led to widespread adoption of Chinese writing, Buddhism, and artistic styles in Japan and Korea. Diplomatic relations, technology transfer, and migration further intertwined these civilizations, leaving lasting impacts on East Asian identity and regional dynamics.

Interaction through trade
-------------------------

*   Trade played a crucial role in fostering interaction between ancient China, Japan, and Korea, facilitating the exchange of goods, ideas, and cultural practices
*   The Silk Road and maritime trade routes served as vital conduits for this interaction, connecting these civilizations and enabling the flow of material culture and knowledge
*   Trade relations had a profound impact on the economic, social, and political development of ancient China, Japan, and Korea, shaping their trajectories and leaving lasting legacies

### Silk Road connections

*   The Silk Road was a network of overland trade routes that connected China with Central Asia, the Middle East, and ultimately, Europe
*   It facilitated the exchange of silk, spices, precious stones, and other luxury goods between China and its western neighbors
*   The Silk Road also served as a conduit for the transmission of ideas, technologies, and religious beliefs (Buddhism)
*   Chinese silk was highly prized in Japan and Korea, and its import via the Silk Road stimulated the development of local silk production

### Maritime trade routes

*   Maritime trade routes, particularly those across the East China Sea and the Sea of Japan, connected China with Japan and Korea
*   Chinese ships carried goods such as ceramics, bronze mirrors, and textiles to Japan and Korea, while bringing back raw materials (timber, gold) and local products (lacquerware)
*   Korean and Japanese ports (Busan, Hakata) emerged as important hubs for maritime trade with China
*   Maritime trade fostered the growth of merchant communities and the development of specialized production centers in coastal regions

### Exchanged goods and materials

*   Silk, ceramics, and bronze mirrors were among the most important Chinese goods traded to Japan and Korea
*   In return, Japan and Korea exported raw materials such as timber, gold, silver, and pearls to China
*   Other exchanged goods included spices, tea, lacquerware, and medicinal herbs
*   The trade in prestige goods (bronze mirrors, gold ornaments) played a significant role in elite gift exchange and diplomacy between the three regions

Cultural exchange and influence
-------------------------------

*   The interaction between ancient China, Japan, and Korea led to a significant exchange of cultural practices, artistic styles, and religious beliefs
*   China, as the dominant civilization in East Asia, exerted a strong influence on the cultural development of Japan and Korea
*   The adoption of Chinese writing systems, the spread of Buddhism, and the emulation of Chinese artistic motifs and styles are testament to the profound cultural impact of these interactions

### Spread of Buddhism

*   Buddhism, which originated in India, was introduced to China via the Silk Road and subsequently spread to Korea and Japan
*   Korean monks (Hyecho) played a crucial role in transmitting Buddhism to Japan, establishing temples and monasteries
*   Buddhist art, architecture, and scriptures from China heavily influenced the development of Buddhism in Japan and Korea
*   The adoption of Buddhism had a profound impact on the religious landscape, social structures, and political ideologies of ancient Japan and Korea

### Adoption of writing systems

*   The Chinese writing system, based on logographic characters, was adopted and adapted by both Japan and Korea
*   In Japan, Chinese characters (kanji) were used to write Japanese, leading to the development of the hiragana and katakana scripts
*   Korea developed its own writing system, hangul, in the 15th century, but continued to use Chinese characters (hanja) for official and scholarly writings
*   The adoption of Chinese writing facilitated the transmission of Chinese literature, philosophy, and historical records to Japan and Korea

### Shared artistic styles and motifs

*   Chinese artistic styles and motifs, particularly those of the Tang Dynasty, heavily influenced Japanese and Korean art
*   Buddhist art, including sculpture and painting, showcased strong Chinese influences in terms of iconography, composition, and technique
*   Chinese bronze mirrors, with their intricate designs and symbolic motifs, were highly prized and imitated in Japan and Korea
*   Ceramic styles, such as green-glazed celadon and white porcelain, were introduced from China and adapted to local tastes and techniques in Japan and Korea

Diplomacy and political relations
---------------------------------

*   Diplomatic relations between ancient China, Japan, and Korea were characterized by a complex web of alliances, conflicts, and power dynamics
*   The Chinese tributary system played a central role in shaping the political interactions between these three regions
*   Embassies and envoys were exchanged to maintain diplomatic ties, negotiate alliances, and resolve conflicts
*   Military conflicts, often fueled by territorial disputes or political rivalries, also marked the history of relations between ancient China, Japan, and Korea

### Tributary system

*   The Chinese tributary system was a hierarchical framework that positioned China as the dominant power, with neighboring states as vassals or tributaries
*   Japan and Korea participated in the tributary system, sending envoys and tribute missions to the Chinese court to acknowledge Chinese suzerainty and maintain trade relations
*   The tributary system served as a means for China to assert its political and cultural hegemony, while also providing a framework for diplomatic exchange and conflict resolution
*   The nature and frequency of tributary relations varied over time, reflecting the shifting power dynamics between China, Japan, and Korea

### Embassies and envoys

*   Diplomatic embassies and envoys were regularly exchanged between the courts of China, Japan, and Korea
*   These missions served to convey official communications, negotiate alliances, and exchange gifts and tributes
*   Chinese envoys to Japan and Korea often brought with them cultural artifacts, such as books, paintings, and musical instruments, which helped to disseminate Chinese culture
*   Japanese and Korean envoys to China were often scholars or monks who studied Chinese language, literature, and philosophy, bringing back knowledge and ideas to their home countries

### Military alliances and conflicts

*   The history of relations between ancient China, Japan, and Korea was punctuated by periods of military conflict and strategic alliances
*   The Korean kingdoms of Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla alternately allied with and fought against Chinese dynasties (Sui, Tang) in their struggles for dominance on the Korean Peninsula
*   The Japanese kingdom of Yamato (later known as Wa) sent envoys and troops to support the Korean kingdom of Baekje in its conflicts with Silla and Tang China
*   The ultimate unification of the Korean Peninsula under the Silla Dynasty and the establishment of a centralized Japanese state (Yamato) were heavily influenced by their interactions with China

Technology transfer
-------------------

*   The interaction between ancient China, Japan, and Korea facilitated the transfer of technologies, innovations, and practical knowledge across a wide range of fields
*   Chinese technologies, particularly in agriculture, metallurgy, and shipbuilding, were adopted and adapted by Japan and Korea, contributing to their economic and social development
*   The transfer of technological knowledge occurred through various channels, including trade, diplomatic exchanges, and the movement of skilled artisans and craftsmen

### Metalworking techniques

*   Chinese bronze casting techniques, particularly those used for ritual vessels and weapons, were introduced to Japan and Korea through trade and cultural exchange
*   The use of iron, which was first developed in China, spread to Korea and Japan, leading to advances in agriculture and warfare
*   Korean and Japanese metalworkers adapted Chinese techniques to create distinctive local styles, such as the Korean Goryeo celadon and the Japanese Yayoi bronzes
*   The exchange of metalworking knowledge also extended to the production of gold and silver ornaments, mirrors, and other luxury goods

### Agricultural practices

*   Chinese agricultural technologies, including irrigation systems, plowing techniques, and the use of iron tools, were adopted and adapted by Japan and Korea
*   The introduction of new crops from China, such as tea, silk, and various fruits and vegetables, diversified the agricultural landscapes of Japan and Korea
*   Korean and Japanese farmers also developed unique local practices, such as the use of raised bed cultivation in Korea and the terraced rice fields of Japan
*   The exchange of agricultural knowledge and practices contributed to the growth of rural economies and the development of regional culinary traditions

### Shipbuilding and navigation

*   Chinese shipbuilding techniques, particularly the use of watertight bulkheads and stern-mounted rudders, were adopted by Korean and Japanese shipwrights
*   The exchange of navigational knowledge, including the use of the magnetic compass and celestial navigation, facilitated the expansion of maritime trade between China, Japan, and Korea
*   Korean and Japanese ships, such as the Korean turtle ship and the Japanese atakebune, incorporated elements of Chinese design while also developing distinctive local features
*   The transfer of shipbuilding and navigation technologies played a crucial role in the growth of maritime trade networks and the exploration of new trade routes

Migration and settlement
------------------------

*   The interaction between ancient China, Japan, and Korea involved the movement of people, leading to the establishment of immigrant communities and the exchange of cultural practices
*   Chinese immigrants settled in Japan and Korea, often as merchants, artisans, or scholars, contributing to the development of local economies and cultural landscapes
*   Japanese and Korean immigrants also established communities in China, particularly in coastal cities and trade hubs, where they engaged in commerce and cultural exchange
*   Intermarriage between Chinese, Japanese, and Korean individuals led to the emergence of mixed-heritage populations and the blending of cultural practices

### Chinese communities in Japan and Korea

*   Chinese immigrant communities were established in various parts of Japan and Korea, particularly in port cities and trade centers (Hakata, Busan)
*   These communities often specialized in particular trades or crafts, such as silk weaving, ceramics production, or medicine
*   Chinese temples, shrines, and festivals were established in these communities, serving as centers of cultural and religious life
*   The presence of Chinese communities in Japan and Korea facilitated the transmission of Chinese language, literature, and cultural practices to local populations

### Japanese and Korean presence in China

*   Japanese and Korean communities were also present in China, particularly in coastal cities and trade hubs (Quanzhou, Ningbo)
*   These communities were often involved in maritime trade, serving as intermediaries between Chinese merchants and their counterparts in Japan and Korea
*   Japanese and Korean temples, shrines, and festivals were established in these communities, serving as centers of cultural and religious life
*   The presence of Japanese and Korean communities in China facilitated the exchange of goods, ideas, and cultural practices between the three regions

### Intermarriage and cultural assimilation

*   Intermarriage between Chinese, Japanese, and Korean individuals was not uncommon, particularly among merchant and elite classes
*   These marriages often served to strengthen commercial and diplomatic ties between families and communities
*   The children of these intermarriages often grew up bilingual or multilingual, and were exposed to a blend of cultural practices and traditions
*   Over time, many of these mixed-heritage individuals and communities underwent processes of cultural assimilation, adopting the language and customs of their host societies

Archaeological evidence of interaction
--------------------------------------

*   Archaeological finds provide tangible evidence of the interaction between ancient China, Japan, and Korea, revealing the extent and nature of cultural exchange and trade relations
*   Chinese artifacts, such as ceramics, bronzes, and coins, have been discovered in various sites across Japan and Korea, attesting to the flow of goods and ideas between these regions
*   Similarly, Japanese and Korean artifacts have been unearthed in China, particularly in coastal regions and along major trade routes
*   Shared burial customs and grave goods also provide insights into the cultural connections and influences between ancient China, Japan, and Korea

### Chinese artifacts in Japan and Korea

*   Chinese ceramics, particularly celadon and white porcelain, have been found in numerous archaeological sites in Japan and Korea
*   Bronze mirrors, coins, and other metal objects of Chinese origin have also been discovered, often in elite burial contexts or in association with Buddhist temples and monasteries
*   Chinese silk textiles and lacquerware have been found in Japanese and Korean tombs, attesting to the prestige and value associated with these goods
*   The presence of Chinese artifacts in Japan and Korea provides evidence of the extent and nature of trade relations, as well as the cultural influence of China on its neighbors

### Japanese and Korean finds in China

*   Japanese and Korean artifacts, including ceramics, metalwork, and lacquerware, have been discovered in various archaeological sites in China
*   These finds are particularly concentrated in coastal regions and along major trade routes, such as the Silk Road and the maritime networks of the East China Sea
*   Japanese and Korean Buddhist statuary and ritual objects have also been found in Chinese temples and monasteries, attesting to the religious connections between these regions
*   The presence of Japanese and Korean artifacts in China provides evidence of the two-way nature of cultural exchange and trade relations between these regions

### Shared burial customs and grave goods

*   Archaeological evidence reveals shared burial customs and grave goods between ancient China, Japan, and Korea, attesting to the cultural connections and influences between these regions
*   The use of stone chambers, coffins, and sarcophagi in elite burials is a common feature across all three regions, with variations in style and construction techniques
*   The inclusion of grave goods, such as ceramics, bronzes, and personal ornaments, is also a shared practice, with regional differences in the types and styles of objects included
*   The arrangement and orientation of burials, as well as the use of burial mounds and tumuli, also exhibit similarities across ancient China, Japan, and Korea
*   These shared burial customs and grave goods provide insights into the cultural beliefs, social hierarchies, and material culture of these ancient societies, as well as the nature of their interactions and influences

*   The interaction between ancient China, Japan, and Korea had a profound impact on the social structures and power dynamics of these societies
*   The adoption of Chinese bureaucratic models, particularly the civil service examination system, led to significant changes in the composition and organization of ruling elites in Japan and Korea
*   The influx of new ideas, technologies, and material culture also contributed to the emergence of new social classes and the restructuring of existing hierarchies
*   The legacy of these ancient interactions can be seen in the lasting cultural influences and the foundation they provided for later historical relations between China, Japan, and Korea

### Adoption of Chinese bureaucratic models

*   The Chinese bureaucratic system, based on a hierarchical structure and the recruitment of officials through civil service examinations, was adopted and adapted by Japan and Korea
*   In Japan, the Taika Reforms of the 7th century introduced a Chinese-style bureaucracy and legal code, laying the foundation for the centralized Japanese state
*   In Korea, the Silla Dynasty adopted the Chinese bureaucratic model, with a system of civil service examinations and a hierarchical ranking of officials
*   The adoption of Chinese bureaucratic models led to significant changes in the composition and organization of ruling elites, with a shift towards meritocratic recruitment and the centralization of power

### Changes in class and hierarchy

*   The interaction between ancient China, Japan, and Korea contributed to the emergence of new social classes and the restructuring of existing hierarchies
*   The growth of trade and commerce led to the rise of merchant classes in all three regions, with varying degrees of social status and political influence
*   The adoption of Chinese cultural practices, such as the use of surnames and the emphasis on literary education, also contributed to the formation of scholar-gentry classes in Japan and Korea
*   The influx of new technologies and material culture, such as iron tools and silk textiles, also had an impact on the economic and social status of artisans and craftsmen

### Emergence of new elites and power dynamics

*   The interaction between ancient China, Japan, and Korea led to the emergence of new elite groups and the reconfiguration of power dynamics within these societies
*   In Japan, the adoption of Chinese bureaucratic models and the influence of continental culture contributed to the rise of the imperial family and the centralization of power
*   In Korea, the Silla Dynasty's unification of the peninsula and its close ties with Tang China led to the emergence of a new aristocratic class and the consolidation of royal authority
*   The exchange of ideas, technologies, and material culture also contributed to the formation of new intellectual and artistic elites, such as the literati painters of Korea and the Buddhist scholars of Japan

Legacy of ancient interactions
------------------------------

*   The interactions between ancient China, Japan, and Korea have left a lasting legacy on the cultural, political, and social landscapes of East Asia
*   The cultural influences of these ancient exchanges can still be seen in the art, literature, and religious practices of modern China, Japan, and Korea
*   The political and economic foundations laid by these early interactions have also shaped the course of later historical relations between these nations
*   The shared cultural heritage and the legacy of these ancient interactions continue to play a significant role in the formation of East Asian identities and the dynamics of regional cooperation and conflict

### Lasting cultural influences

*   The cultural influences of ancient China on Japan and Korea can still be seen in various aspects of modern life, from language and writing systems to art and architecture
*   The legacy of Buddhism, which was transmitted from China to Korea and Japan, remains a significant feature of the religious landscape of East Asia
*   The influence of Chinese literature, particularly the Confucian classics and the works of Tang Dynasty poets, can be seen in the literary traditions of Japan and Korea
*   The aesthetic principles and artistic techniques developed during the period of ancient interactions continue to shape the art and design of modern East Asia

### Foundation for later historical relations

*   The political and economic foundations laid by the ancient interactions between China, Japan, and Korea have had a profound impact on the course of later historical relations between these nations
*   The tributary system and the diplomatic protocols established during the ancient period continued to shape the nature of political exchanges and power dynamics in later centuries
*   The trade networks and economic ties forged during the ancient period also served as the basis for later commercial relations and regional economic integration
*   The legacy of ancient conflicts and alliances, such as the Goguryeo-Sui Wars and the Baekje-Yamato alliance, have also had a lasting impact on the geopolitical landscape of East Asia

### Significance in East Asian identity formation

*   The shared cultural heritage and the legacy of ancient interactions play a significant role in the formation of modern East Asian identities
*   The recognition of a common cultural background, rooted in the exchanges and influences of the ancient period, serves as a basis for regional cooperation and mutual understanding
*   The legacy of ancient interactions also contributes to the sense of cultural pride and the assertion of national identities within the context of East Asian relations
*   The ongoing debates and dialogues surrounding the interpretation and significance of ancient interactions reflect the complex and dynamic nature of East Asian identities in the modern world
