The **Balhae controversies** involve disputes between [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), [Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea "Korea"), [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), and [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), countries that have conducted studies on the historical state of [Balhae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae "Balhae") (Bohai, Po-hai, Parhae). The Korean perspective generally considers Balhae to be the successor state of [Goguryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo "Goguryeo") and part of the [Northern and Southern States period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_and_Southern_States_period "Northern and Southern States period") of Korean history, while Chinese scholars generally consider Balhae to be a state of the [Mohe people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohe_people "Mohe people"), a [Tungusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungusic_peoples "Tungusic peoples") ethnic group, and subordinate to the [Tang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty") (618––907).[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-Kim2012-2) In Russian historiography, Balhae is recognized as the first highly organized independent state formation of the Tungus-Manchurian peoples.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-%D0%A8%D0%90%D0%92%D0%9A%D0%A3%D0%9D%D0%9E%D0%92_%D0%AD%D1%80%D0%BD%D0%B5%D1%81%D1%82_%D0%92%D0%BB%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%BC%D0%B8%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B8%D1%87-3)

Balhae (698–926) is a kingdom that has been studied and debated in [East Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asia "East Asia") since the early 20th century. Central to the issue of scholarship since the 1960s is whether or not Balhae belongs to Korean or Chinese national history. Arguments based on the identity and essential features of Balhae have been made by contemporary states to confirm or question territorial claims by present governments. Academic disputes over the identity of Goguryeo and Balhae are commonly linked to claims in international relations discourse on the legitimacy of the present Sino-Korean border.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane20142%E2%80%933-4)

The general positions of state actors involved in the Balhae dispute:

Koreas:

*   Balhae was a "Korean" state founded by the descendants of Goguryeo and that Balhae and Unified Silla constituted the "[Northern and Southern Dynasties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_and_Southern_dynasties "Northern and Southern dynasties")".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane20144-5)

China:

*   Balhae was a local polity founded by the "Mohe nationality", subordinate to the Tang dynasty.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane20144-5)

Soviet Union/Russia:

*   Balhae was created by a union of Mohe peoples who are the ancestors of tribal groups in Russian territory.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane20144-5)

Empire of Japan:

*   Balhae was founded by a Sumo Mohe tribal leader with no connection to Goguryeo or Korea, and was independent from the Tang dynasty.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane20147%E2%80%938-6)

[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/History_of_Korea-Inter-country_Age-830_CE.gif/250px-History_of_Korea-Inter-country_Age-830_CE.gif)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:History_of_Korea-Inter-country_Age-830_CE.gif)

The [Northern and Southern States period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_and_Southern_States_period "Northern and Southern States period") in 830

[Goryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goryeo "Goryeo") (918–1392) did not write an official history for Balhae, and some modern scholars argue that had they done so, Koreans might have had a stronger claim to Balhae's history and territory.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-7) This was in part because the writer of Korea's first historical record, the _[Samguk sagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samguk_sagi "Samguk sagi")_, was [Kim Pusik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Pusik "Kim Pusik") (1075–1151), who was a direct descendent of the ruling Silla dynasty. Silla was known to have held a hostile attitude towards Balhae, which might explain the exclusion of Balhae from the first complete compilation of Korean History.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-shultz70-8) Although Goryeo did not compile an official history for Balhae, a great portion of the royalty and aristocracy fled to Goryeo, including its Crown Prince [Dae Gwang-hyeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dae_Gwang-hyeon "Dae Gwang-hyeon").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim2019108-9) A text known as the _Jodaegi_ allegedly written by a Balhae refugee contained records of Balhae's history but was lost during the literary purges of [Sejo of Joseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sejo_of_Joseon "Sejo of Joseon") in the 15th century and only fragments remain.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-10) Snippets of its contents are recorded in the _Taebaek Ilsa_, part of the _[Hwandan Gogi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwandan_Gogi "Hwandan Gogi")_ compiled by Gye Yeon-su in 1911.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-11) However, most scholars from South Korea, North Korea and Japan believe that the Hwandan Gogi is a forgery and that its content is unreliable.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-12)

The first inclusion of Balhae in Korean history was in the [Jewang ungi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewang_ungi "Jewang ungi"), a historical book written in the form of rhyming poetry by Goryeo scholar and court official [Lee Seung-hyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lee_Seung-hyu&action=edit&redlink=1 "Lee Seung-hyu (page does not exist)") in 1287, during the late Goryeo dynasty.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-auto1-14)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-auto2-15) According to Myungkyung University Professor Lee Sooyoung, Lee was motivated to write the Jewangungi due to both the internal political turmoil of the Goryeo court as well as the [Yuan dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_dynasty "Yuan dynasty")'s interference in Goryeo politics during [Goryeo under Mongol rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goryeo_under_Mongol_rule "Goryeo under Mongol rule").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-auto1-14) The Jewangungi is considered important as it is the first history book to record the history of Balhae as Korean history, and has been cited by both North and South Korean scholars.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-auto2-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-16)

Some scholars, such as [Pak Chiwŏn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pak_Chiw%C5%8Fn_/(philosopher/) "Pak Chiwŏn (philosopher)") (1737–1805), denied the fact that the [Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty")'s territories extended south of the [Yalu River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalu_River "Yalu River"), and criticized [Kim Pusik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Pusik "Kim Pusik") (1075–1151), the author of the _[Samguk sagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samguk_sagi "Samguk sagi")_, for excluding [Balhae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae "Balhae") (_Bohai_ in Chinese) in Manchuria from the [history of Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Korea "History of Korea"), arguing that the people of Balhae were "descendants" of Goguryeo. [Yi Gyu-gyeong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yi_Gyu-gyeong "Yi Gyu-gyeong") (b. 1788) argued that the exclusion of Balhae from Korean history was "a grave error" since "it occupied a vast area".[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShin200011%E2%80%9312-17) In Joseon's later years, increasing numbers of Korean historians included Balhae in Korean history, despite acknowledging that the state's founders were the [Mohe people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohe_people "Mohe people") and not considered to be "us."[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-Karlsson-18) In the 18th century, there was a divide in opinions. [Seongho Yi Ik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seongho_Yi_Ik "Seongho Yi Ik") (1681–1763) and [An Jeongbok](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=An_Jeongbok&action=edit&redlink=1 "An Jeongbok (page does not exist)") refused to consider Balhae part of Korean history while [Sin Gyeongjun](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sin_Gyeongjun&action=edit&redlink=1 "Sin Gyeongjun (page does not exist)") and [Yu Deuk-gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yu_Deuk-gong "Yu Deuk-gong") (1749–1807) fully incorporated it. In Yu's _[Balhaego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhaego "Balhaego")_, an investigation of Balhae, he argued that Balhae should be included as part of Korean history and that doing so would justify territorial claims on Manchuria.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-Choe-19)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-20) A century later, [Han Chiyun](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Han_Chiyun&action=edit&redlink=1 "Han Chiyun (page does not exist)") and [Han Jinseo](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Han_Jinseo&action=edit&redlink=1 "Han Jinseo (page does not exist)") included Balhae as equal in Korean history to such uncontroversially Korean dynasties like [Silla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silla "Silla").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-Karlsson-18)

Korean historian [Sin Chaeho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sin_Chaeho "Sin Chaeho") (1880–1936) criticized the _Samguk sagi_ for excluding Balhae and [Buyeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buyeo "Buyeo") (Chinese: _Fuyu_, another state in Manchuria) from Korean history.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-21) Writing about [Jiandao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiandao "Jiandao") in the early 20th century, he bemoaned that for centuries, Korean people in their "hearts and eyes considered only the land south of the [Yalu River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalu_River "Yalu River") as their home." He interpreted Balhae's defeat by the [Khitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khitan_people "Khitan people")\-led [Liao dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liao_dynasty "Liao dynasty") (916–1125) as having caused "half of our ancestor [Dangun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dangun "Dangun")'s ancient lands... loss for over nine hundred years". Sin also criticized Kim Pusik for excluding Balhae from his historical work and claiming that [Silla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silla "Silla") had achieved the [unification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unified_Silla "Unified Silla") of Korea.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-Schmid-22) Inspired by ideas of [Social Darwinism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Darwinism "Social Darwinism"), Sin wrote:

> How intimate is the connection between Korea and Manchuria? When the Korean race obtains Manchuria, the Korean race is strong and prosperous. When another race obtains Manchuria, the Korean race is inferior and recedes. Moreover, when in the possession of another race, if that race is the northern race, then Korea enters that northern race's sphere of power. If an eastern race obtains Manchuria, then Korea enters that race's sphere of power. Alas! This is an iron rule that has not changed for four thousand years.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-23)

North Korean scholars—and more recently, some in the [South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea")—have recently tried to incorporate Balhae history as an integral part of Korean history by challenging the view of [Unified Silla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unified_Silla "Unified Silla") (668–935) as the unification of Korea. According to this narrative, [Goryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goryeo "Goryeo") was the first unification of Korea, since Balhae still existed while occupying former Goguryeo territory north of the Korean peninsula.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-Choe-19) In the 1960s, the North Korean scholar [Pak Se-yong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pak_Se-yong "Pak Se-yong") advanced arguments that claimed Balhae as "a part of Korean history."[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a5-24) Central to the argument was Balhae's place as "a state founded by people of Koguryŏ" and its territory as composed of most of the "former territory of Koguryŏ and an expansive, newly-acquired portion."[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a5-24) Pak made broader claims on the continuity of Balhae with modern Korea, contending that "bloodline and culture are an important component of the bloodlines and cultural traditions of the Korean race."[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a5-24)

In South Korea, Chu Yŏnghŏn advocated a Korean identity for Balhae based on findings of joint Chinese-North Korean archaeological excavations in the 1960s. These efforts led to the incorporation of Balhae into Korean history as part of the "Northern and Southern Dynasties" based on instances in which the Silla court referred to Balhae as the "northern court."[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a5-24) Acceptance of this new narrative was not immediate. In 1981, a South Korean scholar called the Northern-Southern Dynasties an "interesting new interpretation"[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a6-25) and as late as 1990, there was still no consensus. However, by now the Northern-Southern Dynasties paradigm is widely accepted in South Korean academia. According to Kim Eun Gug, the adoption of this position was necessary to counter Chinese claims on Goguryeo and Balhae as part of Chinese history as well as to provide a model for North and South Korea's unification. Kim openly declared that, "We have a national responsibility to develop a response to China's [Northeast Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_Project_of_the_Chinese_Academy_of_Social_Sciences "Northeast Project of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences") and its claims that Koguryŏ and Parhae belong to Chinese history."[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a4%E2%80%936-26)

Some Japanese scholarship from the mid-1930s to the early postwar period also supported placing Balhae within Korean history. This position was advanced mostly prominently by Mikami Tsugio and became very popular after Japan severed diplomatic ties with the People's Republic of China in 1949. In the 1980s, Japanese scholars scrutinized new archaeological evidence from China in the hopes of clarifying Balhae's ethnic identity. However, since then, the majority of Japanese scholars have moved away from seeking a singular ethnic paradigm for Balhae and instead focus on local government mechanisms and their relationship with central authority. According to Park Jin Suk, Japan no longer has any territorial interests in Balhae and its scholars offer a more objective position.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a7%E2%80%938-27)

According to Dartmouth historian [Pamela Kyle Crossley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamela_Kyle_Crossley "Pamela Kyle Crossley"), "[Balhae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae "Balhae") as a language, people and state with diverse origins was without doubt part of a spectrum that included [Goguryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo "Goguryeo"), [Buyeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buyeo "Buyeo") and [Baekje](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baekje "Baekje") and was closely connected with the development of medieval Korea."[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrossley201612-28)

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Balhae_Kingdom.png/250px-Balhae_Kingdom.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Balhae_Kingdom.png)

Administrative divisions of Balhae with Chinese and Korean names[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-29)

### Jurchens and Manchus

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Balhae_controversies&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Jurchens and Manchus")\]

Historically, the [Jurchens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurchen_people "Jurchen people") (later renamed the [Manchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchu_people "Manchu people")), believed they shared ancestry with the Mohe. According to the _[History of Jin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jin "History of Jin")_, the history of the Jurchen-led [Jin dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jin_dynasty,_1115%E2%80%931234 "Jin dynasty, 1115–1234") (1115–1234), the Jin founder [Emperor Taizu of Jin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taizu_of_Jin "Emperor Taizu of Jin") once sent ambassadors to Bohai people living in the [Liao dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liao_dynasty "Liao dynasty") (916–1125) to convince them to rebel against the Liao. He claimed that "the Jurchens and Bohai were originally of the same family" (女直渤海本同一家) and that they were "actually one family, because in origin they were consisted of seven Wuji tribes."[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim2011b173-30)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-31)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-32)

> Classical Chinese
> 
> 建州毛怜则渤海大氏遗孽，乐住种，善缉纺，饮食服用，皆如华人，自长白山迤南，可拊而治也。
> 
> English
> 
> The (people of) [Chien-chou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jianzhou_Jurchens "Jianzhou Jurchens") and Mao-lin \[YLSL always reads Mao-lien\] are the descendants of the family Ta of Po-hai. They love to be sedentary and sow, and they are skilled in spinning and weaving. As for food, clothing, and utensils, they are the same as (those used by) the Chinese. (Those living) south of the [Ch'ang-pai mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%27ang-pai_mountain "Ch'ang-pai mountain") are apt to be soothed and governed.
> 
> — 据魏焕《皇明九边考》卷二《辽东镇边夷考》[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-33) Translation from _Sino-J̌ürčed relations during the Yung-Lo period, 1403–1424_ by Henry Serruys[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-34)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/National_Museum_3.jpg/250px-National_Museum_3.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:National_Museum_3.jpg)

A dragon head artifact from [Bohai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae "Balhae") at the [National Museum of Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Korea "National Museum of Korea").

Archaeological materials from the Anan'evskoe site show material evidence of ancestral relations between the Jurchens and Bohai people. Several South Korean scholars believe that after Bohai's destruction in 926, Bohai's population was divided into two groups. Influential Bohai families were sent to the inner part of the Liao dynasty and were referred to as Bohai people, while those who remained under indirect management were called Jurchen. Han Ciu-cheol argues that Jurchens could be considered part of Korean history. Soviet and Russian scholars agree there were hereditary relationships between Mohe and Jurchen and that the Bohai population certainly contributed culturally to the ethnogenesis of the Jurchen. However, some differences remain. The Balhae refugee population was received well in Goryeo while they had a combative relationship with the Jurchens. Goryeo once massacred the ambassador and leaders of a Jurchen delegation during peace talks. They sent an official complaint about the Jurchens to the [Song dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_dynasty "Song dynasty"), calling them greedy liars and other insulting names. The Jurchens described Goryeo people as enemies and often came into military conflict with them.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim2011b171%E2%80%93172-35) The Jurchen and Bohai people also differed in their level of technological and societal sophistication. Chinese sources describe the Jurchens as lacking law, governors, kings, or dignitaries. Prior to the reign of [Wanyan Wugunai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wanyan_Wugunai "Wanyan Wugunai") (1021–1074), in the early 11th century, the Jurchens could not produce iron armor and had to trade for it from other tribes.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim2011b173-30)

In 1778, the [Qianlong Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qianlong_Emperor "Qianlong Emperor") of the [Qing dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty "Qing dynasty") reviewed various history books and commissioned a new comprehensive history of the [Manchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchus "Manchus"), the _[Researches on Manchu Origins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Researches_on_Manchu_Origins "Researches on Manchu Origins")_ ([Manchu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchu_language "Manchu language"): ᠮᠠᠨᠵᡠᠰᠠᡳ  
ᡩᠠ  
ᠰᡝᡴᡳᠶᡝᠨ ‍‍ᡳ  
ᡴᡳᠮᠴᡳᠨ  
ᠪᡳᡨᡥᡝ, [Möllendorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transliterations_of_Manchu "Transliterations of Manchu"): _Manjusai da sekiyen-i kimcin bithe_, [Abkai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transliterations_of_Manchu "Transliterations of Manchu"): _Manjusai da sekiyen-i kimqin bithe_; [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters "Traditional Chinese characters"): 滿洲源流考; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): _Mǎnzhōu Yuánliú Kǎo_). Part of this endeavor was to create a new imperial history of Manchus that was glorious in its own right and not a frontier imitation of Chinese civilization. This new history placed their Jin ancestors, the Jin imperial clan, among the population of the Mohe, who lived in the [Changbai Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changbai_Mountains "Changbai Mountains") and along the [Amur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amur "Amur").[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrossley200220-36) Qianlong repeatedly made references to the Bohai as the origin of various organizational features such as the use of "the five-capitals, a writing system, and a leadership hierarchy that he believed was evident in early Qing history and still in use among Northeastern peoples."[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrossley201611-37)

Finnish linguist [Juha Janhunen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juha_Janhunen "Juha Janhunen") argues that it is possible that the Goguryeo language could have been an Amuric language related to today's [Nivkh language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nivkh_language "Nivkh language") isolate.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-38)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-39)

### People's Republic of China

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Balhae_controversies&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: People's Republic of China")\]

Since 1949, the People's Republic of China has depicted the country as a multi-ethnic state and endeavored to create unity among the country's various minorities to strengthen the nation as a unified construct. According to this narrative, Chinese scholarship has generally characterized Bohai as a "local polity of a minority nationality" subordinate to Tang rule and that the history of Bohai belongs to China.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a6-25) Only in the 1980s did the study of the Bohai become a major enterprise in China. In the mid-2000s, Bohai studies received a new impetus from the Northeast Project. The project was seen by South Korean scholars as a concerted political effort to "contest the role of Koguryŏ and Parhae" as part of Korean history. There was concern that China would seek recognition from [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO"). Park Jin Suk argues that "the Chinese position has been solidified" by the Northeast Project and now presents a united front against other historical interpretations.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a6%E2%80%937-40) Although a standard Chinese position never actually developed and contradictions within Chinese scholars remain, there are no Chinese authors advocating Bohai as Korean.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a7-41)

Chinese research was described as focusing "solely on the relationship between Parhae and Tang, leading to the conclusion that Parhae was only a local government dependent in every respect on Tang."[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a13-42) Such an assessment is no longer entirely true as Chinese scholarship now pays more attention to Bohai's relationship with other polities. A recent Chinese introduction to the topic categorized Bohai's diplomatic exchanges with the Tang as a "relationship between cultures" while other diplomatic actions were "foreign relations".[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a14-43) According to Lei Yijie, Bohai was a "local ethnic polity" ruled by the Tang.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a14-43) Kaneko Shūichi notes that the Tang treated Bohai and Silla the same. Formally, they were "prefectures under loose rule" (_jimizhou_). In 713, the Tang court granted Da Zuorong the post of Commander-in-Chief (_dudu_) of Huhan Prefecture, the Tang name for Bohai's capital.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a14-43)[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-44) In practice, it is hard for Chinese dynasties to claim any state as independent under the "tribute model." This problem is exhibited by states such as Silla, Goryeo, and Joseon, all of which had less political autonomy than Bohai but are not claimed as Chinese.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a15-45) Epigraphic evidence shows that the rulers of Bohai considered themselves emperors and empresses. In communications between Bohai and the Japanese court, Bohai's ruler referred to himself as "Grandson of Heaven" and portrayed the relationship between himself and the ruler of Japan as uncle to nephew. Sakayori Masashi believes this was meant to express his superiority in a "Sinocentric worldview" centered on Bohai and to claim sovereignty over Silla and the Mohe tribes.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a15-45)

An earlier, opposing view comes from Chinese Prime Minister [Zhou Enlai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_Enlai "Zhou Enlai"), who said in 1963 that Korean people have lived in the northeastern region of China since ancient times and excavated relics prove that Bohai is a branch of ancient Korea. The former Chinese premier's remarks have been made public through a document entitled "Premier Zhou Enlai's Dialogue on Sino-Korean Relations."[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-46)

China is accused of limiting Korean archaeologists access to historical sites located within [Liaoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning "Liaoning") and [Jilin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jilin "Jilin"). Starting from 1994, increasing numbers of South Korean tourists began to visit [Goguryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo "Goguryeo") archaeological sites in China and often engaged in nationalistic displays. China perceived this as a threat and restricted foreign access to Goguryeo sites. This perception was aggravated by a series of tomb robberies and vandalism at several of these archaeological sites between 1995 and 2000.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-47) South Korean archeologist Song Ki-ho, a noted professor at [Seoul National University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul_National_University "Seoul National University") who has published several papers criticizing the Chinese government's interpretation of [Bohai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae "Balhae") 's history, made several visits to China in the 1990s, 2000, 2003, and 2004, examining several historical sites and museums. However, he found himself restricted by limitations on note-taking and photography and was even ejected from several sites by museum employees.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-48)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-49)

Balhae as Manchurian
--------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Balhae_controversies&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Balhae as Manchurian")\]

The placement of Balhae within [Manchurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchuria "Manchuria") history was advanced by Japanese scholarship as their political and military interests grew after the [First Sino-Japanese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Sino-Japanese_War "First Sino-Japanese War") in 1895. The Manchurian framework emphasized the distinctiveness of Balhae culture compared to Tang China, Goguryeo, and Silla. The Japanese archaeologist Komai Kazuchika led the excavation of Balhae's [Supreme Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shangjing_Longquanfu "Shangjing Longquanfu") in 1933–1934. In his draft of a "Cultural History of Manchuria," the first ruler of Balhae was described as "a ruler of the Sumo Mohe"[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a7-41) with no connection to Korea or Goguryeo and independent of the Tang dynasty.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a7%E2%80%938-27)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Unified_Silla_map.jpg/250px-Unified_Silla_map.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Unified_Silla_map.jpg)

[Bohai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae "Balhae") at the time of maximum expansion in the 9th century (according to Russian archaeological research).[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-suchan.narod.ru-50)

In traditional Russian historiography, this state is recognized as the first highly organized independent state formation of the [Tungus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungusic_languages "Tungusic languages")\-[Manchurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchu_people "Manchu people") peoples.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-%D0%A8%D0%90%D0%92%D0%9A%D0%A3%D0%9D%D0%9E%D0%92_%D0%AD%D1%80%D0%BD%D0%B5%D1%81%D1%82_%D0%92%D0%BB%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%BC%D0%B8%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B8%D1%87-3)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-51)[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-52)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-53)

On the territory of Russia, over 130 years,[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-54) 18 small objects (detached farm, a watchtower, a smithy far outside village, etc.), 19 villages, and 7 cities of this state have been studied.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-55)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-56)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-57) Also, in Russian academic science there are other data on the borders of this state than in Korea and China.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-suchan.narod.ru-50)

According to Associate Professor Kim Alexander from Vladivostok State University [\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-58) Bohai studies were not left outside the politically driven polemics during the era of the [Sino-Soviet split](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Soviet_split "Sino-Soviet split"). Soviet scholars wrote extensively about the war between the Tang Empire and the state of Bohai, paying great attention to the victories of the Bohai forces and emphasizing the independence of the state, while at the same time trying to downplay the results of the war, which made Bohai re-confirm its inferior position vis-a-vis the Tang Empire in the tributary system.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-:0-59)

Russian Archeologists found in the area an Abbasid drachma from Central Asia which may indicate an economy in which foreign currency may have been used. The archeologists laid stress on the argument that the absence of an independently developed coinage is not sufficient evidence to deny that the Bohai state existed as an independent state.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-:0-59)

Alexander Ivliev stresses that Bohai students are mentioned in Chinese sources (e.g. [New Book of Tang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Book_of_Tang "New Book of Tang")) to have sat for the bingongke (賓貢科) exam, indicating that for the Tang officials, the students were subjects of other states as opposed to subjects of the Tang realm.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-:0-59)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-60)

Also, on the basis of archaeological documentary material (credential tag of the [Tang Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_Empire "Tang Empire")), it was established that the Teli people were not part of Bohai in 795. They directly paid tribute to Tang and received from him a sign recognizing the power over them of their ruler.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-61) there are also two similar tags for Heishui Mohe.

Subjects of contention
----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Balhae_controversies&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Subjects of contention")\]

The ethnicity of Balhae's population is the most widely debated topic in the debate over its historical identity. The generally held position by most scholars is that Balhae society was separated into two ethnic components: descendants of Goguryeo and Mohe tribal groups. However, within this paradigm exists a number of different views on the relationship of the two groups.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a9-62)

Korean scholarship and history textbooks teach that "the ruling class of Parhae were persons of Koguryŏ origins and that the people over whom they ruled were the Malgal, a people whose ethnic origins were different from Koguryŏ."[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane20149-63) This Korean framework portrays Balhae as a country, state, and government founded and dominated by Goguryeo people, an ethnic group equivalent to modern Koreans. The ethnic identity of the rulers is the overriding identity marker of Balhae, placing it within Korean history. Chŏn Hoch'ŏn characterizes Balhae and the peninsular Korean state of Silla as possessing "the same ethnicity."[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane20149-63) Song Ki-ho and No T'aedon argue that the Mohe were Tungusic people who had been assimilated into Goguryeo and Balhae, thereby making Mohe part of Korean history.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim201512-64)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a11-65) A few scholars in Korea, such as Han Ciu-cheol, argue that there was no difference between the Goguryeo and Mohe population and that they were the same ethnicity. Mohe was used as a pejorative term for the lower class. In the same vein, Jang Guk-jong argues that Mohe tribes in Balhae were not Mohe but part of Goguryeo's provincial population.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim201512-64)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a10-66)

In China, the Mohe are generally considered the "main ethnicity" while Goguryeo descendants occupy a secondary minority position. Based on the _New Book of Tang_, Chinese scholars argue that Balhae's founders were from the Sumo Mohe tribe centered on the [Songhua River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songhua_River "Songhua River").[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a9%E2%80%9310-67)

In 1915, Tsuda Sōkichi noted that Tang sources describe the Baishan Mohe as more closely allied to Goguryeo while the Sumo were actually in conflict with Goguryeo. Li Jiancai argues that based on this finding, the founder of Balhae, [Dae Joyeong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dae_Joyeong "Dae Joyeong") or Da Zuorong, was more likely to have been from the Baishan tribe. This position has been adopted by a number of Chinese scholars but remains marginal. Another marginal position presented by Sun Jinji argues that Balhae was not just Mohe but that diverse groups merged to form a Balhae ethnicity. This is directly opposed by Yun Jae-Woon, who points out separate activities by Mohe and Jurchen groups after the fall of Balhae, which demonstrate that they had not been absorbed into Balhae. However, Jesse D. Sloane notes that this does not mean a new ethnicity did not form as well, while not everyone were absorbed into it.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a9%E2%80%9310-67)

Russian scholars argue that the ethnic composition of Balhae cannot be determined with great precision because no materials exist that can confirm either the Chinese or Korean claims. Some Russian scholars claim Balhae as part of Manchurian history while others believe Balhae was neither a Korean state nor a Chinese province and there is no direct link between Balhae and either modern China or Korea.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim2011299-68) E. V. Shakunov believes that Balhae's population also consisted of elements from [Central Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Asia "Central Asia") such as [Sogdians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sogdians "Sogdians") and [Tocharians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tocharians "Tocharians"). Many [Uyghurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs") fled to Balhae after the destruction of the [Uyghur Khaganate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghur_Khaganate "Uyghur Khaganate") in 840 but they failed to adapt to Balhae society and caused social unrest.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim201510%E2%80%9311-69)

Besides the territorial aspirations of both Korean nationalists and those of Joseon rulers during the mid-late period of the Joseon dynasty, Korean claims to Balhae also rest on ethnicity as well as East Asian concepts of state succession. When Balhae was destroyed by the [Liao dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liao_dynasty "Liao dynasty"), a great portion of the Balhae royalty and aristocracy fled to Goryeo, including [Dae Gwang-hyeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dae_Gwang-hyeon "Dae Gwang-hyeon"), the last [crown prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_prince "Crown prince").[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-70)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-71) They were granted land and the crown prince was given the family name Wang (왕; 王), the royal family name of the Goryeo dynasty, and were included in the royal household by [Wang Geon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Geon "Wang Geon"), who was crowned as Taejo of Goryeo. Koreans believe Goryeo thus unified the two successor nations of Goguryeo.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-72) Some other members of the Balhae royalty took the surname Tae (태; 太).[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-Lee_Ki-baik_page_88%E2%80%9389-73) According to the _Goryeosa jeolyo_, the Balhae refugees who accompanied the crown prince numbered in the tens of thousands of households.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-74) As descendants of Goguryeo, the Balhae people and the Goryeo dynasts were related.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTERossabi1983154-75) Taejo of Goryeo felt a strong familial kinship with Balhae, calling it his "relative country" and "married country",[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-%EB%B0%95%EC%A2%85%EA%B8%B0-76) and protected the Balhae refugees.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTERossabi1983323-77) This was in stark contrast to Later Silla, which had endured a hostile relationship with Balhae.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-78)

[Crossley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamela_Kyle_Crossley "Pamela Kyle Crossley") believes that according to Goryeo records, Balhae refugees only arrived in groups of a few hundred to a few thousand. She suggests that the total number could not be more than 100,000, while millions remained in Liao-controlled territories. According to Crossley, it's also unclear whether they stayed, went back to Balhae, or moved on elsewhere like China or Japan.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrossley201628-79) According to Kim, between the 10th and 11th centuries, 30,000 Balhae families (more than 100,000 people) immigrated to Goryeo, 94,000 (470,000 inhabitants) local families were deported by the Liao, and only 20,000 Balhae families lived in the former territories of Balhae, a significantly smaller figure than those that immigrated to Goryeo.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim2019108,_110-80) Korean historians generally estimate that approximately 100,000 to 200,000 fled from Balhae to Goryeo.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-81)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-82) Historian Professor Park Jong-gi estimated that 120,600 people fled from Balhae to Goryeo, and by themselves, comprised approximately 6.3% of early Goryeo's roughly 2 million inhabitants.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-83)

Exodus en masse on part from the Balhae refugees would continue on at least until the early 12th century, during the reign of King Yejong, according to Korean scholars.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-84): 32–33 [\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-86) Due to this constant massive influx of Balhae refugees, the Goguryeo population is speculated to have become dominant[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-87)[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-88) in proportion compared to their Silla and Baekje counterparts that have experienced devastating war and political strife[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-89)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-90)[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-91) since the advent of the Later Three Kingdoms. Later, Baekje fared only little better than Later Silla before its fall in 936. Meanwhile, of the three capitals of Goryeo, two were Kaesong and Pyongyang, which were initially populated by Goguryeoic settlers from the Paeseo Region (패서; 浿西) and Balhae.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-92)

> The problem about Parhae history is that many questions are beyond a simple answer. Different, nearly contemporary, sources represent fundamental questions in very different ways with different possible interpretations.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReckel2015481%E2%80%93482-93)

— Johannes Reckel

While the study of Balhae draws on a wide range of textual sources, most investigations of its ethnicity start from the two official histories of the Tang dynasty.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a11-65) Efforts have been made to seek evidence in other texts but works by Balhae authors are extremely scarce.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a13-42)

According to the _[Old Book of Tang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Book_of_Tang "Old Book of Tang")_, the founder of Balhae, Da Zuorong or Dae Joyeong, was a Mohe but adds that he was _gaoli biezhong_ (高麗別種).[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a12-94)[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-Link-95) Literally speaking, _biezhong_ means "separate kind."[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a12-94) The term _gaoli biezhong_ has been interpreted in different ways. Korean historians believe it means "a branch of the Goguryeo people" while Japanese and Chinese researchers believe it means "distinct from Goguryeo".[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-96)[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a12-94) Lei Yijie and Yao Yucheng argue that _biezhong_ does not indicate ethnicity at all and was used in Chinese official sources in situations where different groups with similar culture occupied the same area.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a12-94) Kaizaburo Hino suggests that Da Zuorong or Dae Joyeoung was a member of the Mohe that were incorporated into the Goguryeo populace, as the need to explicitly mention _gaoli biezhong_ would have otherwise been unnecessary.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-97)

> The Bohai Mohe Da Zuorong was originally a branch of the race of Koguryŏ. Once Koguryŏ had been annihilated \[by the Tang\], Da Zuorong led his relatives to a new home at Yingzhou 營州 \[near modern Chaoyang Municipality 朝陽市, Liaoning\]. In the \[Tang\] Wansui Tongtian 萬歲通天 period \[696–697\], the Khitan Li Jinzhong 李盡忠 rebelled, and Zuorong and the Mohe Qisi Biyu 乞四比羽 each led a group of refugees fleeing east, fortifying an inaccessible position for self-protection. Once Li Jinzhong had died, \[Empress Wu\] Zetian 武則天 ordered Li Kaigu 李楷固 \[d.u.\], Great General of the Right Guards of the Jade Strategy, to lead troops in an attack on \[Li Jinzhong's\] remaining followers. He first defeated and executed Qisi Biyu, and then crossed the Tianmen Range 天門嶺 to press in on Da Zuorong. Zuorong united Koguryŏ and Mohe groups to repel Li Kaigu. The \[Tang\] army suffered a major defeat, and Li Kaigu escaped to return \[to Tang territory\]. All of the Khitan and Xi submitted to the Turks, and with the route \[to Zuorong's position\] cut off, Wu Zutian was able to attack. Da Zuorong thereupon led his group to the east, fortifying the former territory of the Guilou 桂婁 and buttressed by Mt. Dongmou 東牟山, where they built a wall for a settlement.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a11-65)[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-Link-95)

According to Han Ciu-cheol, the _Old Book_ states that the customs of the Balhae, such as coming of age ceremonies, marriages, funerals, and memorial rites, were the same as with the Goguryeo, which Korean historians often cite to support their arguments.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-auto3-98) However the original quotation in the _Old Book_ does not make any specific mention of the social customs that were similar, and compares Balhae not just to Goguryeo but also to the Khitans: "The customs and habits were the same as in Goryeo and Khitan. It had its script, books and documents."[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-99) According to Kim Eun Gug, the _Old Book_ indicates that the Tang court bestowed [Mu of Balhae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mu_of_Balhae "Mu of Balhae") the title of "King of Kyeru Commandery," which is significant because Kyeru (Gyeru) was the name that was used to denote old Goguryeo territory. Kim Eun Gug believe this indicates that the Tang recognized Balhae as Goguryeo's successor.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-100)[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-101)

The _[New Book of Tang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Book_of_Tang "New Book of Tang")_, compiled in the 11th century, refers to Dae Joyeong and his state as Sumo Mohe, affiliated with Goguryeo.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-102)[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim20158-103) The _New Book_ states that "Parhae was originally the Mohe \[tribes\] who had submitted to Koguryŏ; the clan surname \[of its rulers\] was Da."[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a13-42)[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-104) Chinese scholars have argued that Balhae's founder was a member of the Sumo Mohe and Balhae's royalty were Mohe rather than Goguryeo, based on this account. Yun challenged this by arguing that though he may have been Mohe, they "would have already undergone a substantial process of Koguryŏ-ization" while providing military service to Goguryeo over two generations.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a13-42) Han Ciu-cheol notes that Chinese historians often cite the _New Book_ in their arguments, whereas Korean historians often cite the _Old Book_ due to their conflicting viewpoints on the ethnicity of Balhae's founder as well as the nature of Balhae's society.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-auto3-98)

According to Sloane, Tang sources divided Balhae's population into two categories, Goguryeo and Mohe. The royalty and upper class were composed of Goguryeo remnants while the majority of Balhae's population were Mohe.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014366%E2%80%93367-105)

According to [Ch'oe Ch'i-wŏn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%27oe_Ch%27i-w%C5%8Fn "Ch'oe Ch'i-wŏn") (b. 857), who was from Silla, the people of Balhae were Mohe.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim2011293-106) In the conflict between the joint Tang-Silla forces against Balhae, Silla described Balhae as "rebellious barbarians."[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim2011a351-107) Sillan aristocracy tended to view the Balhae population as consisting of solely Mohe people, but this could be due to the antagonistic relations between the two states causing the Sillan nobility to ignore Goguryeo elements of Balhae ethnic composition.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim20158-103)

> As we know in relation to the origin of the Bohai people, when Gouli (Koguryŏ) was not yet destroyed, they \[the Bohai people\] were the useless tribe of Mohe. Many tribes were the same; its name was that of the small barbarian nation Sumo, and in the past \[this tribe\], being in competition with Gouli, moved to the inner region \[China\].[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim20158-103)

The _[Samguk sagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samguk_sagi "Samguk sagi")_, written in the 12th century by [Kim Pusik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Pusik "Kim Pusik"), did not consider Balhae a Korean state.[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim2011292-108) The _[Samguk yusa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samguk_yusa "Samguk yusa")_, a 13th-century collection of Korean history and legends, describes Dae as a Sumo Mohe leader. However, it gives another account of Dae being a former Goguryeo general, citing a now-lost Sillan record.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-109)[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-110) Alexander Kim considers this unlikely since Goguryeo fell in 668 while Dae died in 719, and young men could not receive the rank of general.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim2011297-111)

The _[Ruijū Kokushi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruij%C5%AB_Kokushi "Ruijū Kokushi")_, a 9th-century Japanese text, says that when Balhae was founded, it spanned 2,000 _li_ and was filled with villages, each of which were Mohe tribes.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-112)[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim2011292-108)

> In length and breadth it measures two thousand _li_. It has no prefectures, counties, state lodges, or post stations, but has villages everywhere. All are Mohe tribes. Among its subjects, Mohe are many while natives are few. In all cases, natives are made village headmen; in large villages, they are called Commanders-in-Chief, in smaller \[villages\], Prefects, and below that, all subjects are called Chieftains.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a16-113)

According to Pak Se-yong, the "natives" in the passage refer to people of Goguryeo, and therefore, all officials in the local and central government were Koguryŏ aristocrats. This has been challenged by Han Ciu-cheol, who argues that the term for "native" (J. _dojin_ 土人) should be read as "literati" (J. _shijin_ 士人) instead. The resulting translation would therefore be: "Everywhere there were villages and those villages were all Malgal settlements. There are many Malgal among the commoners but there are few literati."[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a17-114) Han notes that in some editions of the _Ruijū Kokushi_, _dojin_ was replaced with _shijin_ instead. However, Han's position is opposed by Fu Langyun, who argues that _dojin_ does not refer to either Mohe or Goguryeo people but rather, a separate group of native inhabitants, while Yang Jun argues that _dojin_ refers to the Sumo Mohe, who were the natives and referred to themselves as such.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a17-114)

Japanese diplomatic communications with Balhae recognized it as a "state of Go\[gu\]ryeo."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-Kim2012-2) In a diplomatic mission to Japan in 727 or 728, the Balhae envoy said that Balhae has "recovered the lost land of Goguryeo and inherited the old traditions of Buyeo."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-Kim2012-2)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a14-43) [Mun of Balhae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mun_of_Balhae "Mun of Balhae") referred to himself as "King of Goryeo" but Reisa Shimoda suggests that this was not to restore the old name, as noted in the _[Dai Nihonshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dai_Nihonshi "Dai Nihonshi")_, but as a means of gaining Japan's favor by invoking Goryeo.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-115) Examples of Balhae envoys being referred to as Goryeo envoys and Balhae kings as the king of Goryeo are found extensively in the [Nara Period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nara_Period "Nara Period") but have not been found during the later [Heian Period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heian_Period "Heian Period").[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-116) According to Japanese historian Shiratori Kurakichi, 26 of the 85 emissaries dispatched to Japan by Parhae bore the typical Goguryeo surname of Ko (Go), which is still commonly used in Korea, which indicated a substantial Goguryeo presence in Balhae culture.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-117) Some Korean historians believe that a record in the _[Shoku Nihongi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoku_Nihongi "Shoku Nihongi")_ implies that the Balhae and Silla language were mutually intelligible: a student sent from Silla to Japan for Japanese language interpreter training assisted a diplomatic envoy from Balhae in communicating with the audience of a Japanese court.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-Han2008-118)[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-u-119)

Chinese scholars have argued that the use of single-chambered brick tombs shows Tang influence. These single-chamber brick tombs appear later in Balhae history and appear less frequently. It was probably not due to a lack of other material that brick was used as stone was widely used around the capital sites. In the early 1980s, Nishikawa Hiroshi argued that early Balhae tombs resembled the Balhae practice of joint burial and reburial. Earthen pit tombs have also been interpreted as Mohe practice by Japanese and Chinese scholarship. Yun Jae-Woon argues that vertical-slit pits were used by non-elites universally and that earth tombs were more common in early Balhae, but many features found in Balhae tombs are influenced by Goguryeo, such as above ground structures, roof tiles, and the use of stone.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a23%E2%80%9325-120) According to Han Ciu-cheol, Balhae's ruling class used stone lined tombs, stone chambers, and stone coffins which had been used by Goguryeo's ruling class.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-auto3-98)

Balhae's ceramic vessels in China have been divided into three stylistic types: Mohe, Goguryeo, and Tang. Early Balhae vessels were mainly categorized as of the Mohe type and used as evidence that Balhae was founded by Mohe. Chinese archaeologists argue that the geographic distribution of Balhae's ceramics match that of the "wide-mouthed, deep-bellied jars of coarse black-brown material" from proceeding centuries in the same area. Chinese archaeologists refer to the previous culture as "Tongren Culture" while texts refer to the inhabitants of the area as "Mohe" and "Wuji" (K. Mulgil, J. Mukkitsu). Later, Balhae pottery show technical improvement and the introduction of three-color glazes.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a26%E2%80%9327-121)

Wei Cuncheng argues that "deep-bellied cylindrical jars and bowls" were prevalent from before the 8th century until the 10th or 11th centuries, especially in small burials and outside the capitals. He argues that these are indicative of the Sumo Mohe tribe and demonstrate that the majority of Balhae's population, particularly during its founding, was culturally, and ethnically Mohe. Yun Jae-Woon argues that similar jars have been found at Goguryeo sites but it is unclear if these are of the same type and could date later than the jars Wei refers to. Yun also argues that the jars do not indicate ethnic difference and "should be seen as reflecting social and cultural differences between elites and non-elites and between the center and the provinces."[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a27-122)

Lee Byeong Gun argues that the pairing of flat riverside settlements with hilltop redoubts distinguishes Balhae settlements from Tang Chinese urban planning. To Lee, mountain sites represent the indigenous culture of Goguryeo, supporting the continuity and succession from Goguryeo to Balhae. Chinese scholarship does not portray Tang and Balhae styles as identical but rather, emphasizes influences on Balhae.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a20-123) Round eave-end roof tiles show Goguryeo influence while ceramic ornamentation show Tang influence. The patterns of Balhae style eave-end roof tiles have been used in China for reconstruction of a Tang dynasty site in [Shanxi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanxi "Shanxi").[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a20%E2%80%9321-124) Korean scholars argue that the existence of heated platforms in some building sites in the Balhae capital indicate Balhae succession from Goguryeo. Chinese scholars point to the existence of pit dwellings as examples of Mohe culture.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a21%E2%80%9322-125) No consensus has been reached yet on the cultural origin of the Lingguang Pagoda located in [Changbai County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changbai_County "Changbai County"), the only surviving above ground example of Balhae architecture.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae_controversies#cite_note-FOOTNOTESloane2014a22%E2%80%9323-126)

Preface Multiple editions The first edition of this book was published in hardback in 1993 as China, Korea and Japan: the rise of civilization in East Asia (London, Thames & Hudson, 1993). In 1999, that version was reprinted in paperback under a better title using the word ‘archaeology’: The rise of civilization in East Asia: the archaeology of China, Korea and Japan (London, Thames & Hudson, 1999). Only very minor corrections within word count were made in the paperback edition, and these first two editions have exactly the same pagination and format; I refer to them collectively as ‘CKJ’. This current offering is a revised edition of the content of CKJ after twenty years. Most of the text has been rewritten; many photographs are also replaced, since those originally published in CKJ mainly belonged to the Thames & Hudson files. Colleagues and others have been most helpful in supplying photos and illustrations with proper copyright for inclusion here. Other illustrations, particularly line drawings, have been re-used from CKJ when nothing better has superseded them. In trying to bring this book up to date, I have encountered three hurdles. One is the vast amount of information published since 1990, resulting in more detail, in changes of emphasis in the available data, and in changes in our perspectives in viewing those data. Second, it was much easier to condense broad swaths of prehistory into a few paragraphs when I knew less myself. Third, method and theory have become more important in writing any kind of archaeology, so that the setting of East Asian data within these frameworks has become necessary. Data were intentionally selected to illustrate general trends in development, areas of scholarly disagreement, and outstanding florescence in material culture – with a vision of an “East Asian Civilization” at the end of the process. With the increase of information available on the internet, it is no longer necessary nor feasible to indulge in long descriptions of individual sites or cultures – easily obtained elsewhere with a couple of clicks and most likely with enviable color illustrations. Thus, this revision is much more technical than CKJ, though it remains an introduction and is not designed to be comprehensive despite the inevitable generalizations. I have striven to follow the same pattern of discussion as in CKJ, and have also tried to identify corrections to CKJ (in footnotes), particularly in terms of advances in knowledge. I hope that the general reader and beginning student will find the deeper level of detail in this volume still accessible within the overall framework of tracing the development of East Asian societies from the Palaeolithic to the early

historic period. If not, read CKJ first! If so, the framework of time/space/content outlined here will allow deeper forays into those areas of particular interest to the new reader via the Further Readings and the Bibliography. This series of books has two main readerships: those coming from East Asian studies, and those from archaeology. Accommodations have been made for both groups: explanation of many archaeological methods and concepts for the former, and source information from English-language works as much as possible for the latter. Where is East Asia? Commonly this term refers to the territories of the modern states of China, Korea and Japan. However, state boundaries are meaningful to prehistory only in terms of the investigating organizations and the languages in which reports are written today. The locations of sites are usually (but not in this work) given in terms of modern prefectures and provinces of the individual countries, which are displayed in the maps in Figures 2.1–2.3 for reference. Because of the boundary (or boundless) problem, we will often stray into Mongolia, the Altai, Central Asia and Vietnam to illuminate what was happening in East Asia as strictly defined. However, this work does not deal much with the archaeology of the far west and south Mainland; in particular, Silk Road archaeology is entirely another field which deserves separate treatment.

Dating preferences One of the most difficult things for newcomers to archaeology anywhere is shifting between BP or ‘years ago’ and BC/AD (BCE/CE) dates – a 2000-year difference. BP (before present) specifically refers to the ‘present’ as 1950 – the date when radiocarbon dating began – and is used primarily for radiocarbon dates (Appendix A). There are several such methods of scientific dating, and dates tend to be given in ‘years ago’ (BP), whereas archaeologists tend to talk in terms of calendar dates BC/AD or BCE/CE. This book will use two forms of notation: ‘years ago’, and BC/AD; dates for the Pleistocene and Palaeolithic are given as ‘mya’ (million years ago) and ‘kya’ (thousand i  The preface to the paperback edition (p. 15) gives out-of-date information concerning the University of Durham. The current URL for the Society for East Asian Archaeology is www.SEAA-web.org. Dates for an Early Palaeolithic in Japan have since been discredited.

Preface  xv

years ago) in Chapters 3 and 4. Beginning in Chapter 5, dates will be given as BC/ AD. Remember, a 2000-year span separates these two systems of ‘years ago’ and ‘BC’, so that the newly dated end of the Pleistocene (see below) at 11.6kya is 9600 BC – quite different from the previously used Pleistocene/Holocene divide of 10,000 years ago or 8000 BC. As far as possible, calibrated dates (see Appendix A) are cited (as cal.), but often it is difficult to tell from publications whether they are calibrated or not, and conventional radiocarbon dates produced decades ago often are missing metadata that allows them to be calibrated. Thus one must remain flexible in dealing with dates due to the many problems in their calculation and presentation; those presented here are only approximations. Other conventions adopted here are using a small ‘c’ to denote century/centuries and a small ‘m’ for millennium/millennia, as in 5c BC (5th century BC) or 1m AD (1st millennium AD). This saves a lot of text space! A different problem surrounds the designation BC/AD. These are Christian terms specifically referring to Before Christ and Anno Domini (Year of our Lord). There is a recent trend to amend these to BCE (Before Common Era) and CE (Common Era) to get away from the Christian implications. However, this does not solve the problem since the dividing line is still the birth year of Christ in the Gregorian calendarii – very inappropriate for East Asia where there is nothing ‘in common’ about the Christian division. This book will follow the original system of BC/AD merely because it is more visually distinct and therefore potentially less confusing. The date 0 AD refers here to the dividing line between BC/AD, though there is no Year 0; and while it is proper to put ‘AD’ before the date, I am choosing to put it after, as with BC. The overall chronological scheme for East Asia is offered in Table 0.1 (below).

Language issues Out of respect for tradition, I have generally presented East Asian personal names with surname first and given name last. But many East Asian scholars now adopt Western practice and write their surname last. To avoid confusion, when both occur together, I give the surname in small capitals (e.g., Abe Satoshi, Li Liu). Some early individuals are known by only one name. Many abbreviations frequently used in this book are explained in Appendix B. Romanization of foreign words in this book employs the Pinyin system for Chinese, the McCune-Reischauer system for Korean, and the Revised Hepburn system for Japanese. These systems are explained, with examples given, in Appendix C. • For Chinese (indicated in the text as C.), Pinyin is the government-approved transcription system in use since 1979. Wade-Giles, the system previously used by most Western scholars of China, is found in older works and can still crop up in texts by recalcitrant scholars. Chapter 1 Orientation

Prior to nation-states, geography was broad and unbounded, with peoples traveling and intermixing at will. Despite the development of multitudinous regional ‘cultures’ and even states across East Asia, interaction was the name of the game. Thus geography is the basic referent for discussing human occupation of the landscape (Figure 1.1). Since most archaeological reports, however, discuss finds in terms of modern provinces and prefectures, these are given in Figures 2.1–2.3. Now, let’s take a tour of East Asia to get oriented.

Grounding Starting from the Yellow Sea The central geographical point of reference for this text is the ‘Yellow Sea Basin’. The Yellow Sea grades into the East China Sea to the south, but for our purposes, the Yellow Sea Basin is defined as beginning at the Shanghai Delta in the southwest and extending to southern Kyushu in the southeast. The Ryukyu Islands are sandwiched by the East China Sea on the west and the Pacific Ocean on the east. The Yellow Sea is made yellow by the deposits of loess coming off the China Mainland and deposited into Bohai Bay in the northwest, the Bay being formed by the pinching in of the Shandongi and Liaodong peninsulae.ii The Yellow River has changed course many times over the millennia, sometimes draining into the Yellow Sea below the Shandong peninsula. The northeastern Bohai Bay receives the Liao River runoff, draining the Manchurian Basin. East of the Korean Peninsula lies the Eastern Sea, more commonly known as the Japan Sea. The Korean Peninsula and Japanese Islands are divided i  This is the usual English name, as it forms part of Shandong province; its official name is the Jiaodong peninsula. ii  Capitalized Peninsula is reserved for the Korean Peninsula; all others will be in lower case. Both Shandong and Liaodong are used later as geographical locators that take in more than just their peninsulae.

These will simply be referred to here as the Korea Strait. Several terms have been devised here to refer to parts of East Asia without using modern nation-state designations. The ‘China Mainland’ (or just ‘Mainland’) refers to most of the modern state of China, though the far west (Xinjiang province), the southeastern coast, and Tibet are not dealt with here. I devised the terms ‘Pen/ Insular’ and ‘Pen/Insulae’ to refer to the combined areas of the Korean Peninsula and the Japanese Islands, whereas the term ‘Peninsula(r)’ (capitalized) is used specifically to refer to the Korean Peninsula; other peninsulae are not capitalized to make that difference clear. On that Peninsula, names of the five major rivers (the Yalu, Taedong, Han, Kum and Nakdong) are used as geographical locators. The term ‘continent(al)’ embraces both the China Mainland and the Korean Peninsula, and possibly other regions, in contrast to the Japanese Islands. Within the Japanese archipelago, areas on the main island (Honshu) are often referred to by sub-regions: Tohoku, Kanto, Chubu, Tokai, Hokuriku, Kinai, and San’in. In addition, the Inland iii
