[Hanja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanja "Hanja"): 古朝鮮; [RR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revised_Romanization_of_Korean "Revised Romanization of Korean"): _Gojoseon_; [MR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCune%E2%80%93Reischauer "McCune–Reischauer"): _Kojosŏn_) and its contemporary name **Joseon** ([Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"): 조선; [Hanja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanja "Hanja"): 朝鮮; [RR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revised_Romanization_of_Korean "Revised Romanization of Korean"): _Joseon_; [MR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCune%E2%80%93Reischauer "McCune–Reischauer"): _Chosŏn_), was the first kingdom on the [Korean Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea "Korea"). According to [Korean mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_mythology "Korean mythology"), the kingdom was established by the legendary king [Tan'gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tan%27gun "Tan'gun"). Old Chosŏn possessed the most advanced culture in the Korean Peninsula at the time and was an important marker in the progression towards the more centralized states of later periods. The addition of _Go_ (고; 古), meaning "old" or "ancient", is used in [historiography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historiography "Historiography") to distinguish the kingdom from the [Joseon dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseon "Joseon"), founded in 1392 CE. According to the _[Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samguk_yusa "Samguk yusa")_, Old Chosŏn was established in 2333 BCE by Tan'gun, who was said to be born from the heavenly prince [Hwanung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwanung "Hwanung") and a bear-woman, [Ungnyeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ungnyeo "Ungnyeo"). While Tan'gun is a mythological figure of whose existence no concrete evidence has been found,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Gojoseon-1) some interpret his legend as reflections of the sociocultural situations involving the kingdom's early development.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-KimJB-2) Regardless, the account of Tan'gun has played an important role in the development of Korean identity. Today, the founding date of Old Chosŏn is officially celebrated as [National Foundation Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaecheonjeol "Gaecheonjeol") in [North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea")[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-3) and [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"). Some sources claim that in the 12th century BCE, following the establishment of Old Chosŏn, [Jizi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jizi "Jizi") (also known as Gija), a [sage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sage_/(philosophy/) "Sage (philosophy)") who belonged to the royal family from the [Shang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty "Shang dynasty"), immigrated to the northern part of the Korean Peninsula and became the founder of [Gija Joseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gija_Joseon "Gija Joseon").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-:0-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-:1-5) There are many interpretations of Old Chosŏn and Gija Joseon as well as debates regarding Gija Joseon's existence.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-6) In 194 BCE, the ruling dynasty of Old Chosŏn was overthrown by [Wi Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiman_of_Gojoseon "Wiman of Gojoseon") (Wei Man in Chinese), a refugee from the [Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") vassal state of [Yan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yan_Kingdom_/(Han_dynasty/) "Yan Kingdom (Han dynasty)"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-11) who then established [Wiman Joseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiman_Joseon "Wiman Joseon"). In 108 BCE, the Han dynasty, under [Emperor Wu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Wu_of_Han "Emperor Wu of Han"), [invaded and conquered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gojoseon%E2%80%93Han_War "Gojoseon–Han War") Wiman Joseon. The Han established [four commanderies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Commanderies_of_Han "Four Commanderies of Han") to administer the former Old Chosŏn territory. After the fragmentation of the Han Empire during the [3rd century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3rd_century "3rd century") and the subsequent [chaotic 4th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upheaval_of_the_Five_Barbarians "Upheaval of the Five Barbarians"), the area escaped Chinese control and was conquered by [Goguryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo "Goguryeo") in 313 CE. The capital of Old Chosŏn was [Wanggeom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wanggeom-seong "Wanggeom-seong") (modern [Pyongyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongyang "Pyongyang")) from at least the 2nd century BCE. In the southern region of the Korean Peninsula, the [Jin state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jin_/(Korean_state/) "Jin (Korean state)") arose by the 3rd century BCE.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Met-12) There are three different main founding myths concerning Old Chosŏn, which revolve around Tan'gun, Gija, or Wi Man.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-bar0-10-13) [![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Baitou_Mountain_Tianchi.jpg/250px-Baitou_Mountain_Tianchi.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baitou_Mountain_Tianchi.jpg) [Heaven Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaven_Lake "Heaven Lake") of [Baekdu Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baekdu_Mountain "Baekdu Mountain"), where Dangun's father is said to have descended from heaven The myths revolving around Tan'gun were recorded in the later Korean work _[Samguk yusa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samguk_yusa "Samguk yusa")_ of the 13th century.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-bar0-11-14) This work states that [Tan'gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tan%27gun "Tan'gun"), the offspring of a heavenly prince and a bear-woman, founded Old Chosŏn in 2333 BCE, and was succeeded by Gija (Qizi) after King Wu of Zhou had placed him onto the throne in 1122 BCE.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-bar0-11-14) A similar account is found in _[Jewang Ungi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewang_Ungi "Jewang Ungi")_. According to the legend, the Lord of Heaven, [Hwanin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwanin "Hwanin") had a son, [Hwanung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwanung "Hwanung"), who descended to [Baekdu Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baekdu_Mountain "Baekdu Mountain") and founded the city of Shinsi. Then a bear and a tiger came to Hwanung and said that they wanted to become people. Hwanung said to them that if they went in a cave and lived there for 100 days while only eating [mugwort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugwort "Mugwort") and garlic he would change them into human beings. However, about halfway through the 100 days the tiger gave up and ran out of the cave. The bear, in contrast, successfully restrained herself and became a beautiful woman named [Ungnyeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ungnyeo "Ungnyeo"). Hwanung later married Ungnyeo, and she gave birth to [Tan'gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tan%27gun "Tan'gun").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-15) While the Tan'gun story is considered to be a myth,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Gojoseon-1) it is believed it is a mythical synthesis of a series of historical events relating to the founding of Old Chosŏn.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-enc.daum.net-16) There are various theories on the origin of this myth.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes20019%E2%80%9314-17) Seo and Kang (2002) believe the Tan'gun myth is based on integration of two different tribes, an invasive sky-worshipping Bronze Age tribe and a native bear-worshipping neolithic tribe, that led to the foundation of Old Chosŏn.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%EC%84%9C%EA%B0%952002-18) Lee K. B. (1984) believes 'Tan'gun-wanggeom' was a title borne by successive leaders of Old Chosŏn.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee1984-19) Tan'gun is said to have founded Old Chosŏn around 2333 BCE, based on the descriptions of the _[Samguk yusa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samguk_yusa "Samguk yusa")_, _[Jewang Ungi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewang_Ungi "Jewang Ungi")_, _[Tongguk t'onggam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongguk_t%27onggam "Tongguk t'onggam")_ and the _[Annals of the Joseon Dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annals_of_the_Joseon_Dynasty "Annals of the Joseon Dynasty")_.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-%EB%8F%99%EA%B5%AD%ED%86%B5%EA%B0%90%EB%8B%A8%EA%B8%B0%EC%82%B0%EC%A0%95-20) The date differs among historical sources, although all of them put it during the mythical [Emperor Yao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Yao "Emperor Yao")'s reign (traditional dates: 2357 BCE? – 2256 BCE?). _Samguk yusa_ says Tan'gun ascended to the throne in the 50th year of the legendary Yao's reign, _Annals of the King Sejong_ says the first year, and _Tongguk t'onggam_ says the 25th year.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-21) In the 7th century BCE, the [Yan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yan_/(state/) "Yan (state)") pioneered the Northeast regions. According to _The Growth of Yan_ and _The Context of Guanzi_,[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-22) it can be presumed that Old Chosŏn grew through trade in this era. It is estimated that Old Chosŏn developed so far as to be able to wage [war against the Yan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gojoseon%E2%80%93Yan_War "Gojoseon–Yan War") in the 4th century BCE. [Gija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jizi "Jizi"), a man from the period of the [Shang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty "Shang dynasty"), allegedly fled to the Korean peninsula in 1122 BCE during the fall of the Shang to the [Zhou dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_dynasty "Zhou dynasty") and founded [Gija Joseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gija_Joseon "Gija Joseon").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarnes20019%E2%80%9310-23) Gija Joseon is recognized and mentioned in the earliest surviving Chinese record, _[Records of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Records_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Records of the Three Kingdoms")_. No contemporary Korean sources existed for Kija Chosŏn, and the oldest sources produced in Korea were from the Goryeo dynasty. The earliest Korean record about Kija Chosŏn can be seen from _[Samguk Yusa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samguk_Yusa "Samguk Yusa")_,[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-24)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-25) By the middle of [Goryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goryeo "Goryeo") dynasty, a state cult had developed around Gija.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Shim_2002-26) The _[Dongsa Gangmok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dongsa_Gangmok "Dongsa Gangmok")_ of 1778 described Gija's activities and contributions in Old Chosŏn. The records of Gija refer to [Eight Prohibitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight_Prohibitions "Eight Prohibitions") (범금팔조; 犯禁八條), that are recorded by the _[Book of Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Han "Book of Han")_ and evidence a hierarchical society with legal protections of private property.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-daum-27) In pre-modern Korea, Gija represented the authenticating presence of Chinese civilization. Until the 12th century CE, Koreans commonly believed that Tan'gun bestowed upon Korea its people and basic culture, while Gija gave Korea its high culture, and presumably, standing as a legitimate civilisation.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Korea_2010,_pp._4-28) Many modern experts have denied Gija Joseon's existence for various reasons, mainly due to contradicting archaeological evidence and anachronistic historical evidence.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-29)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Shim_2002-26) They point to the _[Bamboo Annals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamboo_Annals "Bamboo Annals")_ and the _[Analects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analects "Analects")_ of Confucius, which were among the first works to mention Gija, but do not mention his migration to Old Chosŏn.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-30) Gija Joseon might have just existed as a symbol of the pre-[Qin dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_dynasty "Qin dynasty") migrants who escaped the chaos of the [Warring States period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warring_States_period "Warring States period").[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-31) [Wi Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi_Man "Wi Man") was a military officer of the [Yan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Yan "Principality of Yan") of northeastern China who fled to the northern Korean peninsula in 195 BCE from the encroaching [Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-bar0-11-14) He founded a principality with [Wanggeom-seong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wanggeom-seong "Wanggeom-seong") as its capital, which is thought to be in the region of present-day Pyongyang.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-bar0-11-14) The 3rd-century Chinese text _[Weilüe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil%C3%BCe "Weilüe")_ of the _[Sanguozhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanguozhi "Sanguozhi")_ recorded that Wi Man usurped [King Jun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jun_of_Gojoseon "Jun of Gojoseon") and thus took over the kingship of Old Chosŏn.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-bar0-11-14)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-32) ### Academic perspectives \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Old_Chos%C5%8Fn&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Academic perspectives")\] Old Chosŏn mythology and history can be divided into three phases, Tan'gun, Gija Joseon, and Wi Man Joseon.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-c-bar0-12-33) 1. Kang & Macmillan (1980), Sohn et al. (1970), Kim J.B. (1980), Han W.K. (1970), Yun N. H. (1985), Lee K.B. (1984), Lee J.B. (1987) viewed the Tan'gun myth as a native product of proto-Koreans, although it is not always associated with Old Chosŏn.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-c-bar0-12-33) Kim J.B. (1987) rejected the Tan'gun myth's association with Old Chosŏn and pushes it further back to the Neolithic period. Sohn et al. (1970) suggested that the Tan'gun myth is associated with the [Dongyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dongyi "Dongyi"), whom they viewed as the ancestors of Koreans. Kim C. (1948) suggested the Tan'gun myth had a Chinese origin, tracing it to a Han dynasty tomb in the [Shandong peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shandong_peninsula "Shandong peninsula"). 2. Gardiner (1969), Henderson (1959), McCune (1962) considered the Gija myth to be a later conflation. Sohn et al. (1970) dismissed the Gija story as a Chinese fabrication. On the other hand, Hatada (1969), gave Old Chosŏn a Chinese identity, exclusively ascribed it to the Gija myth, and moved it to the 3rd century BCE.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-c-bar0-12-33) Shim Jae-Hoon (2002) accepted the eastward migration of Gija, but denied the relationship between Gija and Joseon, suggesting that the existence of Old Chosŏn could not be extended to the second millennium BCE.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Shim_2002-26) 3. Kim C.W. (1966), Han W.K. (1970), Choi M.L. (1983, 1984, 1985, 1992), Han W.K. (1984), Kim J.B. (1987), Lee K.B. (1984) accepted Wi Man as a historical figure.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-c-bar0-12-33) Gardiner (1969) questioned authenticity of the Wi Man myth, although he mentioned there were interactions between Old Chosŏn and the Han dynasty and social unrest in the area during that time period.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-c-bar0-12-33) The first extant Korean text to mention Kija (the Korean pronunciation of Jizi) was [Kim Pusik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Pusik "Kim Pusik")'s _[Samguk sagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samguk_sagi "Samguk sagi")_ (completed in 1145), which claimed that Kija had been enfeoffed in Haedong (海東: Korea) by the Zhou court, but commented that this account was uncertain because of the brevity of the sources.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Shim_276-34) Only in the thirteenth century did Korean texts start to integrate Kija more fully into Korean history. The _[Samguk yusa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samguk_yusa "Samguk yusa")_ (1281) explained that after being enfeoffed by [King Wu of Zhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Wu_of_Zhou "King Wu of Zhou"), Kija replaced [Dangun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dangun "Dangun")'s descendants as the ruler of Old Chosŏn, whereas _[Jewang Ungi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewang_Ungi "Jewang Ungi")_ (1287) identified Tan'gun and Kija as the first rulers of former and latter Joseon respectively.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Shim_276-34) Most premodern Korean historians after that accepted that Kija had replaced another indigenous power (represented by Tan'gun) in Old Joseon.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Shim_276-34) In 1102, during the [Goryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goryeo "Goryeo") period, [King Sukjong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukjong_of_Goryeo "Sukjong of Goryeo") built a [mausoleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mausoleum "Mausoleum") to Kija in a place near [Pyongyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongyang "Pyongyang") that had been identified as [Kija's tomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kija%27s_Tomb "Kija's Tomb").[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-35)[Sadang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancestral_shrine "Ancestral shrine") for Kija called Kijasa (箕子祠) was also built in [Pyongyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongyang "Pyongyang").[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-36) The mausoleum was rebuilt in 1324 and was repaired in 1355, but the cult of Kija spread most widely after the establishment of the Joseon Dynasty in 1392. Because Joseon's state ideology was [Neo-Confucianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Confucianism "Neo-Confucianism") borrowed from China, Joseon intellectuals promoted Kija as a [culture hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_hero "Culture hero") who had raised Korean civilization to the same level as China.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Shim_277-37) By the mid-[Joseon dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseon_dynasty "Joseon dynasty"), the established view among historians traced Korean origins to Chinese refugees, considering Korean history that of a long series of kingdoms connected with China. As such, the [Gija Joseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gija_Joseon "Gija Joseon") and [Silla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silla "Silla") states were valorized, while the Old Chosŏn and [Goguryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo "Goguryeo") states were not considered as important.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-38) According to this view, the first state in Korea, [Gija Joseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gija_Joseon "Gija Joseon"), was founded by [Jizi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jizi "Jizi") in 1122 BCE, who was a disgruntled Chinese advisor to the [Shang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty "Shang dynasty"). The story of how he brought poetry, music, medicine, trade, and a political system to the Korean peninsula was conceived similarly to the proposed [Founding of Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_of_Rome "Founding of Rome") by the [Trojan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_War "Trojan War") refugee [Aeneas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneas "Aeneas").[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Simons70-39) But by the 1930s, under the influence of [Shin Chaeho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shin_Chaeho "Shin Chaeho")'s histories, the Jizi Korean founding story became less popular than that of [Tan'gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dangun "Dangun"), the son of a tiger and a bear – the latter being common in [Japanese folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_folklore "Japanese folklore") – who brought civilization to the Korean peninsula.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Simons70-39) Shin and the other historians who promulgated this myth had been influenced by [Daejonggyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daejonggyo "Daejonggyo"), a [new religious movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_religious_movement "New religious movement") which worshipped Tan'gun,[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-40) but attacked pre-annexation textbook narratives of Tan'gun which portrayed him as the brother of the Japanese god [Susanoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susanoo "Susanoo").[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-41) To Shin, Tan'gun was both the founder of the Korean _minjok_ and the first Korean state (_kuk_), and thus the necessary starting point for Korean history.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-42) In response to a challenge by the Japanese scholars [Shiratori Kurakichi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiratori_Kurakichi "Shiratori Kurakichi") and [Imanishi Ryū](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E4%BB%8A%E8%A5%BF%E9%BE%8D "ja:今西龍") of Tan'gun as a fabrication by the author of the _[Samguk yusa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samguk_yusa "Samguk yusa")_, nationalist historian [Choe Nam-seon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choe_Nam-seon "Choe Nam-seon") attacked [Japanese mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_mythology "Japanese mythology") as being built upon fabrications.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-43) By focusing on a mythological god which founded a "sacred race" (_shinsŏng chongjok_), Korean nationalist historiography aims to portray ancient Korea as a golden age of "gods and heroes" where Korea's cultural achievements rivaled those of China and Japan.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-44) Accordingly, Shin Chaeho elevated Tan'gun to play a similar role as did the [Yellow Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_Emperor "Yellow Emperor") in China and which [Amaterasu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaterasu "Amaterasu") does in Japan.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-45) [Choe Nam-seon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choe_Nam-seon "Choe Nam-seon"), according to his [Purham culture theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Purham_culture_theory&action=edit&redlink=1 "Purham culture theory (page does not exist)") ([ko](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EB%B6%88%ED%95%A8%EB%AC%B8%ED%99%94%EB%A1%A0 "ko:불함문화론")), places Tan'gun even above the Chinese and Japanese emperors, because those rulers were supposedly [Shamanistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shamanism "Shamanism") rulers of the ancient Korean "Părk" tradition.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-46) The Tan'gun story also lends credence to claims that Korean heritage is over 5000 years old. According to Hyung Il Pai, the popularity of Tan'gun studies can be said to "reflect the progressively ultra-nationalistic trend in Korean historical and archaeological scholarship today".[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-47) Shin Chaeho named [Mount Paektu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Paektu "Mount Paektu") in the [Changbai Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changbai_Mountains "Changbai Mountains") on the Sino-Korean border as a part of Korean heritage, by virtue of connection with the mythical Tan'gun. The mountain, however, was also claimed by the [Manchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchu_people "Manchu people") of the [Qing dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty "Qing dynasty") as part of their origin myth at least since the 17th century,[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Pai254-48)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-49) and the mountain range is considered sacred in [Han Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Chinese "Han Chinese") culture as well.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-50) This nationalist identification of Baekdu with Koreans was cemented by the operation of [Korean independence movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_independence_movement "Korean independence movement") partisans operating from the Chinese border and legitimized with associations to the history of the Old Chosŏn and [Balhae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae "Balhae") states.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Pai254-48) The Chinese civilizational connection to ancient Korea continues to be attacked by North Korean historians, who allege that the history of [Gija Joseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gija_Joseon "Gija Joseon") was "viciously distorted by the feudal ruling class, the [sadaejuui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadaejuui "Sadaejuui") followers, and the big-power chauvinists".[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-51) [![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Gojoseon_%28700_BC%29.png/250px-Gojoseon_%28700_BC%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gojoseon_/(700_BC/).png) Approximate location of Old Chosŏn in 700BCE The first mentions of Old Chosŏn are found in historical records of [Guanzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanzi_/(text/) "Guanzi (text)"). It locates Old Chosŏn around [Bohai Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohai_Bay "Bohai Bay") and mentions the state trading with [Qi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qi_/(state/) "Qi (state)") (齊) of China.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-52) The _[Zhanguoce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhanguoce "Zhanguoce")_, _[Shanhaijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanhaijing "Shanhaijing")_, and _[Shiji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiji "Shiji")_—containing some of its earliest records—refers to Joseon as a region, until the text _Shiji_ began referring it as a country from 195 BCE onwards.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-53) By the 4th century BCE, other states with defined political structures developed in the areas of the earlier Bronze Age "walled-town states"; Old Chosŏn was the most advanced of them in the peninsular region.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Met-12) The city-state expanded by incorporating other neighboring city-states by alliance or military conquest. Thus, a vast confederation of political entities between the Taedong and Liao rivers was formed. As Old Chosŏn evolved, so did the title and function of its leader, who came to be designated as "king" ([Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khan_/(title/) "Khan (title)")), in the tradition of the [Zhou dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_dynasty "Zhou dynasty"), around the same time as the [Yan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yan_/(state/) "Yan (state)") (燕) leader.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-naver-54) Records of that time mention the hostility between the feudal state in Northern China and the "confederated" kingdom of Old Chosŏn. Notably, a plan to attack the Yan beyond the Liao River frontier is recorded. This confrontation led to the decline and eventual downfall of Old Chosŏn, described in Yan records as "arrogant" and "cruel". But the ancient kingdom also appears as a prosperous Bronze Age civilization with a complex social structure, including a class of horse-riding warriors who contributed to the development of Old Chosŏn and its northern expansion[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-NYT-55) into most of the Liaodong basin. Around 300 BCE, Old Chosŏn lost significant western territory after a war with the Yan state, but this indicates Old Chosŏn was already a large enough state that it could wage war against the Yan and survive the loss of 2000 [li](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_/(unit/) "Li (unit)") (800 kilometers) of territory.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-daum-27) Old Chosŏn is thought to have relocated its capital to the [Pyongyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongyang "Pyongyang") region around this time.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-naver-54) ### Wiman Joseon and downfall \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Old_Chos%C5%8Fn&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Wiman Joseon and downfall")\] [![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Hangunhyeon.PNG/250px-Hangunhyeon.PNG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hangunhyeon.PNG) [Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") destroys [Wiman Joseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiman_Joseon "Wiman Joseon"), establishing [Four Commanderies of Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Commanderies_of_Han "Four Commanderies of Han") in the northern Korean peninsula. In 195 BCE, [King Jun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jun_of_Gojoseon "Jun of Gojoseon") appointed a refugee from Yan, [Wi Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiman_of_Gojoseon "Wiman of Gojoseon"), to guard the frontier.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-56) Wi Man later rebelled in 194 BCE and usurped the throne of Old Chosŏn. King Jun fled to [Jin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jin_/(Korean_state/) "Jin (Korean state)") in the south of the [Korean Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Peninsula "Korean Peninsula").[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Lee-57) In 109 BCE, [Emperor Wu of Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Wu_of_Han "Emperor Wu of Han") invaded near the [Liao River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liao_River "Liao River").[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Lee-57) A conflict would erupt in 109 BCE, when Wi Man's grandson King [Ugeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugeo "Ugeo") (우거왕; 右渠王) refused to let Jin's ambassadors through his territory in order to reach the Han dynasty. King Ugeo refused and had his son, Prince [Wi Jang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi_Jang "Wi Jang") (長降) escort the ambassador back home. However, when they got close to Han's borders, the ambassador assassinated [Wi Jang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi_Jang "Wi Jang") (長降) and claimed to Emperor Wu that he had defeated Joseon in battle. Emperor Wu, unaware of this deception, made him the military commander of the Commandery of Liaodong. The outraged King Ugeo made a raid on Liaodong and killed She He. Scholars also hypothesize that the initiation of war may also have been because the Han dynasty was concerned that Old Chosŏn would ally with the [Xiongnu against the Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han%E2%80%93Xiongnu_War "Han–Xiongnu War").[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-58) In response, Emperor Wu commissioned a two-pronged attack, one by land and one by sea, against Old Chosŏn.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Lee-57) The two forces attacking Old Chosŏn were unable to coordinate well with each other and suffered large losses. Eventually, the commands were merged, and Wanggeom fell in 108 BCE. Han took over the Old Chosŏn lands and established [Four Commanderies of Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Commanderies_of_Han "Four Commanderies of Han") in the western part of former Old Chosŏn.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Kang-59) Old Chosŏn disintegrated by the 1st century BCE as it gradually lost the control of its former fiefs. Many successor states sprang from its former territory, such as [Buyeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buyeo_kingdom "Buyeo kingdom"), [Okjeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okjeo "Okjeo"), [Dongye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Ye "Eastern Ye"). [Goguryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo "Goguryeo") and [Baekje](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baekje "Baekje") arose out from Buyeo. Around 2000 BCE, a new pottery culture of painted and chiseled design was developed. These people practiced agriculture in a settled communal life, probably organized into familial clans. Rectangular huts and increasingly larger [dolmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolmen "Dolmen") burial sites were found throughout the peninsula. Bronze daggers and mirrors have been excavated, and there is archaeological evidence of small walled-town states in this period.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-NYT-55)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-60) [Dolmens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolmen "Dolmen") and bronze daggers found in the area are uniquely Korean and cannot be found in China. A few dolmens are found in China, mostly in the [Shandong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shandong "Shandong") province.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-61) In the [Mumun pottery period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumun_pottery_period "Mumun pottery period") (1500 – 300 BCE), plain coarse pottery replaced earlier comb-pattern wares, possibly as a result of the influence of new populations migrating to Korea from Manchuria and Siberia. This type of pottery typically has thicker walls and displays a wider variety of shapes, indicating improvements in kiln technology.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Met-12) This period is sometimes called the "Korean Bronze Age", but bronze artifacts are relatively rare and regionalized until the 7th century BCE. Rice cultivation was extensive in the lower parts of South Korea and Manchuria in the periods between 1900 BCE to 200 CE. The beginning of the [Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") on the peninsula is usually said to be 1000 BCE, but estimates range from the 13th to 8th centuries BCE.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-62) Although the Korean Bronze Age culture derives from the [Liaoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning_bronze_dagger_culture "Liaoning bronze dagger culture") and Manchuria, it exhibits unique typology and styles, especially in ritual objects.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-63) By the 7th century BCE, a Bronze Age material culture with influences from Manchuria, eastern Mongolia, as well as Siberia and Scythian bronze styles, flourished on the peninsula. Korean bronzes contain a higher percentage of zinc than those of the neighboring bronze cultures. Bronze artifacts, found most frequently in burial sites, consist mainly of swords, spears, daggers, small bells, and mirrors decorated with geometric patterns.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Met-12)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-64) Gojoseon's development seems linked to the adoption of bronze technology. Its singularity finds its most notable expression in the idiosyncratic type of bronze swords, or "mandolin-shaped daggers" (비파형동검; 琵琶形銅劍). The mandolin-shape dagger is found in the regions of [Liaoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning "Liaoning"), [Hebei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebei "Hebei"), and Manchuria down to the Korean Peninsula. It suggests the existence of Old Chosŏn dominions. Remarkably, the shape of the "mandolin" dagger of Old Chosŏn differs significantly from the sword artifacts found in China. Megalithic dolmens appear in Korean peninsula and Manchuria around 2000 BCE to 400 BCE.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-65)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-66) Around 900 BCE, burial practices become more elaborate, a reflection of increasing social stratification. Goindol, the [dolmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolmen "Dolmen") tombs in Korea and Manchuria, comprising upright stones supporting a horizontal slab, are more numerous in Korea than in other parts of East Asia. Other new forms of burial are stone [cists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cist "Cist") (underground burial chambers lined with stone) and earthenware jar coffins. The bronze objects, pottery, and jade ornaments recovered from dolmens and stone cists indicate that such tombs were reserved for the elite class.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Met-12)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Unesco-67) Around the 6th century BCE, burnished red wares, made of a fine iron-rich clay and characterized by a smooth, lustrous surface, appear in dolmen tombs, as well as in domestic bowls and cups.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Met-12) #### Other types of tombs \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Old_Chos%C5%8Fn&action=edit§ion=14 "Edit section: Other types of tombs")\] In 1964, through a joint excavation by China and North Korea, Gangsang tomb (강상무덤; 崗上墓) and Nusang tomb (누상무덤; 樓上墓) were found in 1964 at the [Liaodong peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaodong_peninsula "Liaodong peninsula"). Nusang was found earlier prior to the excavation in 1958[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-68)[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-gangsang-69) Gangsang and Nusang tombs are considered to be burial [cairn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairn "Cairn") tombs of local nobilities of Old Chosŏn. Some consider the tombs as the evidences of the slavery that could have existed,[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-gangsang-69)[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-70) but others find that the evidences are inadequate and lacking to deduce such conclusion.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-71) Around this time, the state of [Jin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jin_/(Korean_state/) "Jin (Korean state)") occupied the southern part of the Korean peninsula. Very little is known about this state except that it was the apparent predecessor to the [Samhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samhan "Samhan") confederacies. Around 300 BCE, iron technology was introduced into Korea from Yan state. Iron was produced locally in the southern part of the peninsula by the 2nd century BCE. According to Chinese accounts, iron from the lower [Nakdong River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakdong_River "Nakdong River") in the southeast was valued throughout the peninsula and Japan.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-Met-12) In the book of Gogeumju ([古今注](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%8F%A4%E4%BB%8A%E6%B3%A8 "zh:古今注")) written by Cui Bao (崔豹) of the [Western Jin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jin_dynasty_/(266%E2%80%93420/) "Jin dynasty (266–420)") period, poetry called Gonghuyin (箜篌引) or [Gongmudohaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gongmudohaga&action=edit&redlink=1 "Gongmudohaga (page does not exist)") ([ko](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EA%B3%B5%EB%AC%B4%EB%8F%84%ED%95%98%EA%B0%80 "ko:공무도하가")) (공무도하가; 公無渡河歌) is said to be of Old Chosŏn origin.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn#cite_note-72) The poetry is as follows: 公無渡河 "Don't cross the river, my love." 公竟渡河 "My love eventually crossed the river.' 墮河而死 "Now that my love is drowned," 當奈公何 "There's nothing that I can do." Proto–Three Kingdoms of Korea ----------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Old_Chos%C5%8Fn&action=edit§ion=17 "Edit section: Proto–Three Kingdoms of Korea")\] Numerous small states and confederations arose from the remnants of Old Chosŏn, including [Goguryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo "Goguryeo"), the [Buyeo kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buyeo_kingdom "Buyeo kingdom"), [Okjeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okjeo "Okjeo"), and [Dongye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Ye "Eastern Ye"). Three of the Chinese commanderies fell to local resistance within a few decades, but the last, Nakrang, remained an important commercial and cultural outpost until it was destroyed by the expanding [Goguryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo "Goguryeo") in 313 CE. [Jun of Gojoseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jun_of_Gojoseon "Jun of Gojoseon") is said to have fled to the state of [Jin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jin_/(Korean_history/) "Jin (Korean history)") in the southern Korean Peninsula. [Jin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jin_/(Korean_history/) "Jin (Korean history)") developed into the [Samhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samhan "Samhan") confederacies, the beginnings of [Baekje](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baekje "Baekje") and [Silla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silla "Silla"), continuing to absorb migration from the north. The Samhan confederacies were [Mahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahan_confederacy "Mahan confederacy"), [Jinhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinhan_confederacy "Jinhan confederacy"), and [Byeonhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byeonhan_confederacy "Byeonhan confederacy"). King Jun ruled Mahan, which was eventually annexed by Baekje. The Beginnings of Korea’s History (Prehistoric Period – Gojoseon)
-----------------------------------------------------------------

The history of the Korean nation began in Manchuria and the Korean Peninsula when people started settling there 700,000 years ago. Representative historic sites associated with the Paleolithic Age, when people made tools of animal horns and chipped stone tools, include the Komun Moru ruins in Sangwon, Pyeongannam-do, the Jeongok-ri Site in Yeoncheon, Gyeonggi-do, the Seokjang-ri Prehistory Site in Gongju, Chungcheongnam-do, and the Durubong Cave Site in Cheongju, Chungcheongbuk-do. The early inhabitants of the peninsula survived by hunting animals and collecting edible plants in groups.

  
  

![Image 7: Hand Axe](https://www.korea.net/upload/content/editImage/handaxe_500.jpg)**Hand Axe**  
This multifunctional tool dates back to the Paleolithic period, which was discovered in Jeongok-ri, Yeoncheongun, Gyeonggi-do.

  
  
The history of the Korean nation began in Manchuria and the Korean Peninsula when people started settling there 700,000 years ago. Representative historic sites associated with the Paleolithic Age, when people made tools of animal horns and chipped stone tools, include the Komun Moru ruins in Sangwon, Pyeongannamdo, the Jeongok-ri Site in Yeoncheon, Gyeonggi-do, the Seokjang-ri Prehistory Site in Gongju, Chungcheongnam-do, and the Durubong Cave Site in Cheongju, Chungcheongbuk-do.  
  
In Korea, the Neolithic Age began around 8,000 B.C.E.. People started farming, cultivating cereals such as millet, and used polished stone tools. They started settling down permanently in places and formed clan societies. One of the most representative features of the Neolithic Age is comb-patterned pottery, examples of which have been found all across the Korean Peninsula, including in Amsa-dong, Seoul, in Namgyeong, Pyongyang, and in Suga-ri, Gimhae.  
  

![Image 8: Comb-pattern Pottery](https://www.korea.net/upload/content/editImage/20231215101505375_SQTHJLLJ.jpg)**Comb-pattern Pottery**  
This comb-pattern vessel with a pointy bottom was discovered in Amsa-dong, Seoul, a representative historic site of the Neolithic Age.

  
  
The Bronze Age started around the 10th century B.C.E. on the Korean Peninsula and the 15th century B.C.E. in Manchuria. Historic sites associated with the Bronze Age are found in Liaoning and Jilin provinces, China and across the Korean Peninsula. With the development of the Bronze Age culture, a society emerged in which the head of a clan exercised great influence. The strongest clan leaders started merging many clans into one, and these groups very gradually developed into early states.  
  
The tribes that played a central role in the establishment of Gojoseon, which emerged as the first recognizable state of the Korean people, believed in the King of Heaven and worshipped bears, respectively. The two factions jointly upheld Dangun Wanggeom as their chief priest and political leader. Gojoseon fostered an independent culture in Liaoning, China and along the Daedonggang River. By the 3rd century B.C.E., kings such as King Bu and King Jun had become powerful and bequeathed the throne to their sons. They established a solid system of rule, backed by high-ranking retainers and military officers.  
  
Towards the end of the 3rd century, the Qin dynasty was replaced by the Han dynasty in China, creating a period of social upheaval. Many people moved southward to Gojoseon. Their leader, Wiman, acceded to the throne in 194 B.C.E. and Gojoseon expanded its territory under his rule. By this time, Gojoseon had adopted Iron Age culture, developed agriculture and various handicrafts, and increased its military strength. It tried to monopolize profits, while serving as an intermediate in the trade between the Korean Peninsula and China, taking advantage of its geographical proximity to China. This led to confrontation between Gojoseon and the Han dynasty. Han attacked Gojoseon with a large number of ground and naval forces. Gojoseon defiantly resisted the attack and won a great victory in the early stage of the war, but its capital at Wanggeomseong Fortress fell after a year of war, and Gojoseon collapsed in 108 B.C.E..  
  

![Image 9: Table-type dolmen in Bugeun-ri, Ganghwa](https://www.korea.net/upload/content/editImage/20231215101542173_5BJ2M42T.jpg)Table-type dolmen in Bugeun-ri, Ganghwa

  
  
**Dolmen**  
  
The Seven Wonders of the World include sites such as the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Great Wall of China, and Stonehenge among others. However, Korea’s dolmens are no less mysterious. About half of all the dolmens in the world — or around 40,000 dolmens — have been found on the Korea Peninsula.  
  
Diverse artifacts, including human bones, stone objects, and jade and bronze artifacts, have been unearthed from the dolmens. The construction methods are hard to guess, and the existence itself still remains a mystery.  
  
The dolmens are classified into table-type and go-board dolmens, depending on their shape. The former, mainly found in the northern part of the Korean Peninsula, was made by positioning four stones to make the walls of a box, which were then capped by a stone lying on top of the supports. The latter is characterized by underground burial with stones that supported the capstone. They are often seen in the southern part of the Korean Peninsula.  
  
Dolmens are often referred to as tombs, but it is difficult to conclude that they are. Yi Gyu-bo, a great scholar of Goryeo in the 12th century, left the following remarks about dolmens: “People say that the saints put the dolmens there in the olden days. It is indeed a wonderful technique (that enabled men to position such huge rocks in that way).”  
  
In the early 20th century, American missionary Horace Grant Underwood claimed that dolmens were not tombs but rather that they were put there for sacrificial rituals offered to the gods of the earth. Korean folklorist Son Jin-tae claimed it was an altar pointing to a folktale in which dolmens were believed to be the houses of witches (Mago halmeoni in local legends).  
  
Dolmens are rarely found in China, except for Manchuria, or Japan, yet many thousands of them can be seen across the Korean Peninsula. They were erected over many thousands of years, but this process stopped sometime before the Common Era.  
  
As this became known, scholars around the world are paying attention to the importance of Korean dolmens in terms of the whole cultural history of mankind. Dolmens in Ganghwa (Incheon), Hwasun (Jeollanam-do), and Gochang (Jeollabuk-do) were listed as UNESCO World Heritage sites in 2000. In addition, many experts have been studying the correlation between dolmens in Korea and ones in Europe and India, other than the reasons why dolmens are concentrated on the Korean Peninsula.  
  

![Image 10: Dolmen Park in Suncheon, Jeollanam-do](https://www.korea.net/upload/content/editImage/20231215101628222_OMIUYJK3.jpg)Dolmen Park in Suncheon, Jeollanam-do
